lessons.plain: Think of a company's cloud account as a building. The organization is the whole building, folders are floors or departments, and projects are the rooms where the actual work happens. Organization policies are house rules posted at a level, such as only storing data in certain cities. A rule posted on a floor applies to every room on that floor, including rooms built later. Building the tree and posting the rules at the right level keeps a new team from accidentally doing something the company forbids.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company wants every new project in its production area to store data in only one country, where would you set that rule: on each project one by one, or once on the folder that holds the production projects? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. An organization is the top node of the resource hierarchy, tied to your company's domain. A folder is an optional grouping node that sits under the organization or under another folder. A project is the basic unit where resources live, and where billing and APIs are attached; every resource belongs to exactly one project. An organization policy is a setting, called a constraint, that limits what may be configured, for example which locations resources may be placed in. A policy is attached to a node and flows down to everything beneath it.

Why it works: inheritance. A policy set on a node applies to all descendant folders and projects, including ones created later. You set the rule once where the boundary naturally sits, and the tree carries it downward. Organization policies restrict configuration; they do not grant anyone access. Access is a separate concept, handled by IAM allow policies.

Worked example: organization acme.example, folder Production, and projects fleet-prod and fleet-prod-dr. Step 1: set a location constraint on the Production folder that allows only two European regions. Step 2: create project fleet-prod-dr under Production. Step 3: the new project inherits the constraint with no extra action. Step 4: an attempt to create a virtual machine in a US region inside fleet-prod-dr is refused, because the constraint is evaluated from the folder downward.

Common mistake: applying the policy to one project and assuming it covers future projects, or treating an organization policy as if it granted permissions.

Consequence: a project created outside the Production folder, for example directly under the organization, has no such restriction, so the rule silently fails to protect it. Place each project in the correct folder before it holds data.

questions.prompt: A new organization, brightpath.example, has a folder named Analytics directly under the organization. Step 1: a location constraint is set on the Analytics folder that allows only two Australian regions. Step 2: project sensor-lake is created under Analytics. Step 3: project sensor-archive is created directly under the organization, not under Analytics. Step 4: a storage bucket is created in a US region inside sensor-lake and the request is refused. Step 5 is missing: what happens when a bucket is created in a US region inside sensor-archive?
choices: It is refused, because a constraint on any folder applies to every project in the whole organization.
It is created only if the person creating it holds an IAM role on the Analytics folder.
It is created, because sensor-archive sits outside the Analytics folder, so the constraint never reaches it.
It is refused, because sensor-archive inherits the constraint from the organization node above it.
questions.why: A policy flows down only to descendants of the node where it is set, and sensor-archive is not a descendant of Analytics, so nothing restricts it.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an organization policy constraint in Google Cloud?
choices: It is a list of users who are allowed to create projects inside a folder, and it applies only to the node where it is attached.
It is a billing limit that stops spending once a project passes a set amount, and it applies across the whole organization.
It is a permission bundle that a project owner grants to a team, which then overrides the rules set on folders above.
It is a rule that limits what may be configured on the nodes beneath the point where it is attached, and it grants no one any access.
questions.why: A constraint restricts configuration, flows down to descendant folders and projects, and does not grant access, which is handled separately by IAM allow policies.

questions.prompt: A team in organization northwind-labs sets a location constraint only on project ml-train-a, which sits in the Research folder. Next week they create project ml-train-b in the same folder and place a GPU cluster in a region the constraint would forbid. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The cluster is refused, because any new project created in a folder automatically copies the constraints of its sibling projects.
The cluster is created, but the constraint is applied later when the project's billing account is linked.
The cluster is refused, because the constraint flows up from the project to the folder and then to every project beneath it.
The cluster is created, because the constraint was attached to ml-train-a, a single project, and does not reach its sibling ml-train-b.
questions.why: The constraint sits on one project rather than on the folder, so it flows only downward from that project and cannot protect a sibling project.

questions.prompt: Finance-reports is a project created directly under the organization root, not inside the Finance folder. The Finance folder has a location constraint that allows only European regions. Someone stores sensitive data in a bucket in an Asian region inside finance-reports. Why was the rule not enforced?
choices: The constraint is evaluated only for folders with a billing account attached, and the root has none.
The constraint is evaluated only when a project is first created, so it cannot affect later resource placement.
Organization policies apply only to virtual machines, so storage buckets are never restricted by them.
The constraint is not attached to the organization root or to any ancestor of finance-reports, so it never flows down to that project.
questions.why: Constraints flow only downward from the node where they are set, and finance-reports is not beneath the Finance folder, so no ancestor of it carries the rule.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud how you would decide where an organization policy should be set in a company's resource hierarchy, and name one limit or tradeoff of setting a policy high up in the tree.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the boundary the rule is meant to protect. If a rule covers a whole group of projects that share a purpose, such as all production work, I attach it to the folder that holds them, so every current and future project under that folder inherits it. Setting it on the organization would be broader, which is right only for company-wide rules. The tradeoff of setting it high is that it reaches everything below, including teams that may legitimately need an exception. Some policies allow child nodes to override or add rules, so I check how a specific constraint behaves before relying on it. Also, an organization policy only limits what can be configured; it never grants anyone access, so I still handle who can do what with IAM separately.
rubricPoints: Explains that a policy set on a folder or organization is inherited by all descendant folders and projects, including new ones.
Explains that organization policies restrict configuration and do not grant access, which is handled by IAM.
Names the tradeoff that a high-level policy reaches many teams and may block legitimate exceptions.
Notes that a project placed outside the intended folder escapes the policy, so placement matters.

suggested.rationale: Working out which rules reach which resources as they inherit down a tree is close to the reasoning an authorization policy evaluator would model.

lessons.plain: When you let someone work on a shared cloud project, you decide what they are allowed to do there. In Google Cloud this decision is written as a role granted to a member. A member is a person, a group of people, or an automated account that acts on its own. A role is a named bundle of permissions, where each permission is one specific action such as reading a file or starting a server. Granting a role means attaching that bundle to a member on a particular project, so it applies there and nowhere else. Think of it like handing someone a key card that opens certain doors in one building.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor needs to view the logs of one project but must not change anything. Before reading further, what would you give them: their own account with full control, or something narrower, and why?
lessons.teach:
A member, also called a principal, is whoever is asking to act: a user account, a group, or a service account (an identity used by software rather than a person). A permission is one action on one kind of resource, for example reading objects from a storage bucket. A role is a named set of permissions. Google Cloud IAM, the identity and access management system, stores an allow policy on each resource, such as a project. That policy is a list of bindings, and each binding pairs one role with one or more members. Access is additive: a member can do whatever any binding naming them, or a group they belong to, permits.

Why it works: you rarely grant permissions one at a time. You bind a role to a group once, and staff changes are handled by changing group membership. Bindings on a parent such as a folder or the organization are inherited by every project beneath it, so a grant high up reaches far down. Predefined roles are maintained by Google and cover common jobs. The basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer are very broad and older than the fine-grained roles.

Worked example. A new team, the group staging-deployers, must deploy services to the project shop-staging but must not change billing or other projects. Step 1: identify the member, which is the group staging-deployers. Step 2: choose the narrowest predefined role that covers deploying services. Step 3: add a binding on the project shop-staging that pairs that role with the group. Step 4: check that no folder-level binding already gives the group more. The result is that group members can deploy in that project only.

Common mistake: granting Owner or Editor because it makes errors disappear, or granting a role to one person's account so it is forgotten when they leave. A broad basic role lets its holder change IAM itself and delete resources, which is hard to undo in a running system.

Consequence: removing someone from the group withdraws their access through that group, but a grant at folder level keeps applying to every project below it until it is removed at that level.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Northwind Freight, has a project named parcel-tracking-prod. The group route-analysts needs to read Cloud Logging entries from that project, but must not change anything. Step 1: the member is the group route-analysts. Step 2: the narrowest predefined role covering reading logs is Logs Viewer. Step 3: add a binding on the project parcel-tracking-prod that pairs Logs Viewer with the group route-analysts. Step 4 is not yet done: check whether any binding on a parent folder or the organization gives route-analysts more than Logs Viewer.
choices: Also add each analyst's personal account as a separate member, so the access survives changes to the group.
Grant route-analysts the Owner basic role on parcel-tracking-prod so that no log-reading tool ever fails for them.
Move the Logs Viewer binding onto the service account that exports logs, since that account is easier to audit.
Check the folder and organization bindings above parcel-tracking-prod for any grant that gives route-analysts more than Logs Viewer.
questions.why: Bindings on a parent folder or organization are inherited by every project beneath them, so a broader grant above would silently give the group more access than the intended Logs Viewer role.

questions.prompt: A nightly database export runs as a service account named export-runner in the project ledger-archive. In an IAM binding, which item is the member?
choices: The service account export-runner, because it is the identity asking to act.
The database itself, because the export reads from it.
The project ledger-archive, because bindings are stored on the project.
The role that allows exporting, because the role is the thing being granted.
questions.why: A member is whoever is asking to act, and here the software identity export-runner is the one acting, while the project holds the policy, the role is the granted set of permissions, and the database is the resource.

questions.prompt: A contractor with a personal account needs to read objects in one storage bucket in the project tidewater-web. Which approach best follows the principle of binding roles to groups?
choices: Bind the Owner basic role to a new group so the contractor cannot be blocked by a missing permission.
Create a service account for the contractor and give it the Viewer basic role on the whole organization.
Add the contractor to a group such as tidewater-contractors and bind a narrow read role to that group on the project.
Give the contractor's personal account the Editor basic role on tidewater-web, since it is quick to remove later.
questions.why: Binding a narrow predefined read role to a group lets staff changes be handled through membership, while the other options either give broad basic roles or attach access to one person's account that is easy to forget.

questions.prompt: An engineer was removed from the group dev-operators, but can still delete virtual machines in the project harbor-dev. Which explanation best fits how IAM access works?
choices: A binding naming the engineer's personal account still exists on harbor-dev or a parent folder, and access is additive, so that binding still grants the permission.
The Viewer role automatically includes delete rights, so removing the group had no effect on the engineer's access.
Group membership changes only take effect after the project is restarted, so the engineer keeps access until the next restart.
Removing someone from a group deletes the roles the group held, but the engineer's cached login token keeps the old permissions for the rest of the day.
questions.why: Because access is additive and a direct or inherited binding naming the person still applies, removing them from a group does not remove a grant made to their account or a parent folder.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a new contractor group read-only access to the logs of one project, without giving broader access. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the contractors in one Google group, say contractors-logs, and grant that group a predefined role that only lets it read logs, on the one project they need. I would not grant Viewer on the project, because it reads far more than logs, and I would not add each person's individual account, since removing them later is easy to forget. The tradeoff is that the grant is only as narrow as the predefined role allows. If no predefined role matches exactly, I would consider a custom role, but I would then own its permissions and maintenance. I would also check the folder and organization for inherited bindings, because a broad grant higher up would add to my narrow one. When the contract ends, I remove the people from the group rather than editing the project policy, so access ends in one place.
rubricPoints: Grants the role to a group rather than individual accounts, and says why
Chooses a predefined role narrow enough for the task instead of a basic role
Notes that bindings are additive and can be inherited from folders or the organization
Names a tradeoff, such as custom roles adding maintenance or broad roles risking over-access

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right member, role and level for a new team is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission covers cloud IAM directly.

lessons.plain: Cloud Identity is the service that keeps the list of people and automated accounts allowed to sign in to your company's cloud. Managing users means creating, changing, suspending and removing those accounts. Managing groups means creating named collections of accounts, such as all the platform engineers, so that access can be handed to the collection rather than to each person. You can do this by hand in an admin console, or with a script or sync tool that makes the same changes for you from a source of truth such as an existing company directory. The skill is knowing which approach to use and why groups are usually the thing you grant access to.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company has 40 engineers who all need the same access to a set of cloud projects, would you rather grant that access to each person separately or to one named collection they all belong to? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A user is a single identity, usually one person, with a sign-in name inside a domain your organization has proven it owns. A group is a named collection of users (and sometimes other groups or service accounts) that can be treated as one unit. Cloud Identity is the directory that holds these users and groups. Manual management means an administrator creates or edits each record in the admin console. Automated management means a program makes those changes through an API, or a sync tool copies users and group membership from an existing directory, such as an on-premises Active Directory, on a schedule.

Why it works. Access is granted by attaching a role to a member, and a member can be a user or a group. Granting a role to a group means one change covers everyone currently in it. Adding or removing a person from the group changes their access without touching the project settings. The directory answers who exists and belongs where; the access grants answer what those members may do.

Worked example. A new engineer, Priya, joins the platform team. Step 1: an admin creates a user account for Priya inside the verified domain in Cloud Identity. Step 2: the admin adds her to the group platform-team. Step 3: platform-team already holds a viewer role on the production project, so Priya gains that access without any direct grant. Step 4: when she leaves, removing her from the group or disabling her account ends the access that came through it.

Common mistake. Granting roles to individual users one by one. It works at first, but when someone changes teams the old grants stay behind, and nobody remembers they exist.

Consequence. An automated sync is only as accurate as its source. If the source directory removes someone, the sync removes that account too, and a manual edit to a synced record can be overwritten at the next sync. Teams should edit the source, not the copy.

questions.prompt: Northwind Foods keeps its staff list in an on-premises Active Directory and syncs it into Cloud Identity every night. On Friday, HR deletes contractor Lena Ortiz from the on-premises directory. The chain so far is: step 1, HR deletes Lena's record in the on-premises directory. Step 2 is missing. Which step belongs there, between HR's deletion and Lena's account disappearing from Cloud Identity?
choices: Cloud Identity keeps the account until someone revokes each of Lena's roles on every project
Deleting Lena's project role grants automatically deletes her user account
An admin deletes Lena's account by hand in the Cloud Identity admin console before the sync runs
The nightly sync copies the removal from the source directory, so Lena's record is removed in Cloud Identity
questions.why: The sync reads the source directory and carries the removal across on its scheduled run, whereas deleting role grants does not delete the user account itself.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Identity, which statement correctly separates a user from a group?
choices: A user is one identity; a group is a named collection of users treated as one unit
A group is a sign-in name, and a user is a shared password many people use
A group holds only service accounts, while a user can contain other users
Users and groups are the same record, differing only in who created them
questions.why: A user is a single identity, usually one person with a sign-in name, while a group is a named collection of members that can be handled as one unit.

questions.prompt: A synced account for Marco was edited by hand in Cloud Identity to add him to an extra group. The next scheduled sync runs. What most likely happens?
choices: The hand edit can be overwritten, so the extra group may disappear at that sync
The extra group is copied back into the on-premises directory automatically
The sync stops and waits until an admin removes the hand edit first
Nothing changes, because the sync never reads records it has already copied
questions.why: A manual edit to a synced record can be overwritten at the next sync, so changes belong in the source directory.

questions.prompt: A team of 40 engineers needs viewer access to one production project, and people join and leave the team often. Which setup needs the fewest changes over time?
choices: Create 40 separate projects, one per engineer, and grant each engineer access to their own
Put the 40 users in one group and grant the viewer role to that group
Grant the viewer role to each of the 40 user accounts one at a time
Grant the viewer role to each of the 40 user accounts one at a time, then review each grant every quarter to confirm it still applies
questions.why: A single grant to the group covers everyone currently in it, so joins and leaves become group membership changes rather than new project grants.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests giving each engineer their own individual role on the project so it is clearer who has what. Explain to them, in your own words, how Cloud Identity users and groups should be used for this, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create one user account per person in Cloud Identity, then put people into groups that match their job, such as platform-team or data-readers. The project roles then go to the groups, not to individuals. Joining or leaving a team becomes a group membership change, and nothing in the project has to be edited. The tradeoff is that you now have to keep the groups honest. If someone is added to a group for a temporary task and nobody removes them, they keep the access. So the group list needs regular review, and group names should say what access they carry, so the review is easy to do.
rubricPoints: Users are individual identities; groups are collections of users used as the unit for granting access.
Granting roles to groups means access changes through membership, not through each project grant.
Automation (API or directory sync) keeps membership consistent with a source of truth, and manual edits can be overwritten.
A real limit: group membership must be reviewed, or stale members keep access.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is reasoning about users versus groups and naming the tradeoff, which is best practised by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers Cloud Identity directly.

lessons.plain: A cloud project is a container that holds the services and resources you use. Each large service a cloud provider offers, such as file storage, databases, or a messaging queue, has to be switched on for that project before anything can use it. Think of a new building where each utility, like power or water, must be connected before tenants can move in. Until the service is switched on, requests to it are turned away, even if your account is allowed to use it in principle. Switching a service on is called enabling its API. This is a per-project step, so a service that is on in one project can still be off in another.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new team creates a project and immediately tries to create a virtual machine and a storage bucket, but both requests fail with a message that the service is not enabled, even though the engineer has full rights to create those resources. What do you think is missing, and at what level does it need to be fixed?
lessons.teach:
An API here is the interface a Google Cloud service exposes so that your code, other tools, and the console can ask it to do work. Enabling an API means turning that service on for one specific project. Until it is enabled, the service refuses calls made against that project, whatever permissions the caller holds.

Why it works this way: a project is the boundary for billing, quotas, and access. Google Cloud does not switch every service on in every project by default, so a project only exposes the services someone has deliberately chosen. That keeps the surface small and makes clear what the project is allowed to use. Enabling takes a permission of its own, held by roles such as Service Usage Admin, Editor, or Owner, so a person who can create a bucket may still be unable to enable the storage service.

Worked example. A team sets up a new project called orders-dev. Step 1: an engineer tries to create a Cloud Storage bucket, and the request fails with a service-disabled error. Step 2: they check the project's list of enabled services and find the storage API is off. Step 3: someone with the enable permission turns it on for orders-dev. Step 4: the same create request succeeds, because nothing else changed. Some services also need a billing account linked to the project before they can be enabled; that is a separate step.

Common mistake: granting a resource role and assuming the work is unblocked. A resource role controls who can use a service once it is on. It does not turn the service on, so the failure persists.

Consequence: a service disabled by mistake, or a deployment script that assumes an API is on, causes outages that look like permission errors. Disabling an API can also break every resource that depends on it, so it should be treated as a change with real impact, not a cleanup step.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IT team creates a new project called intake-qa to test a patient-scheduling tool. Step 1: a tester runs a query against a BigQuery dataset in intake-qa and gets a service-disabled error. Step 2: an admin opens the project's list of enabled services and sees the BigQuery API is off. Step 3: ___. Step 4: the same query now succeeds, and nothing else in the project changed.
choices: Enable the BigQuery API on intake-qa using an account that holds the enable permission, such as Service Usage Admin.
Raise the query quota so the service accepts more requests.
Create a new dataset in a different project and point the tool at it.
Grant the tester the Owner role on the dataset so the query is allowed to run.
questions.why: The API must be switched on for this specific project by someone holding the enable permission, because a resource role alone cannot turn a disabled service on.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does enabling an API do for a Google Cloud project?
choices: It copies the service's settings from another project into this one.
It turns the service on for that one project, so calls made against the project can succeed.
It gives every user in the organisation permission to call that service in any project.
It links a billing account to the project and sets its spending limit.
questions.why: Enabling is a per-project switch that makes a service available in that project; it does not grant permissions or handle billing by itself.

questions.prompt: A developer on the lumen-api-test project holds the Cloud Functions Developer role and still gets a service-disabled error when deploying a function. A colleague suggests adding the Storage Admin role to fix it. What is the most accurate diagnosis and fix?
choices: The deploy failed because the function's code is invalid, so the API state is irrelevant.
The colleague is right; the developer needs a broader storage role before the deploy can start.
The developer's role is too narrow, so the fix is to upgrade them to Project Owner.
The API is off for this project, so someone with the enable permission must turn it on; a different resource role will not help.
questions.why: A service-disabled error means the API is not enabled for the project, and only the enable permission can change that, not extra resource roles.

questions.prompt: An admin disables the Compute Engine API in ridge-batch-prod to tidy up unused services, without checking what depends on it. Which outcome best describes the risk?
choices: Nothing happens until someone tries to create a new resource, and then only that request fails.
Disabling an API only blocks the admin's own account, so other users are unaffected.
The API is removed from the organisation entirely and every project loses it.
Existing resources that depend on the API may break, so disabling it should be handled as a change with real impact.
questions.why: Disabling an API can break every resource in that project that depends on it, which is why it must be treated as a consequential change rather than cleanup.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that since they have Owner on the project, they can now deploy anything. Explain to them what enabling APIs within a project means, why it is a separate step from granting roles, and one limit or tradeoff of turning on every API up front.
lessons.modelAnswer: Owner lets you do a lot, but it does not turn services on by itself. Each Google Cloud service exposes an API that must be enabled per project before calls to it succeed. Enabling is a project-level switch, separate from the roles that decide who can use a service once it is on. The enable action needs its own permission, which Owner and Editor include. So if a deployment fails with a service-disabled error, the fix is to enable that API in that project, not to hand out more roles. The tradeoff of enabling everything up front is convenience against a wider surface: more services mean more things to secure, monitor, and possibly pay for, and quotas apply per service. I would enable only what the project's workloads need and record why each one is on.
rubricPoints: Enabling an API is a per-project switch that must happen before a service accepts calls in that project.
Enabling is separate from granting roles; a resource role does not turn a service on.
The enable action requires its own permission, which broad roles such as Owner or Editor include.
Enabling everything up front widens the attack and cost surface, so enable only what is needed.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly precise facts about the console and permissions, and no listed mission or planned engine covers Google Cloud API enablement.

lessons.plain: Observability means being able to see what your systems are doing: how busy they are, whether they are healthy, and what went wrong. On Google Cloud, a set of built-in services collects that information. Provisioning these products means turning them on and pointing them at the things you want to watch, so measurements and logs start arriving somewhere you can look at them. Think of it like installing gauges, a logbook, and a smoke alarm in a new building before anyone moves in. Done early, you find problems before customers do. Skipped, you have no evidence when something breaks.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 40 virtual machines spread across three projects. Would you set up monitoring separately inside each project, or once in one central place that can see all three? Say what you would gain and what you would risk with each choice.
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A metric is a numbered measurement recorded over time, such as CPU use or request count. A log entry is a timestamped record that a service or program writes, either as text or as structured fields. Cloud Monitoring is the Google Cloud product that stores metrics, draws dashboards, runs uptime checks and fires alerts. Cloud Logging stores log entries in log buckets, which are containers with their own retention period. A metrics scope is the grouping that lets one Monitoring view read data from several projects: one project hosts it, and the others are added to it. An alerting policy is a rule that watches a metric or log condition and notifies a channel when the condition holds for a set duration.

Why it works. Many signals are produced automatically by managed services, but some come only from software you install. On virtual machines, the Ops Agent is a program that collects host metrics and application logs and sends them onward. Without it, the platform sees only what it can observe from outside the operating system.

Worked example. A team owns a web service in project web-prod running on one virtual machine. Step 1: choose the project that will host the metrics scope. Step 2: add web-prod to that metrics scope. Step 3: install the Ops Agent on the VM. Step 4: create an uptime check that requests the service health URL every minute. Step 5: create an alerting policy that opens an incident if the check fails for five minutes, and send it to the on-call notification channel.

Common mistake. Teams often build dashboards and alerts before confirming that data arrives, then find empty charts during an outage. Check that each metric or log appears before you rely on it.

Consequence. If logs are routed to a short-retention bucket, an investigation a month later finds nothing. Set bucket retention to match your audit needs before an incident, not after.

questions.prompt: A retail team runs a nightly batch job on one virtual machine named batch-vm in project shop-eu-batch. They want Monitoring to watch that VM from a separate project, shop-monitor. Their plan so far reads: Step 1, choose shop-monitor to host the metrics scope. Step 2, add shop-eu-batch to that scope. Step 3 is missing from the plan and is left blank here. Step 4, create an alerting policy that fires when error log entries exceed 10 within 10 minutes and notifies the email channel. Which item belongs in the blank Step 3, and why is it needed?
choices: Enable an uptime check that requests the batch job's URL every minute
Install the Ops Agent on batch-vm so its host metrics and application logs are sent onward
Create a new log bucket with 400-day retention so the alert has somewhere to write
Create a second metrics scope that is hosted by shop-eu-batch
questions.why: Without the Ops Agent on the VM, the platform sees only what it can observe from outside the operating system, so the application error logs that Step 4 depends on never arrive.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has three projects, fleet-a, fleet-b and fleet-c. An engineer wants one Monitoring view that reads CPU metrics from all three. Which setup does this correctly?
choices: Create three separate dashboards and export each one to a spreadsheet each morning
Create one metrics scope hosted by one chosen project, then add the other two projects to it
Create a log bucket in each project and point the dashboard at the bucket names
Move all VMs from fleet-b and fleet-c into fleet-a so one project holds everything
questions.why: A metrics scope is the grouping where one project hosts the view and the others are added to it, which lets one Monitoring view read data from several projects.

questions.prompt: A team created an alerting policy that notifies their on-call channel when a VM's CPU metric stays high for five minutes. During an outage, no notification arrived, and the metric's chart for that VM shows no data at all since the VM was created. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The alerting policy was stored in a different region from the VM, which blocks notifications
The metric never reached Monitoring, so the condition could never hold and the alert could not fire
The uptime check ran too often, which disabled the alerting policy automatically
The alert only fires when the VM is restarted, so a running VM never triggers it
questions.why: An alerting policy can only fire when the watched metric or log condition actually holds, and a metric with no data cannot meet that condition, so the team should confirm data arrives before relying on the alert.

questions.prompt: A company routes its application logs into a log bucket with a short retention period. A security review a month later finds no entries for the period it needs. What should the team do to prevent this next time?
choices: Delete the metrics scope so that old data is not lost in the shared view
Keep the logs only as dashboard charts in Monitoring, since charts never expire
Set the bucket's retention period to match the audit needs before any incident happens
Lengthen the alerting policy's duration so it holds the logs open longer
questions.why: A log bucket keeps entries only for its own retention period, so the retention must be chosen to match audit needs in advance, since entries past that period cannot be recovered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging for a new project with several virtual machines. Name one limit or tradeoff of the setup you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first pick one project to host the metrics scope, then add the other projects to it so one Monitoring view shows all the machines. On each VM I would install the Ops Agent, because the platform alone does not see inside the operating system, so memory, disk and application logs would be missing otherwise. For logs I would check which log bucket receives them and set its retention to match our audit needs. Then I would create an uptime check and one alerting policy for the service, and confirm the data shows up before trusting it. The tradeoff is that a central host project becomes a single place to manage access and visibility, and the scope has to be set up deliberately. Also, the agent adds a little work to every new machine, so it must be part of the build, not an afterthought.
rubricPoints: A metrics scope lets one Monitoring view read several projects, with one host project.
The Ops Agent is needed on VMs for in-guest metrics and logs.
Log buckets have retention periods that must match audit needs, set before incidents.
Verify data arrives before relying on dashboards or alerts.
Name a real tradeoff, such as central access control or agent maintenance.

suggested.rationale: Choosing alert thresholds and durations is a core part of setting up observability, and the planned metric alarm builder would let the learner practise that reasoning.

lessons.plain: A quota is a cap that a cloud provider places on how much of something your account can use. Think of it like a daily allowance on a shared service: it keeps one customer from taking more than their share and gives you a limit you can plan around. Quotas apply to things like how many machines you can run in one region, how many addresses you can hold, or how many requests you can send per minute. When you hit a quota, the platform refuses the new request even if you have money in the account and the right permissions. Most quotas can be raised by asking, and the request is reviewed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's deployment fails with an error saying it cannot create more instances, even though billing is active and the account has the right role. What do you think is limiting it, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A quota is a limit on how much of a resource your project may use. Quotas are counted per project, and often per region. There are two broad kinds. A rate quota limits how many requests you can make within a time window, such as API calls per minute. An allocation quota limits how many things you can hold at the same time, such as the number of virtual CPUs in one region. Each quota tracks a specific metric, which is the thing being counted. Some quotas can be raised by submitting a quota increase request, which is reviewed and may be approved in full, in part, or not at all. Others are fixed.

Why it works: before creating a resource, the platform checks whether the request would push current usage above the limit. If it would, the request fails with a quota error. Permission and quota are separate gates, so a correct IAM role does not get around a quota.

Worked example: a team wants 40 virtual machines with 4 vCPUs each in one region, which is 160 vCPUs. The regional CPU quota is 120. Step 1: note current usage, which is 0. Step 2: add the request, 160. Step 3: compare 160 with the limit, 120. Step 4: the creation fails with a quota error naming the region and metric. The fix is to request an increase to at least 160 with some headroom, or to split the work across regions if the design allows it.

Common mistake: treating a quota error as a billing or permission problem and granting more roles. That wastes time and changes nothing.

Consequence: during a traffic surge, autoscaling can stall because new instances cannot be created. The service stays at its current size while everything else looks healthy, so the shortfall is easy to miss until users notice slow responses.

questions.prompt: Harbor Robotics runs a nightly batch job in one region. Its project already uses 30 vCPUs in that region, and the regional CPU quota is 150. The team plans to create 25 new instances with 8 vCPUs each. Step 1: note current usage, which is 30. Step 2: this step is missing. Step 3: compare the resulting total with the limit of 150. Step 4: if the total is above 150, the creation fails with a quota error. Which choice correctly fills in step 2?
choices: Check whether the project owner role is granted, because a quota error means a missing permission.
Ignore the 30 vCPUs already in use, since only the new request is checked against the limit.
Add the 200 vCPUs requested (25 times 8) to the 30 already in use, giving 230.
Divide 200 by 8 to count instances, then compare that instance count with 150.
questions.why: The platform checks current usage plus the new request against the limit, so the 200 requested vCPUs must be added to the existing 30 to get the total of 230 that gets compared with 150.

questions.prompt: Which pair of statements correctly describes the two broad kinds of quota?
choices: A rate quota limits how many things you hold at once, and an allocation quota limits requests per time window.
A rate quota limits requests within a time window, and an allocation quota limits how many things you can hold at the same time.
A rate quota can never be raised, and an allocation quota can always be raised by an administrator.
Both kinds limit requests per minute, and the only difference is which region they apply to.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a rate quota as a limit on requests within a time window and an allocation quota as a limit on how many things you can hold at the same time.

questions.prompt: A team's project shows a quota error for a resource whose limit cannot be changed by a request. What is the most sensible response?
choices: Grant the team additional IAM roles so the quota check is bypassed.
Redesign the workload to fit within the fixed limit, or spread it across regions or projects if the design allows.
Ask billing support to remove the quota because the account is paid.
Submit a quota increase request and wait for it to be approved in full.
questions.why: Some quotas are fixed and cannot be raised, so the practical options are to stay within the limit or distribute the work, since quotas are counted per project and often per region.

questions.prompt: A service account has the Editor role on a project, but creating new instances fails with a quota error. What explains this?
choices: Permission and quota are separate gates, so a correct role does not get around a quota limit.
Billing has not been enabled yet, and the quota error is a symptom of that.
The Editor role is too weak, so the team needs the Owner role to get past quota checks.
The Editor role was assigned at the wrong level, and quota checks only apply at the organisation level.
questions.why: Quota is checked independently of IAM permissions, so holding a sufficient role does not remove the limit; the fix is to raise the quota or reduce the requested usage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a failed resource creation is caused by a quota, what you would request, and one limit or tradeoff of asking for a quota increase.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first read the error. A quota error names the region and the metric, such as CPUs or addresses. Next I would compare current usage with the limit for that metric in that region, using the quotas page for the project, and add the new request to see whether it goes over. If it does, I would request an increase to a value that covers the request with some headroom, and say why I need it. The main limit is that the increase is a request, not a guarantee: it is reviewed, may be approved only in part, and some quotas cannot be raised at all. Approval can also take time, so for a launch I would start early or plan a fallback, such as another region or a smaller first step. I would avoid granting extra IAM roles, because permissions do not affect quota.
rubricPoints: A quota is a per-project, often per-region limit on a metric, separate from permissions and billing
Check current usage against the limit before creating resources
Increase requests are reviewed, may be partial, and some quotas are fixed
Plan lead time or a fallback, since approval is not instant

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers quotas, so reading the quota facts and reasoning through a failing deployment scenario is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Before you can build anything in Google Cloud, you need a company-level container that everything else sits inside. Setting up a standalone organization means creating that top container for a business that is not part of some larger parent company. It is tied to a web domain the business already owns, such as its email domain, and the first administrator who signs in becomes the most powerful person in it. Getting this step right first matters because later choices, like who can do what and which rules apply everywhere, all hang off this one node.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new company wants one place where a single security rule automatically applies to every project it ever creates. What would it need to set up first, and why would creating projects before that exist cause trouble?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. An organization is the root node of Google Cloud's resource hierarchy: every folder and project in a company sits beneath it. A standalone organization is one you create for your own business, rather than one that a larger parent already controls. Its identity comes from a Cloud Identity or Google Workspace account, which is a directory of users and groups tied to a domain name you can prove you own. Proof is usually a DNS record you add at your domain registrar, showing you control the name. The first user who signs up and verifies the domain becomes the super admin, the highest administrative role, able to grant every other role.

Why it works. Permissions and organization policies are inherited downward. A rule set at the organization node applies to every folder and project beneath it, unless a lower level is allowed to override it. So the organization is the one place where company-wide guardrails and access are set once. Without it, projects exist with no shared root, so no company-wide rule can reach them.

Worked example. A new company owns example-corp.com. Step 1: create a Cloud Identity account for that domain. Step 2: prove domain ownership by adding the verification record. Step 3: the organization resource appears, and the first admin is its super admin. Step 4: that admin creates a second, named break-glass administrator, a backup account kept for emergencies, and assigns day-to-day roles to groups rather than to individuals. Step 5: only then are folders and projects created under the organization.

Common mistake. Signing up with a personal consumer email, or creating projects before the organization exists, leaves resources detached from the company root, so organization policies cannot reach them until they are moved.

Consequence. If the super admin account is lost or the domain registration lapses, the company can lose control of its whole cloud estate, so that account must be protected and recovery options kept in place.

questions.prompt: Ridgeline Freight owns ridgeline-freight.net and wants a standalone organization. Before the organization existed, an engineer created a project called rf-tracking while signed in with a personal consumer email. The steps so far: Step 1, create a Cloud Identity account for ridgeline-freight.net. Step 2, prove domain ownership by adding the DNS verification record at the registrar. Step 3, the organization resource appears and the first verified admin becomes its super admin. Step 4, [missing step]. Step 5, the admin sets a company-wide organization policy at the organization node, and that policy now applies to rf-tracking.
choices: Re-create the project's billing account under the company domain so the project can be billed.
Move the rf-tracking project into the organization so it sits beneath the organization root node.
Rename the domain to match the project name so the project is recognized as belonging to the company.
Set the same organization policy directly on rf-tracking, because policies only flow down from individual projects.
questions.why: A project created before the organization exists is detached from the root, so organization policies cannot reach it until it is moved beneath the organization node.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud's resource hierarchy, which node is the root that every folder and project in a company sits beneath?
choices: The organization
The project with the lowest ID number
The billing account
A single folder named Production
questions.why: The organization is the root node of the hierarchy, and every folder and project in a company sits beneath it.

questions.prompt: A company's super admin account is lost, and the domain registration for the company's identity domain then lapses. What is the most serious consequence described for this situation?
choices: Existing virtual machines stop running immediately and cannot be restarted.
Folders can no longer be created, but existing projects keep working normally.
Billing charges stop being applied to the company's projects.
The company can lose control of its whole cloud estate, which is why the account and its recovery options must be protected.
questions.why: The teaching text states that losing the super admin account or letting the domain registration lapse can cost the company control of its entire cloud estate.

questions.prompt: A company sets a rule at the organization node of its standalone organization. Which resources does that rule reach by default?
choices: Every folder and project beneath the organization, unless a lower level is allowed to override it.
Only projects whose names match the company's domain name.
Only the organization node itself, and nothing beneath it.
Only the first project that the super admin created.
questions.why: Permissions and organization policies are inherited downward from the organization node to every folder and project beneath it, unless a lower level is allowed to override them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests creating projects first on a personal email account and setting up the company domain later. Explain to them why the standalone organization should come first, and name one limit or tradeoff of their approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Set up the standalone organization first because it is the root that everything else depends on. The organization is tied to a domain the company proves it owns, through a Cloud Identity account, and the first super admin is created at that point. Folders, projects, and organization policies all sit beneath that root, and policies set at the top flow down to every project. If we create projects on a personal account, those projects have no company root, so company-wide rules cannot reach them and we would have to migrate them later, which is extra work and risk. The tradeoff of doing the organization first is that it takes some up-front effort, like verifying the domain and protecting the super admin account, before anything can be deployed. That cost is worth paying because it is set up once and governs everything afterward.
rubricPoints: Organization is the root node that folders and projects sit beneath
Standalone organization is tied to a verified domain via a Cloud Identity or Workspace account
The first super admin is created at setup and must be protected, with a backup
Projects created outside the organization are not reached by org-level policies until moved

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why the organization root must come first and what depends on it, which a learner can practise by articulating it to a teammate.

lessons.plain: When you set up a new cloud account, one early job is deciding how your computers will talk to each other and to the outside world. Cloud networking is that plan. You create a private network the cloud provider runs for you, divide it into address ranges, and write rules that say which traffic is allowed in and out. Get this wrong and either your services cannot reach each other, or things that should stay private are exposed to the internet. The steps are simple to repeat once you know the parts and why each one exists.
lessons.guessPrompt: You create two virtual machines in a brand-new cloud project and add no extra rules. Should a computer on the public internet be able to open an SSH connection to one of them? Give your reasoning before reading on.
lessons.teach:
A VPC network (virtual private cloud) is a private network that exists inside your cloud project. Machines on it can reach each other over private addresses, and outside traffic reaches them only if you allow it. In Google Cloud a VPC network is global, meaning it spans every region, but the subnets inside it are regional. A subnet is a block of private IP addresses tied to one region, such as 10.10.0.0/24, which gives 256 addresses, a few of them reserved by the platform. Each virtual machine takes one address from the subnet in its region.

Traffic is governed by firewall rules that belong to the VPC network, not to individual machines. A rule matches a direction (ingress for traffic coming in, egress for traffic going out), a source or destination, a protocol and port, and an action (allow or deny). Each rule has a priority number, and a lower number wins. Rules are stateful: if an inbound connection is allowed, the reply travels back without a separate rule. A new network denies all inbound traffic by default and allows outbound traffic.

Worked example: a web server should accept port 443 from anywhere, and a database on port 5432 should accept connections only from the web tier. Step 1: create a custom-mode VPC with one subnet in one region. Step 2: create an ingress allow rule, source 0.0.0.0/0, port 443, applied to machines tagged web. Step 3: create an ingress allow rule whose source is the web tag, port 5432, applied to machines tagged db. Step 4: the default deny blocks everything else.

A common mistake is keeping the old default network, which comes with broad pre-made firewall rules and a subnet in every region, instead of planning your own address ranges. On a running system, the consequence shows up later: if you need to connect two networks whose address ranges overlap, they cannot be joined without rebuilding one of them. Creating networks and firewall rules also needs a network admin role in the project, which is separate from the role that lets you create virtual machines.

questions.prompt: Lumen Labs is setting up SSH access through a bastion host. Its custom-mode VPC lumen-core has one subnet, 172.20.0.0/22, in europe-west1. Step 1 is done: the VPC and subnet exist. Step 2: create an ingress allow rule with source 203.0.113.0/24, TCP port 22, applied to machines tagged bastion. Step 3 is missing from the list. Step 4: confirm the network's default deny still blocks all other inbound traffic. Which missing step 3 makes api machines (tagged api) accept SSH only from the bastion?
choices: Lower the priority number of the default deny so it wins over the bastion rule.
Create an ingress allow rule with source 0.0.0.0/0, TCP port 22, applied to machines tagged api.
Create an ingress allow rule with source tag bastion, TCP port 22, applied to machines tagged api.
Add a second subnet 172.20.4.0/22 in europe-west2 so the api machines get a closer address range.
questions.why: An ingress rule that names the bastion tag as its source and the api tag as its target limits SSH to bastion machines, because firewall rules match by tag as well as by address.

questions.prompt: A team created its VPC in us-east1 and now wants a VM in europe-west1 on the same network. Which step makes that possible?
choices: Move the VPC to europe-west1, since a VPC is tied to a single region.
Add a subnet in europe-west1 to the existing VPC, since VPCs are global and subnets are regional.
Create a second VPC in europe-west1 and then reconnect the machines to it through the console so each region has its own network.
Enable a VPC peering link between the two regions, because regions cannot share a VPC.
questions.why: A VPC network spans all regions while each subnet belongs to one region, so adding a subnet in the new region lets machines there join the same network.

questions.prompt: Network A uses 10.4.0.0/16 and network B uses 10.4.8.0/21. Both hold production workloads and must talk privately. What is the constraint?
choices: Joining works only when both networks use the same subnet mask length, which these two do not.
Their ranges overlap, so one must be rebuilt with a non-overlapping range before they can be joined.
Firewall rules on each side can allow the overlapping addresses through, so no rebuild is needed.
The platform renumbers machines automatically when two networks are connected.
questions.why: The 10.4.8.0/21 block sits inside 10.4.0.0/16, so the ranges overlap, and overlapping networks cannot be joined without rebuilding one of them.

questions.prompt: A VPC has two ingress rules for TCP 3306. Rule X: allow, source 10.8.0.0/24, priority 50. Rule Y: deny, source 0.0.0.0/0, priority 60. A machine at 10.8.0.5 connects to port 3306. What happens?
choices: Denied, because the default deny overrides any explicit allow rule in the network.
Allowed, because rules are stateful so the reply path is always permitted.
Allowed, because rule X has the lower priority number and wins over rule Y.
Denied, because the deny rule matches a wider source range and so takes precedence.
questions.why: Both rules match this source, and the lower priority number wins, so rule X's allow decision applies.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the new web server is running but nobody can reach it. Explain to them how VPC networks, subnets and firewall rules fit together to decide whether traffic gets through, and name one tradeoff between putting everything in one subnet and splitting it into several.
lessons.modelAnswer: The machine is running, so the block is at the network layer. The VPC network is the private network, and its subnet gives the machine an address in one region. Firewall rules attach to the network and decide which traffic gets through. A new network denies inbound traffic by default, so we need an allow rule for the web port, scoped to a tag or a source range. Rules are stateful, so replies to allowed connections go back without extra rules. The tradeoff: one big subnet is simpler to manage, but it is one address pool and one place where broad rules apply. Several subnets separate tiers and regions more cleanly, but each needs its own planned range, and ranges that overlap with another network you later connect cannot be joined without rework.
rubricPoints: A VPC network is a private, global network; subnets are regional blocks of addresses inside it.
Firewall rules live on the network, are evaluated by direction, priority and port, and deny inbound traffic by default.
Rules are stateful, so replies to allowed connections need no separate rule.
Splitting into several subnets trades simpler management for careful address planning, since overlapping ranges block future connections.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which firewall rule admits or blocks a packet across a virtual network is the hands-on skill this objective needs, and the planned tracer would build it.

lessons.plain: Google Cloud runs its services in many physical places. A region is a broad geographic area, and a zone is a separate location inside a region. Not every service, machine type, or hardware option is offered in every region or zone. Before you choose where to build something, you check that the product you need is actually sold there, in the zone you plan to use. A quick check now saves a failed deployment later, and it stops you from planning redundancy that a location cannot provide. It is like checking that a restaurant has the dish you want before you drive across town.
lessons.guessPrompt: You plan to create a service in a region your team has used before, and the create button fails with a message saying the option is not available in that location. What do you think might be different about that location or that option?
lessons.teach: A region is a named geographic area, such as a cluster of data centers in one part of the world. A zone is an isolated deployment area inside a region, built so that a failure in one zone should not take down the others. Google Cloud products are not all offered everywhere. Each product has a scope: a zonal resource lives in one zone, a regional resource is spread across zones in one region, and some products are multi-regional or global. Availability also varies by location and by feature. A product may exist in a region while a specific machine type, accelerator, or version is offered only in some zones. Why this matters: a deployment names a location, and if the product or feature is not offered there, the create call fails, or the design quietly loses the redundancy you planned. Worked example: you need a regional group of virtual machines that uses a specific GPU type in region R. Step 1: list the zones in R. Step 2: check which of those zones offer that GPU type. Step 3: find that only zones a and c offer it. Step 4: choose a and c for the group rather than assuming all three zones work. Step 5: confirm that the organization's location policy allows region R before you create anything. Common mistake: assuming that because a product works in one zone of a region, every zone in that region has it. Consequence: if the group's only spare zone lacks the GPU type, a zone outage can leave the service unable to replace failed machines. Verify availability before you design, not after the first deployment fails.

questions.prompt: Priya is setting up a regional group of batch virtual machines in region us-west9, which has zones a, b, c and d. Step 1 is done: she listed all four zones. Step 2 is done: she checked that machine family M3 is offered in zones a, b and d, but not in zone c. Step 3 is missing: she has not yet confirmed that her organization's location policy allows region us-west9. Which action completes the plan correctly?
choices: Move the group to a global resource so that zone availability for M3 no longer matters to the design.
Create the group in all four zones, because zone c will simply fail to start machines and the group will retry them elsewhere.
Create the group in zones a, b and d only, after confirming that the organization's location policy allows us-west9 before any create call is made.
Create the group in zones a and b only, because a region with three working zones is always enough for redundancy.
questions.why: The teaching text says to confirm that the organization's location policy allows the region before creating anything, and to choose only the zones that actually offer the required feature.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a zonal resource?
choices: A resource that lives in exactly one zone.
A resource that exists only on the organization level and is not tied to any location.
A resource that is available in every region of the world at once.
A resource spread automatically across every zone in one region.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a zonal resource as one that lives in one zone, in contrast to regional and multi-regional or global resources.

questions.prompt: A team confirms that a managed database product works in zone a of region R. They conclude it will also work in zone b of region R, so they can skip checking zone b. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because zones in the same region always offer identical products and features.
The flaw is that zones cannot host managed databases at all, only virtual machines.
The team must instead check every region in the world before trusting any single zone.
Availability varies by location and by feature, so product support in one zone does not guarantee support in another zone of the same region.
questions.why: The teaching text warns against assuming that a product working in one zone means every zone in that region offers it, because specific features and versions may be limited to some zones.

questions.prompt: Before designing a new deployment that needs a specific accelerator in a particular region, what check should come first according to the availability guidance?
choices: Rename the deployment so that the location is chosen automatically by the platform.
Create one test resource and wait to see whether the deployment fails.
Assume the accelerator is offered everywhere the product is offered and proceed.
Confirm that the organization's location policy allows the region, and verify the specific feature is offered in the zones you plan to use.
questions.why: The teaching text says to verify availability before design, including checking the organization's location policy for the region and confirming feature support in the chosen zones, rather than discovering a failure after deployment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would confirm that a product you need is available in a chosen region and zone before you design a deployment there. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a location's availability.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by listing the zones in the target region, then check the product catalogue or the command-line listing for that region to see whether the service and the specific feature I need, such as a machine type or accelerator, are offered. Availability is per zone, so I check each zone I plan to use rather than trusting one zone to represent the whole region. I also confirm that the organization's location policy allows that region, because a product can exist there and still be blocked. The main tradeoff is that offerings change over time and a region can run short of a specific resource, so a check done at design time is not a guarantee at deploy time. For a redundant design, I keep a fallback zone or region in mind and verify it too.
rubricPoints: Availability is checked per region and per zone, not assumed for the whole region.
Products differ by scope (zonal, regional, multi-regional or global) and by specific features.
Verify with the catalogue or command listing before designing, and confirm the organization's location policy allows the location.
Offerings can change or run short, so a design-time check does not guarantee deploy-time success.

suggested.rationale: Location availability is catalogue-style reference knowledge checked through console and command listings, which a reading and checklist serve better than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Cloud Asset Inventory is a record-keeping service that lists the cloud resources you own, such as virtual machines, storage buckets and networks, along with the access rules attached to them. It can cover a whole organization, a folder, or a single project. Think of it as a catalogue that updates as things change, so you can ask what exists, where it sits in your folder tree, and what changed recently. Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI helper built into the Google Cloud console. You ask it questions in plain language about a resource or a problem, and it reads the configuration and logs you are allowed to see and suggests explanations and next steps. It is a helper, not an authority, so you still check its answers against the inventory and your own records.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your new company has forty projects under one organization, and nobody can say which of them have publicly readable storage buckets. Before any teaching, what kind of tool would you reach for to answer that across every project at once, and why would checking project by project by hand be risky?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Asset Inventory is a Google Cloud service that collects metadata about resources and their IAM policies. IAM means identity and access management, the system that decides who can do what. A resource is anything you create, such as a bucket, a virtual machine or a network. The inventory works at a chosen scope: an organization, a folder, or a project. Scope matters because the inventory only covers resources below the scope you pick. Inventory data can be queried directly, exported to BigQuery (a data warehouse for analysis) or Cloud Storage (object storage), and sent as change feeds through Pub/Sub (a messaging service) so other tools can react when something changes. Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI assistant in the console that explains and troubleshoots using the same configuration and logs your permissions allow.

Why it works: the service gathers resource data from many services into one place, so you query a single record instead of visiting every console. Worked example: scope the search to the organization, enable the Cloud Asset API in the project that hosts the query or export, grant yourself a viewer role at organization scope, search for storage bucket asset types, then read each result's project field to see which team must fix it.

Common mistake: assuming you see everything. You only see resources your roles allow, so a gap in results may mean missing permissions rather than a clean estate.

Consequence: if a change feed's Pub/Sub topic is deleted, downstream security checks stop receiving updates and fail silently, so the system looks healthy while going blind.

Cloud Asset Inventory tells you what exists and how it is set up; Gemini Cloud Assist helps you interpret that evidence, but it never replaces verifying the source data before you change anything.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Co. has a folder called EU-Retail with four projects under it. Its analyst, Dana, wants a monthly BigQuery table of every network resource in those projects. The steps so far: Step 1, set the inventory scope to the EU-Retail folder. Step 2, enable the Cloud Asset API in the project lumen-audit, which hosts the export. Step 3, ____ (this step is missing). Step 4, create the export to the BigQuery dataset eu_assets inside lumen-audit. Which missing Step 3 completes the setup so the export shows what Dana needs?
choices: Grant Dana the viewer role at the EU-Retail folder scope, because the results she can see depend on the roles she holds
Set the BigQuery dataset location to match the region of each of the four projects
Create a Pub/Sub topic in lumen-audit so the export becomes a continuous feed instead of a one-time pull
Narrow the scope to a single project so the export finishes faster
questions.why: The inventory only returns what the person running it is allowed to see, so Dana needs a viewer role covering the folder's resources, which the other choices do not provide.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Asset Inventory, what does the chosen scope (organization, folder, or project) decide?
choices: Only the resources below the selected organization, folder, or project are covered by the inventory
Which people are permitted to sign in to the Google Cloud console
How often the inventory refreshes its stored records
Which file format the exported records are written in
questions.why: The scope sets the boundary of what the inventory covers, and anything outside that boundary will not appear in results.

questions.prompt: Quill Logistics has nine storage buckets across three projects under the Ops folder. An analyst whose viewer role covers only the project qv-dev runs a bucket search at the organization scope and sees just two buckets. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The other seven buckets were deleted last week
The analyst's roles only allow seeing some resources, so the gap may reflect missing permissions rather than an empty estate, and the analyst should check their roles before concluding anything
Gemini Cloud Assist ranks results and dropped the lower-ranked buckets from the list
The Cloud Asset API was switched off for the whole organization
questions.why: Inventory results are limited to what the viewer's roles allow, so a short result list can reflect missing permissions instead of a clean estate.

questions.prompt: A team's Pub/Sub topic, which carries change feed messages from Cloud Asset Inventory to a security check tool, is accidentally deleted. What is the consequence?
choices: Only Cloud Storage exports stop, because Pub/Sub feeds run on a separate system that the deletion does not touch
The security check stops receiving updates and can fail silently, so the environment looks healthy while the checks are blind to changes
The inventory deletes all records it had previously collected for the scope
Gemini Cloud Assist notices the gap and automatically recreates the topic with the same name and settings
questions.why: Downstream tools depend on the change feed's Pub/Sub topic, so deleting it stops their updates without any obvious error in the console.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can just ask Gemini Cloud Assist which buckets are public and fix them based on its answer. Explain to them what Cloud Asset Inventory gives you that the assistant alone does not, and name one limit of each tool they should keep in mind before acting.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud Asset Inventory is the record of what exists: it collects resources and their IAM policies across an organization, folder, or project, and lets you search that data or export it for analysis. That gives us a repeatable, scoped picture we can check, not a one-off answer. Gemini Cloud Assist is useful for explaining what a resource's configuration means and suggesting next steps, but its answer is only as complete as what our permissions let it see and it can be wrong. The limit of the inventory is that it only covers the scope we chose and only shows resources our roles allow us to view. The limit of the assistant is that it advises rather than proves. So before we change any bucket, we confirm the finding in the inventory, check the owning project, and make the fix through our normal review.
rubricPoints: Cloud Asset Inventory records resources and IAM policies at a chosen scope and can be searched or exported.
Gemini Cloud Assist explains and suggests, drawing on what the user's permissions allow it to see.
The inventory only covers resources within its scope and visible to the user's roles.
AI suggestions must be verified against source data before any change is made.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console facts, scope rules and service setup that a listed mission does not practice, so reading the material is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Most companies already keep staff accounts in one central system, such as a corporate login service. Workforce Identity Federation lets people sign in to Google Cloud using that existing login, so you do not have to create a separate Google account for each person. Think of it as a trusted doorman. Google accepts the identity proof the company's login system issues, checks a few rules about who may come in, and then grants access based on the permissions already set on cloud resources. You set the trust up once for the organization, and people do not have to manage a second password for the cloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's staff already sign in to their corporate identity system every morning. Without creating a Google account for each person, what would you need to decide before those staff could use the cloud console, and which side should be trusted to vouch for them?
lessons.teach:
An identity provider, or IdP, is the outside system that holds staff accounts and proves who someone is. Workforce Identity Federation sets up a trust relationship between that IdP and Google Cloud, and the trust is built from two pieces. A workforce identity pool is a container for external identities, attached at the organization level. Inside a pool sits a provider, which records the details of one specific IdP: the protocol it speaks (OIDC or SAML 2.0), its issuer address, and the signing information Google needs to confirm that a sign-in statement is genuine.

Why it works: when someone signs in, the IdP issues a signed statement, called an assertion, that lists claims such as an email address or group membership. Google checks the signature, then applies attribute mapping, a set of rules that copies claims into attributes Google can use, such as setting the subject to the email. An attribute condition is a filter written over those attributes. If it evaluates to false, sign-in is refused even when the password was correct. Access comes from IAM bindings, where you grant roles to a principal or principalSet that stands for the federated identity, just as you would for a Google account. The pool itself grants nothing.

Worked example: the IdP asserts the email alice at example dot com and a group called platform-ops. The mapping sets the subject to that email and records the group. The condition allows only identities in platform-ops. Alice signs in, passes the condition, and is represented as a member of the group principalSet. A role granted to that group on a project applies to Alice, and she has no other grant.

Common mistake: configuring the pool and provider, then forgetting the IAM grant. The person signs in successfully and then sees nothing, or the team grants a broad role at organization level just to make things work.

Consequence in a running system: if the attribute mapping is wrong, several people can map to the same subject, and audit logs stop showing who actually made each change.

questions.prompt: Lumen Bay Foods has a workforce identity pool at the organization level with an OIDC provider for its IdP. A staff member, Bianca, signs in. Trace what happens, then identify the missing step. Step 1: the IdP issues a signed assertion listing the email bianca at lumenbay dot test and the group dock-auditors. Step 2: Google verifies the signature. Step 3: attribute mapping sets the subject to the email and records the group, and the attribute condition allows only identities in dock-auditors, so Bianca passes. Step 4: [missing].
