Bianca is represented as a member of the principalSet for dock-auditors, and the project's storage bucket is still not visible to her. What step 4 is missing?
choices: Grant a role to the principalSet for dock-auditors on the project or resource that she needs to use
Add a new OIDC provider with the same issuer address so the signature check is repeated
Change the attribute mapping so the subject is set to the group name instead of the email
Create a second workforce identity pool at folder level so the group can be seen there
questions.why: Membership in a principalSet grants nothing by itself; an IAM role binding on the target resource is the step that gives access, as with any other principal.

questions.prompt: In a workforce identity setup, what is a workforce identity pool?
choices: The signing key that Google uses to check the sign-in statement from the IdP
A container for external identities attached at the organization level, which holds one or more providers
A set of IAM roles bundled together and granted to a project's service accounts
A filter written over attributes that decides whether a sign-in is allowed
questions.why: The teaching text defines the pool as an organization-level container for external identities, and it is the providers inside it that describe a specific IdP.

questions.prompt: A supplier's staff member, Ravi, is set up through a correctly configured pool and provider. He types the right password at sign-in but is refused. The attribute mapping is correct and the signature check passes. Which cause best explains the refusal?
choices: The attribute condition evaluated to false for his claims, so sign-in is refused despite the correct password
The provider uses SAML 2.0 instead of OIDC, which always blocks sign-in
The pool was created at project level instead of organization level
Ravi's IAM role on the project is too narrow to allow him to sign in
questions.why: The teaching text says an attribute condition that evaluates to false refuses sign-in even when the password was correct, and this is the only option that matches the described checks passing.

questions.prompt: A team maps the subject attribute to a department code, procurement, which twelve people share. The sign-in works for everyone. What is the main consequence for a running system?
choices: Sign-in will fail for all twelve people because the subject is not unique
The organization-level pool is automatically deleted after the first sign-in
Roles granted to the group stop applying to any of the twelve people
Audit logs can no longer show which individual made a given change, because several people map to the same subject
questions.why: When several people map to one subject, the subject in the logs cannot identify the individual actor, which the teaching text names as the consequence of a wrong attribute mapping.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we do not just create Google accounts for every contractor who needs console access. Explain how Workforce Identity Federation grants access, what the pool and the provider each do, and one limit or tradeoff we should weigh before adopting it.
lessons.modelAnswer: We would only create Google accounts if we had no existing directory to trust. With federation, the company's identity provider keeps authenticating people, and Google trusts its signed sign-in statements. The workforce identity pool is the organization-level container for these external identities. The provider inside it records which IdP to trust, the protocol it uses, and how to verify its signatures. Attribute mapping translates the IdP's claims into Google attributes, and an attribute condition decides who may sign in at all. Access is still controlled by IAM: we grant roles to the federated principal or group, so the pool by itself gives no permissions. The main tradeoff is dependency. If the IdP is down, nobody new can sign in, and offboarding relies on removing the person in the IdP and on how long sessions last, so we should test that revocation path before relying on it.
rubricPoints: Explains that the external IdP keeps authenticating people and Google trusts its signed assertions.
Distinguishes the workforce identity pool (container) from the provider (one specific IdP trust).
States that access is granted through IAM roles on a federated principal or group, not by the pool itself.
Names attribute mapping and attribute conditions as the parts that translate claims and restrict who may sign in.
Names a real limit, such as dependency on the IdP's availability or revocation timing tied to session lifetime.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a federated group should receive a role involves reasoning through authorization policy outcomes, which the planned policy evaluator would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A billing account is the payment arrangement that covers the cost of cloud usage. A project is a container that holds your cloud resources, such as servers and storage. Linking means attaching a project to a billing account so that the charges from that project are paid through it. A project can exist without any billing account, but paid services will not run in it until one is attached. Think of it like putting a utility account in the name of a building: the building uses the power, and the bill goes to whichever account it is connected to. One billing account can pay for many projects, but a project is connected to only one billing account at a time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you create a new project and never attach it to a billing account, what do you think happens when someone tries to start a paid virtual machine inside it?
lessons.teach:
A billing account is the Google Cloud object that holds payment details and collects charges for usage. A project is the unit that owns resources and usage. Linking is the act of setting a project's billing account, which decides where that project's charges go. Creating a project does not create a billing account, and creating a billing account does not automatically pay for any project. Two kinds of permission matter. The first is a billing role on the billing account, such as Billing Account User, which lets a person attach projects to it. The second is a permission on the project itself, such as being an owner or holding a billing manager role there, which lets a person change that project's billing link. Someone needs both sides to make the link.

Worked example: a team lead creates a project called checkout-dev. The lead opens the billing page for that project and sees no billing account linked. The lead has Billing Account User on the shared account Finance-Shared and Owner on checkout-dev. The lead selects Finance-Shared and confirms. Now the project's paid services are allowed to run, and their charges appear under Finance-Shared.

A common mistake is assuming that an organization administrator role is enough. Organization roles do not by themselves let someone attach a project to a billing account. The consequence in a running system is serious: if a project's billing link is removed or the billing account is closed, paid resources in that project stop working, and services that depend on them can go down.

A project and its billing account are separate objects, and the link between them is what lets paid usage run.

questions.prompt: A small agency sets up a project called ledger-staging for a client trial. The sequence is: Step 1, Dana creates ledger-staging and holds Owner on it. Step 2, Sam, who administers the agency's billing account Client-Trial-Billing, is asked to help. Step 3, [missing step]. Step 4, Dana opens the billing page for ledger-staging, selects Client-Trial-Billing, and confirms, and the project's paid services can now run. Which entry correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Dana grants herself Owner on the Client-Trial-Billing account.
Sam converts ledger-staging into a folder under the organization.
Dana creates a second billing account so the project has its own payment record.
Sam grants Dana the Billing Account User role on Client-Trial-Billing.
questions.why: Dana already has the project-side permission from Step 1, so she still needs the billing-account-side role, which Sam can grant, before she can attach the project in Step 4.

questions.prompt: A developer opens the billing page for a project named reports-eu and sees that no billing account is linked. What does this status mean?
choices: The billing account was closed automatically when the project was made.
The project is on a free tier that never incurs charges, so no link is needed.
The project was deleted and must be recreated before anything runs.
The project has no billing account attached, so its paid services cannot run until one is linked.
questions.why: A project without a linked billing account cannot use paid services, and the link is what allows that paid usage to run.

questions.prompt: An engineer holds the Organization Administrator role for a company and also holds Owner on the project media-prod. The engineer has no billing role on the billing account Corp-Main. Can the engineer attach media-prod to Corp-Main?
choices: Yes, because organization administrators can attach any project to any billing account.
Yes, because Owner on the project is enough to change its billing link without any billing-account role.
No, because the link needs a billing-account role on Corp-Main in addition to the project-side permission.
No, because only the person who originally created Corp-Main can ever link a project to it.
questions.why: Linking requires both a billing role on the billing account and a permission on the project, and an organization role alone does not supply the billing-account side.

questions.prompt: A team runs a web service and a batch job in a project called orders-live, which is linked to the billing account Retail-Ops. The billing account is closed by mistake. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: Only new projects fail to link, while existing projects keep running normally.
The project is automatically moved to a free billing account and keeps running.
The paid resources in orders-live stop working, and services that depend on them can go down.
Nothing changes until the next monthly invoice is generated.
questions.why: When a project's billing account is closed or its link is removed, paid resources in that project stop, and dependent services can fail.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to link a new project to the company's shared billing account what permissions they need, and name one limit or tradeoff of sharing one billing account across many projects.
lessons.modelAnswer: Linking a project is a two-sided permission check. The teammate needs a billing role on the shared billing account, such as Billing Account User, so they can attach projects to it. They also need an owner-level or billing manager role on the new project, so they can change its billing link. An organization administrator role alone is not enough. The main tradeoff of sharing one billing account is that all linked projects' charges roll up into one place. That makes cost attribution harder unless projects are labeled and reviewed, and it means anyone who can unlink or close that account can stop paid services in every project tied to it. So before linking, confirm the owner, the cost purpose of the project, and who else depends on that account.
rubricPoints: Linking needs a billing role on the billing account and a suitable role on the project
An organization-level role alone does not allow a project to be linked
One billing account can cover many projects, but each project has only one billing account at a time
Unlinking or closing the billing account stops paid services in every linked project

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console steps and account-and-role facts, and none of the listed missions or planned engines covers billing account linking directly.

lessons.plain: A billing budget is a spending target you set for a cloud account, such as 500 units of currency for the month. Alerts are warning points attached to that target, such as 50, 90 and 100 percent of the amount. When spending reaches one of those points, the system notifies the people responsible for billing so they can act before a surprise invoice arrives. A budget watches costs; by itself it does not stop anything from running.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your cloud project's monthly costs quietly climb to twice what you expected, what do you think a budget with an alert at 90 percent would do automatically, and what would it not do?
lessons.teach:
A billing account is the account that receives the charges for your cloud usage. A budget is a spending target attached to a billing account, with a chosen amount and a time period, usually monthly. You can narrow what the budget counts by scope, such as particular projects, particular services, or resources carrying particular labels (key-value tags you attach to resources). Threshold rules are the warning points, expressed as percentages of the budget amount. Each rule can compare against actual spend so far or against forecasted spend for the period. Notifications go by email to billing administrators and users with billing roles, and can also be published to a Pub/Sub topic, which is a messaging channel that other software can subscribe to and react to.

Worked example: a budget of 400 for the month, with rules at 50, 90 and 100 percent of actual spend. On day 15 spend reaches 210, which passes 50 percent (200), so an email goes out. On day 25 spend is 370, passing 90 percent (360), so another email goes out. On day 28 spend is 405, passing 100 percent (400), so a final alert goes out. Each rule fires once as its line is crossed.

The common mistake is assuming a budget caps spending. It does not. Cost data can lag by hours, so an alert often arrives after the money is already spent. A runaway job keeps running unless a person or your own automation stops it. Automated responses, such as a function that reacts to the Pub/Sub message, must be built and tested separately.

A budget is an early warning on a delayed signal, not a spending limit.

questions.prompt: A data team sets a monthly budget of 1,500 scoped to one project, with a single rule at 75 percent of forecasted spend. On day 9 the forecast for the whole month is 1,640. Step 1: 75 percent of 1,500 is 1,125, which is the warning line for this rule. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the rule fires once and an email goes to billing administrators and users with billing roles.
choices: Stop the project automatically, because a budget acts as a cap and spend cannot pass 1,125 without being halted.
Compare the forecast with the full 1,500 budget. Since 1,640 is above it, the 75 percent rule waits until spend reaches 100 percent.
Compare the forecast of 1,640 with the 1,125 line. The forecast is above it, so the rule's line is crossed and the alert fires.
Add the 1,640 forecast to the 1,125 line to get 2,765, and treat that sum as the new threshold to watch.
questions.why: A rule fires when the chosen measure, here forecasted spend, crosses the threshold line, and 1,640 is above 1,125, so the alert goes out.

questions.prompt: A billing administrator creates a budget of 2,000 on a billing account and limits its scope to resources carrying the label env=staging. Which statement about this budget is correct?
choices: It counts spend on all projects in the billing account, because labels only change how invoices are grouped.
It counts only spend on resources carrying the env=staging label, and it automatically shuts those resources down at 2,000.
It counts spend on every resource in the organisation, since a label applies to the whole organisation rather than one resource.
It counts only spend on resources carrying the env=staging label, and its alerts warn people but do not stop those resources.
questions.why: A budget's scope narrows what it counts, a label is one way to scope it, and a budget only sends notifications without stopping anything.

questions.prompt: A team sets one alert at 100 percent of actual spend on an 800 budget for a nightly export job. The job has no other controls. The team assumes the export will stop once spend reaches 800. What is the most accurate correction?
choices: The alert will fire at 800 exactly and the export is paused until a billing administrator approves more spending.
Cost data is updated in real time, so the export stops within seconds of spend reaching 800 without any further action.
The alert may arrive hours after spend has passed 800, and the export keeps running unless a person or separate automation stops it.
The job will stop at 800 because the budget enforces its amount automatically on any resource in scope.
questions.why: Budgets are early warnings on delayed cost data, so nothing stops the export unless a separately built and tested control does.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants VMs in a development project to be shut down when a budget alert fires at 90 percent. They publish budget notifications to a Pub/Sub topic. Which statement describes the correct setup?
choices: Publishing to Pub/Sub makes the budget itself shut down the VMs, so the team only needs to subscribe to the topic.
Pub/Sub delivers the alert as a message, and the team must build and test a subscriber that reacts by stopping the VMs.
The budget rule can be set to stop VMs directly once the 90 percent line is crossed, with no subscriber needed.
Pub/Sub messages are sent only to billing administrators, so the VMs must be shut down by hand after each email.
questions.why: A Pub/Sub topic carries the alert as a message, and any automated response is a separate piece of software that must be built and tested.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a budget alert does and does not do, and name one tradeoff in how you choose the alert thresholds.
lessons.modelAnswer: A budget is a spending target on a billing account, and its alerts are warning points at percentages of that target. When actual or forecasted spend crosses a point, the billing contacts get an email, and optionally a message goes to a Pub/Sub topic. The alert does not stop spending. Charges can show up hours late, and nothing shuts down a runaway resource unless we build automation that reacts to the message and disables something. The tradeoff in thresholds is timing: a low threshold like 50 percent gives early warning but may fire during normal busy periods and get ignored, while a high threshold like 100 percent gives fewer false alarms but leaves little time to react before the budget is gone. Forecast-based rules can warn earlier, but forecasts are estimates and can be wrong in either direction.
rubricPoints: A budget is a spending target attached to a billing account, with optional scope filters
Threshold alerts are percentages of the amount, based on actual or forecasted spend
Budget alerts notify people and can publish to Pub/Sub, but do not cap or stop spending by default
Cost data is delayed, so alerts can arrive after charges are incurred

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console configuration and the difference between alerting and capping, which is best learned from reading the setup steps and concepts.

lessons.plain: A billing export is an automatic, regular copy of your cloud spending records, delivered to a place where you can analyze them with queries. Think of a bank that sends a statement every day, except the rows land in a database table you can sort and total yourself. Setting one up is a one-time configuration on the billing account, not on each project. The export only records spending from the moment you turn it on, so it cannot reconstruct the past. Knowing which account owns the setting, and where the data lands, decides whether anyone can see costs later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company turns on a billing export today. Will a query run tomorrow show what was spent last month, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A Cloud Billing export is a continuing feed of cost records. Google Cloud writes rows describing usage charges into a BigQuery dataset, which is a managed analytics database where data is kept in tables and queried with SQL. Three terms first: a billing account is the container that charges are billed to; a project is the unit that consumes resources and is linked to a billing account; a dataset is a named container of tables in BigQuery, with a location such as a region or multi-region that is fixed once the dataset is created.

Why it works: the billing system pushes new records on a regular schedule, so you never have to download invoices by hand. The export is configured at the billing account level, so the costs of every linked project flow into the same destination. Permissions are split. Someone who administers billing needs rights over the billing account to switch the export on, while people who read the results need read access to the dataset.

Worked example. Step 1: a team lead creates a dataset named finops_export in the EU location. Step 2: in the billing account's export settings, they choose that dataset as the destination for the detailed usage cost export. Step 3: they save the setting on 3 March. Step 4: on 4 March, rows dated 3 March and later appear in the table. There are no rows for 1 February, because the export never saw those charges.

Common mistake: assuming the export is retroactive, or that turning it on for one project covers the whole billing account. The consequence in a running system is that if a cost spike happened before the export existed, the only record may be the invoice, and any cost query written against the table will show a gap that looks like zero spending.

A dataset's location cannot be changed after creation, so it should be chosen before the export is enabled.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Analytics has one billing account with three linked projects. Its finance lead wants daily cost rows in BigQuery. The steps so far: Step 1: on 12 May, an engineer creates a dataset named cost_feed in the US multi-region. Step 2: [missing step, which you must supply]. Step 3: a billing administrator saves the setting on 13 May. Step 4: on 14 May, rows dated 13 May and later appear in cost_feed. Which choice completes Step 2?
choices: Link each of the three projects to cost_feed separately, so each one writes its own export.
Copy the April invoices into a table inside cost_feed so that the history is complete.
In the billing account's export settings, select cost_feed as the destination for the detailed usage cost export.
Change cost_feed's location to the EU, because a multi-region dataset cannot receive export data.
questions.why: The export is configured at the billing account level, so the destination dataset is chosen in that account's export settings, which then covers every linked project.

questions.prompt: A contractor needs to read the daily cost rows in a dataset but must not be able to change the billing account's export settings. Which access is appropriate?
choices: Owner rights on every linked project, so they can see all costs.
Read access on the dataset that holds the export tables.
Permission to change the dataset's location, so they can reorganise the data.
Billing administrator rights over the billing account, so they can see the export settings.
questions.why: Readers of the results need read access to the dataset, while switching the export on or off requires rights over the billing account, so the two are separate permissions.

questions.prompt: Kestrel's team turned the export on for 1 September. A cost spike on 20 August appears on the invoice, but a query over the export table returns zero for that day. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The export only records charges from the moment it was enabled, so no rows exist for 20 August.
The contractor's read access hides rows from before September from query results.
The export is only partly working, so the query is missing rows that did get written.
The dataset location is wrong, so the 20 August rows are stored in a different region.
questions.why: The export is not retroactive and only receives records from when it was switched on, so a query over the table shows a gap that looks like zero spending.

questions.prompt: A team created a dataset in us-central1 for their billing export and now wants the data held in an EU location. Which approach is correct?
choices: Create a new dataset in an EU location and point the billing export at it, accepting that earlier rows remain in the original dataset.
Edit the dataset's location in its settings and keep all existing rows, since the data is copied automatically to the new region.
Delete the export and wait for the billing system to rebuild the history in the new region.
Move the billing account into an EU region, which relocates every dataset linked to it.
questions.why: A dataset's location is fixed once it is created, so the fix is a new dataset in the wanted location with the export pointed at it, and the old rows stay where they were.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Cloud Billing export is, where its rows land, and one limit they must plan for before turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Cloud Billing export is a regular feed of cost line items that Google Cloud writes into a BigQuery dataset, so we can query spending with SQL instead of reading invoices. It is set on the billing account, which means every linked project's charges go to the same place. The main limit is that it starts recording only from the moment it is enabled and does not backfill earlier months. So we should enable it early, and before we do, we need to pick the dataset location deliberately, because it cannot be changed later. Someone also needs billing administration rights to switch it on, and readers need access to the dataset. Until we have an export, a cost spike from last month can only be checked against the invoice.
rubricPoints: Defines the export as a regular automatic feed of billing line items into a BigQuery dataset
Notes that the export is configured at the billing account level, covering all linked projects
States that it records only from the enable date and is not retroactive
Mentions that the dataset location is fixed once created and must be chosen first

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console settings, permission boundaries and facts about where data lands, which no listed mission or planned engine covers.

lessons.plain: Before you can run an application on Google Cloud, you have to decide what kind of computer it runs on. Some options give you a whole virtual machine that you fully control. Others give you a container or a single function and let Google handle the machines underneath. Choosing is a tradeoff: more control means more work to keep things running, and less control means less to manage but fewer choices. This lesson gives you a way to match a workload's shape to the option that fits, so you do not end up looking after servers you never needed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a stateless web API packaged as a container. Traffic is quiet overnight and spikes at lunchtime, and nobody on the team wants to patch servers. Which compute option would you try first, and what would make you switch to a different one?
lessons.teach:
A compute option is the way your code gets processor time, memory, and an operating environment. The options differ mainly in how much of the stack you manage yourself. Compute Engine gives you virtual machines, which are software computers, and you control the operating system, its patches, and the machine size. Google Kubernetes Engine, or GKE, is a managed Kubernetes cluster. Kubernetes is a system that schedules containers, which are packaged application bundles, across many machines. Cloud Run runs a container image without you managing servers, scales down to zero when idle, and suits services that respond to requests. Cloud Run functions run a single piece of code triggered by an HTTP call or an event, and Google builds the packaging for you. Agent Runtime, part of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, is a managed place to host AI agent code, so the team can focus on the agent's logic rather than the hosting.

The principle is that the more the provider manages, the less you operate, but you give up control over the machine and some freedom in how it runs.

Worked example: a team has a stateless HTTP API in one container, with quiet nights, lunchtime spikes, and no appetite for patching servers. Step one: the app needs no special operating system, so Compute Engine offers more control than they need. Step two: it is a single container, so a full cluster is overhead. Step three: it responds to requests and should scale to zero, which points to Cloud Run.

Common mistake: choosing GKE because Kubernetes sounds like the industry standard, when the team has nobody who can run cluster upgrades. In a running system, node pools then fall behind on patches, and each upgrade becomes a risk to live traffic that someone has to handle at night.

The choice decides who is on call for what, so match the option to the team's operating capacity as well as to the workload.

questions.prompt: A small research lab wants a Python script to run each time a new CSV file lands in a storage bucket. The script takes about 20 seconds and reads only the file it was given. The team has no container experience and does not want to build or patch images. Step one: the work is one piece of code started by an event, so a function-style option fits better than a full VM or cluster. Step two: [missing step, to be chosen below]. Step three: because the team does not need to pick the operating system or machine size, a Compute Engine virtual machine would add control they will never use, so the managed function option is the match.
choices: Step two: confirm the script does not need a custom operating system or system-level software installed by the team.
Step two: confirm the script needs a Kubernetes cluster with several node pools to run in parallel.
Step two: confirm the team has someone able to run cluster upgrades every quarter.
Step two: confirm the script can run as a long-lived service that scales to a fixed number of replicas.
questions.why: The missing step checks the one requirement that would rule out the managed function option, namely whether the team must control the operating system or install system software, and the scenario states it does not.

questions.prompt: A regulated bank runs a legacy trading tool that needs a specific operating system kernel version and a manually tuned machine size. Which compute option gives the team the control they need?
choices: Cloud Run, because it scales to zero and so keeps the machine size flexible.
Agent Runtime, because it hosts any code the team needs in a managed place.
Compute Engine, because it provides virtual machines where the team controls the operating system and machine size.
Cloud Run functions, because Google builds the packaging for the tool.
questions.why: Compute Engine provides virtual machines where the customer controls the operating system, its patches, and the machine size, which is the control this bank needs.

questions.prompt: A logistics company chooses GKE for one stateless container that handles order lookups. Nobody on the team has run a Kubernetes cluster before, and no one is scheduled to handle cluster upgrades. What is the most likely problem in operation?
choices: Node pools will fall behind on patches, and each later upgrade becomes a risky change to live traffic that someone must handle at night.
Compute Engine will automatically replace the cluster with a managed virtual machine, removing the upgrade work.
Cloud Run functions will be forced onto the cluster, so the order lookups will run as single-purpose events.
The container will scale to zero during quiet hours and then fail to start on the next request.
questions.why: Without people able to run cluster upgrades, node pools drift behind on patches, and each upgrade turns into a risk to live traffic that someone has to manage out of hours.

questions.prompt: A startup builds an AI assistant that calls a language model and a few internal tools to answer customer questions. The founders want to focus on the assistant's logic and avoid running any servers. Which option matches this need best?
choices: Compute Engine, because the founders can install whatever agent libraries they like on a virtual machine.
Cloud Run functions, because each tool call is a single function and Google builds the packaging.
GKE, because a Kubernetes cluster is the most flexible place to run agent code.
Agent Runtime, because it is a managed place to host AI agent code so the team can focus on the agent's logic instead of hosting.
questions.why: Agent Runtime is the managed hosting option described for AI agent code, so it lets the team spend its effort on the agent's logic rather than on servers or clusters.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions for a new service. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the shape of the workload. If it needs a specific operating system, kernel settings, or long-running processes I fully control, Compute Engine fits. If we have many containers that need to talk to each other and a team that can run cluster upgrades, GKE fits. If it is a container that serves requests and can scale to zero, Cloud Run is my default because we do not manage servers. If it is one small function reacting to an event or an HTTP call, Cloud Run functions is simpler still. The tradeoff with Cloud Run is that each request has a time limit and the service has less control over the machine, so long batch jobs or special hardware push me toward Compute Engine or GKE. I would also ask who will be on call for patching and upgrades, because that decides how much management overhead we can afford.
rubricPoints: Matches the option to the workload shape, such as containers, requests, events, or need for OS control
Names how much management each option leaves to the team
States at least one concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen option
Considers the team's operating capacity alongside the technical fit

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic workload shape against several options adds the most beyond reading the descriptions.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine, often called an instance, is a computer that runs in a cloud provider's data center but behaves like a server you control. When you launch one, you make two kinds of choices that matter long after launch. The availability policy decides what happens to the machine when the physical hardware under it needs planned maintenance or fails: keep it running by moving it, or stop it and start it again. SSH keys decide who can log in. An SSH key is a pair of files: a public half you place on the machine and a private half you keep secret on your own computer. Get these right at launch and the server stays up and reachable.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server runs on a physical machine in a data center, and that machine must be patched tonight. What do you want to happen to your server during that patch, and how would you tell the cloud platform?
lessons.teach:
A Compute Engine instance is a virtual machine: a computer that Google runs on shared physical hardware inside one zone, which is a single data center location. The availability policy is the set of settings that tells the platform how to treat that instance when the hardware under it has trouble. It has two main parts. The on-host maintenance setting says what happens during planned maintenance of the physical host. MIGRATE moves the running instance to other hardware without a reboot, while TERMINATE stops it. The automatic restart setting says whether the platform should start the instance again after it stops unexpectedly, such as after a host failure or crash. It does not apply when you stop the instance yourself. SSH keys are a pair: a public key you place on the instance and a private key that never leaves your machine. The instance accepts a login when the caller proves possession of the matching private key. You can attach a key to one instance's metadata, or to project-wide metadata so every instance in the project accepts it.

Worked example. You launch a web server in one zone. Step 1: set on-host maintenance to MIGRATE, so planned host work moves the server live. Step 2: turn automatic restart on, so an unexpected host failure brings the server back. Step 3: paste your public key into the instance's SSH key metadata. Step 4: connect with your private key. The guest operating system checks the key you present against the stored public key and admits you only if they match.

Common mistake: pasting the private key into metadata, a ticket, or a chat, which exposes the secret to anyone who can read it. A related mistake is choosing TERMINATE for a server you expect to stay up, then being surprised when planned maintenance stops it. In a running system, TERMINATE with no automatic restart means planned host maintenance takes your service offline until someone starts the instance again.

A single zone is still a single point of failure. The availability policy keeps one machine alive; it does not make a whole service resilient.

questions.prompt: Ledgerline, a small accounting firm, launches a file-sync virtual machine (a VM, meaning a computer Google runs on shared hardware) in one zone. Step 1: it sets on-host maintenance to MIGRATE, so planned host work moves the VM without a reboot. Step 2: it turns automatic restart on, so a host crash brings the VM back. Step 3 is missing: the team must decide where the contractor's public key goes, and it wants only this one VM to accept that contractor. Step 4: the contractor connects with the matching private key, and the VM admits them. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Send the contractor the private key so they can paste it into the instance's metadata.
Add the contractor's public key to this one instance's metadata, since only this VM needs to accept it.
Put the public key into project-wide metadata so every VM in the project accepts it.
Turn automatic restart off so the contractor's session is not restarted by the platform.
questions.why: Attaching the public key to this instance's own metadata limits access to that one VM, while project-wide metadata would let every instance in the project accept the key.

questions.prompt: A nightly report VM can be paused during planned host maintenance, but if its host crashes it must start again without anyone intervening. Which availability policy fits?
choices: On-host maintenance MIGRATE with automatic restart on
On-host maintenance TERMINATE with automatic restart off
On-host maintenance TERMINATE with automatic restart on
On-host maintenance MIGRATE with automatic restart off
questions.why: TERMINATE accepts that planned maintenance stops the VM, and automatic restart on brings it back after an unexpected host failure.

questions.prompt: A developer stopped a VM by hand on Friday to save money. On Monday it is still stopped, and the team suspects the automatic restart setting is broken. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The VM is probably stopped because automatic restart never applies when a person stops the instance.
The public key in metadata expired, which blocks the VM from starting.
The host crashed over the weekend and automatic restart failed to run.
Planned maintenance was set to TERMINATE, which stops VMs permanently.
questions.why: Automatic restart only applies to unexpected stops such as host failures, so a VM stopped on purpose stays stopped until someone starts it.

questions.prompt: A colleague needs to log in to a VM you manage. Which item is safe to give them, and which is never to be shared?
choices: Give them a renamed copy of your private key, which is safe because the name has changed.
Give them your private key file, and keep only a copy of the public key for yourself.
Give them both keys together so they can set up their own login without asking you again.
Give them the public key to place in metadata, and keep the private key only on your own machine.
questions.why: The public key can be shared freely because it only verifies a login, while the private key must stay on the machine that owns it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the two availability settings on a new VM do, and how an SSH key pair lets you log in without sending a password. Name one limit or tradeoff of each setting.
lessons.modelAnswer: The on-host maintenance setting decides what happens when the provider must maintain the physical machine under our VM. MIGRATE keeps the VM running by moving it live to other hardware, which suits most web servers, though some machine types and accelerators cannot migrate and workloads may see brief slowdowns. TERMINATE stops the VM, which is only acceptable when the workload tolerates a stop. Automatic restart brings the VM back after an unexpected host failure, but it does not save data that existed only in memory, and it does nothing when we stop the VM on purpose. For SSH, we generate a key pair: the public key goes into instance or project metadata, and the private key stays on our laptop. The server checks that we hold the matching private key, so no password crosses the network. The tradeoff is that anyone holding the private key can log in, so we must protect that file and remove keys when people leave the team.
rubricPoints: Explains MIGRATE versus TERMINATE for on-host maintenance and what each does to the running VM.
Explains automatic restart as recovery after unexpected stops, not after a deliberate stop.
Explains the SSH key pair: public key placed on the instance, private key kept secret by the user.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as termination causing downtime or a leaked private key granting access.

suggested.rationale: Launch settings and their defaults are product facts best checked in the console, and no listed mission or planned engine covers VM availability policy or SSH key setup.

lessons.plain: A Compute Engine virtual machine (VM) needs a disk to hold its operating system and data. Google Cloud offers network-attached block storage for this, which behaves like a hard drive connected to the machine over the network but kept separate from it, so the data survives when the machine stops. You choose where the disk lives: in one zone, copied across two zones in the same region, or in a newer disk family where you set speed and size separately. Choosing well means balancing how fast the disk must be, how much failure it must survive, and what it costs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database VM needs fast storage for a modest amount of data, and the service must keep running if one data center area in its region fails. Which kind of disk would you reach for first, and what would worry you about your choice?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A region is a geographic area, such as a city-sized part of the world, that contains several zones. A zone is an isolated data center area inside a region. A persistent disk (PD) is durable block storage that a VM attaches over the network, and its data persists after the VM stops. A zonal persistent disk exists in one zone. A regional persistent disk is synchronously replicated to two zones in one region, so a write is confirmed only after both copies have it. Hyperdisk is a newer block storage family in which you provision performance separately from capacity. IOPS means input and output operations per second, and throughput means the amount of data moved per second.

Why it works. On a zonal PD, the speed you get grows with the disk's size, so reaching a high IOPS target can force you to buy far more capacity than you need. Hyperdisk separates those dials, so you can set size and speed independently. Regional PD trades some write speed and extra cost for survival: if one zone fails, the workload can be restarted in the other zone and attach the replica.

Worked example with illustrative numbers. A database needs 500 GB and 20,000 IOPS. Step 1: on a zonal PD, estimate the size needed to reach 20,000 IOPS, which may be much larger than 500 GB. Step 2: on Hyperdisk, set 500 GB and 20,000 IOPS directly. Step 3: if the database must survive a zone outage, check whether a zone-redundant option exists for that disk type; if you need that protection with the simpler PD model, regional PD gives it at the cost of some write speed.

Common mistake. Treating regional PD as a backup. Replication copies accidental deletions and corruption to both zones at once. Backups are made with snapshots.

Consequence. A zonal disk in a failed zone leaves its VM unavailable until that zone recovers. With regional redundancy, the workload can be restarted elsewhere in the region with its data intact.

The disk type is a design decision made before launch, and changing it later is usually a migration project, so decide from the workload's speed, survival, and cost needs.

questions.prompt: A checkout service's VM needs 300 GB of disk and must keep its data if one zone in its region fails. Step 1: a zonal persistent disk lives in one zone, so if that zone fails, the VM is unavailable until the zone recovers. Step 2: a regional persistent disk keeps a synchronously replicated copy in a second zone of the same region, so the workload can be restarted in the other zone with its data. Step 3: [missing step] Which decision completes the reasoning?
choices: Choose zonal PD and rely on nightly snapshots to recover after a zone loss.
Choose regional PD, accepting some write-speed cost, to survive a zone outage.
Choose zonal PD, because copies in two zones would also copy accidental deletions.
Choose Hyperdisk, since separating speed from size makes zone survival unnecessary.
questions.why: Regional PD is the option that meets the stated survival requirement, and the text says it trades some write speed and cost for that protection.

questions.prompt: A media startup's render VM has a persistent disk. The VM is stopped overnight and started the next morning. Which statement best describes what happens to the disk's data?
choices: The data persists, because a persistent disk keeps its data after the VM stops.
The data is kept only if the disk is regional, because zonal disks are cleared on stop.
The data is erased at stop, because disks only hold data while a VM is running.
The data survives only if a snapshot was taken before the stop.
questions.why: A persistent disk is durable block storage whose data persists after the VM stops, regardless of disk location type.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's reporting database needs 2 TB of capacity and 45,000 IOPS. Under the teaching model, which storage choice lets the team set those two values independently?
choices: Snapshots, which supply extra IOPS on demand.
Zonal PD, where speed rises with size so the 2 TB figure sets the speed.
Regional PD, where replication to two zones determines the IOPS available.
Hyperdisk, which provisions size and performance separately.
questions.why: Hyperdisk separates provisioned performance from capacity, while on zonal PD the speed grows with size, so the two cannot be set independently.

questions.prompt: A team keeps its only copy of an order-history dataset on a regional persistent disk and considers that enough protection. An engineer accidentally deletes a folder. What is the likely result?
choices: The deleted folder is still safe in the second zone, which keeps an older version.
The folder is removed from both zones, because replication writes the deletion to both copies at once.
The VM stops working until the folder is restored from the other zone.
Only the first zone's copy is removed, and the second zone keeps the folder.
questions.why: Regional PD is synchronous replication, not a backup, so the deletion is confirmed in both zones and recovery requires a snapshot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick a zonal persistent disk, a regional persistent disk, or Hyperdisk for a database VM, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the database needs. If it is a non-critical workload that can be rebuilt, a zonal persistent disk is the cheapest and simplest choice, and I would accept that a zone outage makes it unavailable until the zone recovers. If the database must survive losing a zone, a regional persistent disk replicates writes to two zones in the region, so I can restart the VM in the other zone with its data. The tradeoff is that every write waits for both copies, so write latency and cost go up. If the database needs high speed on a modest size, Hyperdisk lets me set IOPS and throughput directly, avoiding buying extra capacity just for speed. The limit I would flag is that none of these is a backup. Replication copies a mistaken delete everywhere, so I would still take snapshots.
rubricPoints: Zonal persistent disk lives in one zone and is simplest, but a zone outage takes it offline
Regional persistent disk replicates synchronously to two zones, improving survival at the cost of write latency and price
Hyperdisk lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of capacity
Replication is not a backup; snapshots are needed to recover from deletion or corruption

suggested.rationale: Choosing a disk for a given workload is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario, and no existing mission or planned engine covers Compute Engine disks directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a shop that opens extra checkout lanes when the queue grows and closes them when it shrinks. In Google Cloud, a managed instance group is a set of identical virtual machines created and managed together. An instance template is the recipe that describes each machine, including its size, operating system image, and startup script. Autoscaling means the group adds or removes machines by itself based on load, between a minimum and a maximum you choose. You do not have to start or stop servers by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a web app's traffic doubles every lunchtime and falls at night, would you rather run a fixed number of servers all day, or let the number change with demand? What would you need to tell the system so it knows when to add one?
lessons.teach: An instance template is a saved blueprint for a virtual machine: machine type, boot image, disk, labels, and a startup script that runs on first boot. You cannot edit a template after it is created; to change anything, you create a new template version. A managed instance group (MIG) is a set of identical VMs built from one template, which the platform keeps running and replaces when one fails a health check. An autoscaler is the part that changes the group size. You set a minimum and maximum number of instances and a target for a signal, such as average CPU utilization of 60 percent, and the autoscaler adds or removes VMs to move that signal toward the target. A cooldown period tells it to ignore a new VM's early metrics while the VM boots, so it does not overreact. Worked example: the group has 2 VMs, minimum 2, maximum 10, target CPU 60 percent. Average CPU rises to 90 percent. The autoscaler estimates the needed count as current size times observed divided by target, which is 2 times 90 divided by 60, giving 3. It adds one VM. After the cooldown and once the new VM is serving, it recalculates. Later, load drops to 20 percent across 3 VMs. The estimate is 3 times 20 divided by 60, which is 1, but the minimum of 2 stops the group going lower. Common mistake: assuming that editing the template updates running VMs. It does not. New VMs use the new template, and existing VMs are replaced only when you start a rolling update. Consequence: a maximum set too low leaves requests queuing during a surge, a minimum set too low leaves no spare capacity while new VMs boot, and a cooldown shorter than the startup script's run time makes the group add and remove VMs repeatedly. An autoscaled MIG grows and shrinks inside your limits, and its template is the only thing that defines what each new machine looks like.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a managed instance group that started with 4 VMs. Its autoscaler has a minimum of 4, a maximum of 5, and a target average CPU of 50 percent. Average CPU rises to 75 percent. Step 1: the current size is 4. Step 2: the estimate is 4 x 75 / 50, which is 6. Step 3: the group cannot go past its maximum, so the final size after scaling out is ___.
questions.why: The maximum of 5 caps the group, so even though the estimate is 6, the autoscaler stops at 5.

questions.prompt: A team edits the instance template used by a running managed instance group to add a new label. What happens to the VMs that are already running?
choices: They are deleted and recreated automatically within the minute.
They are restarted immediately with the label applied.
They keep their existing configuration, and only new VMs or a rolling update will use the edited template.
The template change is rejected because templates cannot be edited while in use.
questions.why: A template cannot be edited in place, so the team must create a new template version, and running VMs are only replaced when a rolling update is started.

questions.prompt: A managed instance group's startup script takes about 6 minutes to finish on each new VM, but the autoscaler's cooldown period is set to 60 seconds. What is the most likely result?
choices: The startup script is skipped so that the VM can join the group sooner.
The autoscaler reads the half-started VMs' early metrics and keeps adding and removing VMs repeatedly.
The group stays at its current size because the cooldown is shorter than the boot time, which blocks scaling.
The group scales smoothly because the cooldown only affects the maximum size.
questions.why: A cooldown shorter than the startup run time lets the autoscaler act on metrics from VMs that are still booting, causing repeated add-and-remove cycles.

questions.prompt: A managed instance group has 5 VMs, a minimum of 3, a maximum of 8, and a target average CPU of 60 percent. Current average CPU is 24 percent. What size does the autoscaler settle at?
questions.why: The estimate is 5 x 24 / 60 = 2, but the minimum of 3 stops the group from going lower, so it settles at 3.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an autoscaled managed instance group decides how many VMs to run, and name one limit or tradeoff of using CPU utilization as the scaling signal.
lessons.modelAnswer: The group is built from one instance template, which defines every VM it creates. The autoscaler watches a signal, usually average CPU across the VMs, compares it to a target such as 60 percent, and works out roughly how many VMs would bring the signal to that target. It adds or removes VMs but never goes outside the minimum and maximum I set. There is a cooldown so it does not react to a new VM that is still booting. The limit is that CPU is only a proxy. A service can be slow because of memory, disk, or waiting on a database while CPU stays low, so the group will not scale even though users are suffering. Another tradeoff is that a low target keeps headroom for spikes but costs more, and a high target saves money but risks queuing when traffic jumps. I would pick a signal that matches the real bottleneck and test the target under load.
rubricPoints: An instance template is a read-only blueprint, and every VM in the group is built from it
The autoscaler adds or removes VMs to move a chosen signal toward a target, within a minimum and maximum
A cooldown period stops the autoscaler from reacting to VMs that are still booting
Editing a template does not change running VMs; a rolling update is needed
CPU utilization is only a proxy and may miss real bottlenecks, or trade cost against headroom

suggested.rationale: The planned autoscale engine lets the learner tune min, max, target, and cooldown and watch the group respond, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When you need to log in to a Linux server in the cloud, someone has to decide who is allowed in and what they can do once inside. OS Login answers that by linking server logins to your company's cloud identity system, so access is granted and removed in one place instead of by copying SSH keys onto each machine. VM Manager is a set of tools that keeps many servers healthy as a group: it tracks what software each machine has, schedules security updates, and reports which machines are out of date. Think of OS Login as the building's keycard system and VM Manager as the maintenance crew that checks every room.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 40 Linux servers and a new engineer joins your team. If access is handled by copying that person's public key onto each server, what do you have to do when that engineer leaves, and how could you make it a single change instead?
lessons.teach:
OS Login is a way of controlling SSH access to Linux virtual machines using identities from your cloud account. SSH is the encrypted remote-login protocol administrators use to type commands on a server. Normally each server keeps its own list of public keys in instance metadata, the key-value settings attached to a VM or project, so access changes must be pushed to every machine. With OS Login on, the server asks the cloud identity system whether a person may log in, then creates or maps a local Linux account for them, called a POSIX account (the traditional Unix user record). Access is governed by IAM roles, which are permission grants that say which identity may do which action. The role roles/compute.osLogin gives ordinary login rights, roles/compute.osAdminLogin also allows administrator (sudo) commands, and roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser covers people outside your organization. You enable it by setting the metadata key enable-oslogin to TRUE, at project level so every VM inherits it, or on one instance to override.

VM Manager is the suite for running many VMs. Its OS inventory records installed software, and its patch management schedules updates and reports compliance. It needs the OS Config agent, a small program on each VM that reports back.

Worked example: Ana needs to log in to vm-web-3. You enable OS Login at project level. You grant Ana roles/compute.osLogin on the project. Ana runs an SSH connection to vm-web-3; the platform checks her IAM role, creates her POSIX account, and lets her in as a regular user. She cannot run sudo. When she leaves, you remove that binding and her access ends on every VM at once.

Common mistake: adding a public key to instance metadata and expecting it to work after OS Login is on. OS Login ignores those keys, so the login fails. The fix is to check the IAM binding, not the keys.

In a running fleet, stale keys on each machine let former staff keep logging in until someone cleans every server by hand. With OS Login, revoking access is one change, and the audit log records who logged in and when.

questions.prompt: Tomas leads a build team at Harbor Freight Labs. His project is forge-dev and his VM is build-agent-7. The project already has enable-oslogin set to TRUE, so every VM inherits OS Login, which is the setting that makes the server check IAM (cloud permission grants) and create a local Linux account for each person. The team lead grants Tomas roles/compute.osLogin on the project. Tomas connects over SSH and gets in as a regular user. He then runs a sudo command to restart a service and is refused. The one change needed is to grant Tomas the role that also permits administrator commands. Which change completes the fix?
choices: Grant Tomas roles/compute.osAdminLogin on the project
Add Tomas's public key to the instance metadata of build-agent-7
Grant Tomas roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser on the project
Set enable-oslogin to FALSE on build-agent-7
questions.why: The role roles/compute.osAdminLogin is the one that adds sudo rights on top of ordinary login, and Tomas's refusal comes from having only the ordinary login role.

questions.prompt: A contractor on a company's OS Login project needs access removed from 40 VMs at once. Which action ends their SSH access on every one of those VMs with a single change?
choices: Rotate the project's SSH host keys
Turn enable-oslogin to FALSE across the project
Delete the contractor's public key from each VM's metadata, one VM at a time
Remove the contractor's IAM binding for roles/compute.osLogin at the project level
questions.why: With OS Login, access is decided by the IAM binding, so removing that binding at project level ends login on every inheriting VM at once, while the other options either touch 40 machines by hand or break access for everyone.

questions.prompt: An engineer's SSH login to vm-batch-12 is refused. The project has enable-oslogin set to TRUE, and the engineer holds roles/compute.osLogin. However, vm-batch-12 has its own metadata key enable-oslogin set to FALSE. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The engineer needs roles/compute.osAdminLogin before any login is allowed
VM Manager's OS Config agent blocks SSH on all instances in the project
The instance-level FALSE setting overrides the project-level TRUE, so OS Login is off on that one VM
The engineer lacks a POSIX account because the Linux home directory is missing
questions.why: The metadata key can be set at project level or on one instance, and an instance setting overrides the inherited project value, so OS Login is disabled on that VM and the IAM role is never consulted there.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants to see which software packages each of its 200 VMs has installed and to track which machines are missing security updates. Which VM Manager feature and supporting program are needed on each machine?
choices: OS inventory and patch management, supported by the OS Config agent running on each VM
OS Login and roles/compute.osAdminLogin, supported by a VPN tunnel to each VM
Instance metadata keys and a public key list, supported by the SSH daemon alone
Patch management only, which works without any agent installed on the VMs
questions.why: VM Manager's OS inventory records installed software and patch management reports update status, and both depend on the small OS Config agent reporting back from each VM, while OS Login only governs who may log in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how OS Login changes who can SSH into a Linux VM compared with managing public keys in instance metadata, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on OS Login.
lessons.modelAnswer: With instance metadata keys, every VM holds its own list of allowed public keys, so granting or revoking access means editing each machine. With OS Login, the VM checks the cloud identity system at login time. A person's access comes from an IAM role on the project or instance, and the Linux account is created automatically. Granting access means adding a role binding, and removing it stops logins everywhere that OS Login is enabled. The tradeoff is dependence on IAM and on the metadata setting: if someone turns OS Login off or a VM lacks the right role, login fails, and admin rights need the separate admin role. Keys in metadata also stop working once OS Login is on, which can surprise people who expect them to still apply.
rubricPoints: OS Login maps SSH access to IAM identities instead of per-VM key lists.
Access is granted or revoked centrally through IAM role bindings.
Admin (sudo) access requires a separate admin role.
OS Login is enabled through the enable-oslogin metadata setting, which overrides keys in metadata.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which IAM role gives a person login versus admin rights on a VM is an exam-style situation that is best reasoned through rather than read as a list.

lessons.plain: Think of a cloud server as something you rent by the hour. Google sometimes offers spare capacity at a much lower price, on the condition that it can take that machine back when another customer needs the space. That cheaper, reclaimable machine is a Spot VM. A custom machine type is the other tool in this lesson: instead of picking from fixed sizes, you choose exactly how many processors and how much memory the machine gets. Together they let you pay less for work that can survive interruption, and buy only the size you actually need.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly batch job can save its progress and restart from where it stopped. You want the lowest price. Would you run it on a normal, guaranteed machine or on a cheaper machine the provider can take back at any time? Give your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
A Spot VM is a Compute Engine virtual machine sold at a steep discount because Google can reclaim it when it needs the capacity for other customers. This reclaiming is called preemption. Before a Spot VM is preempted, Compute Engine sends a short warning, about 30 seconds, through the instance metadata and the operating system shutdown signal, so your software can save its state. Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime, but they are not guaranteed to keep running, and they do not get live migration, the feature that moves a running machine to new hardware without stopping it. When you create one, you choose what happens on preemption: stop the VM or delete it.

A predefined machine type is a fixed size, such as a set number of vCPUs (virtual CPU cores) with a set amount of memory. A custom machine type lets you pick the vCPU count and memory yourself within allowed limits, so you pay for the shape you need rather than a larger preset. Memory above the standard amount per core costs extra, so asking for far more memory than the work uses raises the bill.

Worked example: a nightly image-resize batch needs 6 vCPUs and 10 GB of memory. The nearest predefined size has 8 vCPUs and 32 GB. The team builds a custom type with 6 vCPUs and 10 GB and runs it as Spot. The job writes a checkpoint to Cloud Storage every 50 images. Step one: the VM is preempted at 02:14. Step two: the shutdown signal arrives and the job flushes its last checkpoint. Step three: a replacement instance starts and the job resumes from the saved checkpoint.

Common mistake: running a Spot VM as the only host for a stateful database or a user-facing service with no fallback, then treating a preemption as a rare bug. In a running system, preemption is routine, so the design must tolerate a machine disappearing with about 30 seconds of notice, usually by pairing Spot instances with a standard baseline of machines that are not reclaimed.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a log-indexing job that needs 4 vCPUs and 12 GB of memory. Their setup follows these steps. Step one: they build a custom machine type with 4 vCPUs and 12 GB, instead of a predefined size with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, so they pay only for the shape the job needs. Step two: they run that custom type as a Spot VM, which Compute Engine may reclaim at any time. Step three is missing from the plan. Step four: the job is interrupted by a reclaim at 14:40 and must finish its index on another machine. Which choice correctly fills step three?
choices: Run a small baseline of standard machines that are not reclaimed, so progress is never held only on a Spot VM that might disappear.
Keep the whole job on Spot and rely on live migration to move it to new hardware if the VM is reclaimed.
Switch the custom machine type back to a predefined size, because custom types cannot be used on Spot VMs.
Raise the memory to 32 GB so the job finishes before any preemption can happen.
questions.why: Because Spot VMs have no guaranteed runtime and get no live migration, a standard baseline of non-reclaimed machines keeps the job from depending on a single preemptible host.

questions.prompt: A fintech team's reporting service runs on a Spot VM. Which statement correctly describes what Compute Engine does before it reclaims that VM?
choices: Compute Engine sends a warning of about 30 seconds through instance metadata and the operating system shutdown signal before reclaiming a Spot VM.
Preemption happens only when the customer's own quota is exceeded, and no warning is given.
Spot VMs have a fixed 24-hour maximum runtime, after which they are reclaimed without notice.
Spot VMs are live-migrated to new hardware when reclaimed, so no warning is needed.
questions.why: The teaching text states the roughly 30-second warning arrives through metadata and the shutdown signal, and that Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime and no live migration.

questions.prompt: A team's job needs 2 vCPUs and 3 GB of memory. Which custom machine type is most likely to raise the bill without helping the job?
choices: A custom type with 2 vCPUs and 3 GB, matching the job's measured need.
A custom type with 1 vCPU and 3 GB, since the job runs on a single thread.
A custom type with 2 vCPUs and 24 GB, so the job has plenty of memory in case it grows.
A custom type with 4 vCPUs and 4 GB, one core of headroom above the need.
questions.why: Memory above the standard amount per core costs extra, so asking for 24 GB when the work uses 3 GB adds cost with no benefit.

questions.prompt: An analytics company's export job needs about 90 seconds to flush its buffer to storage once it is told to stop. It runs on a Spot VM with no standby machine. What is the main risk of this design?
choices: The export will be billed at the predefined machine rate instead of the Spot rate.
The flush may be cut short by a reclaim, since the shutdown warning is only about 30 seconds, so progress should be saved in small increments as the job runs.
Nothing, because a Spot VM keeps running until the job's flush has fully completed.
The job will be live-migrated to new hardware and the flush will finish there.
questions.why: With only about 30 seconds of warning, a flush that needs 90 seconds cannot be relied on, so the design must save state incrementally rather than at shutdown.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would put a workload on Spot VMs and when you would not. Name the main limit you must design around, and say what a custom machine type gives you and what it can cost you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use Spot VMs for work that can be interrupted and restarted, such as batch jobs, rendering, or test runs, because they cost much less than standard machines. The main limit is preemption: Google can reclaim the VM at any time, with a warning of roughly 30 seconds, and there is no live migration. So the job has to save checkpoints and resume cleanly, and a user-facing service needs a standard baseline. A custom machine type lets us choose the exact vCPU and memory we need instead of an oversized preset, which saves money. But memory beyond the standard ratio per core costs extra, so we should size memory based on measured usage.
rubricPoints: Spot VMs are cheaper because Google can preempt them with a short warning.
Interrupted work must checkpoint and resume, or it should not run on Spot.
Custom machine types let you choose vCPUs and memory to match the workload.
Extra memory beyond the standard ratio costs more, so size from measured usage.

suggested.rationale: Comparing Spot and standard prices against the cost of rework after preemption is a tradeoff a cost model can practise, though the engine is still planned.

lessons.plain: kubectl is a command-line program you type into a terminal to talk to a Kubernetes cluster. A cluster is a group of machines that runs your containerized applications, and Kubernetes is the system that schedules those applications and keeps them running. Think of kubectl as a remote control: it sends your instructions, such as list the running apps or scale one up, to the cluster's control point, and prints the reply. Before the remote can work, it must be installed on your computer and must know which cluster to point at. Installing and configuring it is the one-time setup that makes every later cluster task possible.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop has no tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster yet. Before you can list the running applications there, what two things do you guess must be true on your laptop?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. kubectl is the command-line client for a Kubernetes cluster. The cluster has a control point called the API server, which accepts requests over the network and checks who is asking. A kubeconfig file is a settings file kept on your computer, usually in a hidden folder in your home directory, that records which clusters you know about and how to log in to each. A context is a named entry in that file that bundles one cluster, one identity, and an optional default namespace, where a namespace is a labelled section inside a cluster that keeps groups of resources apart. The current context is the one every command uses unless you override it. Why it works: kubectl does no magic of its own. Each time you run a command, it reads the kubeconfig, picks the current context, presents that identity, sends the request to the chosen API server, and prints the answer. Worked example: first, install the kubectl program and confirm the client version with a version check that does not need a cluster. Second, log in to your cloud account and ask the cloud tooling to fetch credentials for a named cluster in a named region. That adds a cluster entry and a context to your kubeconfig and makes it current. Third, check the current context and confirm it names the cluster you meant. Fourth, list the nodes. A list of machines means the whole path works: program, file, identity, network, cluster. Common mistake: trusting a stale current context. If yesterday you pointed at a production cluster and today you run a delete command without checking, you act on production. In a running system, a scale-down or delete issued this way can drop live traffic within seconds, so check the context before any change and keep test and production in separate contexts. Consequence: a correctly configured kubectl only changes things when you ask it to, but a wrong context turns every later command into an action against the wrong place.

questions.prompt: Ravenna Foods keeps two clusters in the europe-west1 region: 'basket-staging' and 'basket-prod'. A new engineer follows this sequence. Step 1: install kubectl and run a client version check, which needs no cluster. Step 2: log in to the cloud account and fetch credentials for 'basket-staging' in europe-west1, which adds a cluster entry and a context and makes it current. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: list the nodes of 'basket-staging'. Which action correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Skip the check, because the client version check in Step 1 already confirmed which cluster is in use
Run the node list first, because a successful list proves the context is correct
Check the current context and confirm it names basket-staging before issuing any change
Delete the kubeconfig file so that the next command rebuilds it cleanly
questions.why: Kubectl acts on whichever context is current, so confirming that the current context names the intended cluster before any change is what prevents acting on the wrong place.

questions.prompt: A developer's laptop holds a settings file that lists three clusters and how to log in to each. What is this file called, and where is it usually kept?
choices: A namespace manifest, kept beside the kubectl program
The API server file, kept in the system temporary folder
A context file, kept in the cluster's namespace folder
A kubeconfig file, kept in a hidden folder in the home directory
questions.why: The teaching text defines the kubeconfig as the settings file on your computer, usually in a hidden home-directory folder, that records clusters and how to log in to them.

questions.prompt: An engineer's current context still points at 'ledger-prod' from last week. Today they need to scale a workload in 'ledger-test'. What should they do first?
choices: Fetch new credentials for ledger-prod so the context is refreshed
Run the scale command and then check which cluster it changed
Check the current context, and switch to the context for ledger-test before running the change
Delete the ledger-prod context so that the default is cleared
questions.why: Commands use the current context unless overridden, so the engineer must confirm the context names ledger-test before making any change, rather than trusting a stale one.

questions.prompt: An engineer runs the client version check and it succeeds. Running the node list then fails with an authentication error. Where does the problem most likely lie?
choices: In the kubectl program itself, so it should be reinstalled
In the namespace labels, which must be renamed before any list works
In the version check, which must be rerun with a different flag
Past the program: the identity or the cluster access path is failing, not the installed client
questions.why: The version check needs no cluster, so the program works; the failing step lies later in the chain of kubeconfig, identity, network and cluster, which is where authentication happens.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what installing and configuring kubectl involves, and name one risk or limit of this setup that they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Installing kubectl means getting the client program onto your machine and checking its version. Configuring it means making sure the kubeconfig file holds an entry for the cluster you want, with a context that carries your identity and points at that cluster's API server. Once that is set, kubectl reads the file on every command, picks the current context, and sends the request there. The main risk is the current context. It silently decides where commands go, so a context left over from another environment can send a delete or scale command to production. Before any change, I check the current context and the namespace. Another limit is version skew: kubectl should be within one minor version of the cluster, or some commands may behave oddly. So my setup check is simple: confirm the client version, confirm the context, and list nodes before doing anything else.
rubricPoints: Describes kubectl as a client that sends requests to the cluster's API server
Explains that kubeconfig holds clusters, identities, and contexts that kubectl reads on each command
Names the current context as the thing that decides which cluster a command targets
Identifies a concrete risk, such as acting on production through a stale context, and a check to prevent it

suggested.rationale: Installation and configuration steps and the kubeconfig vocabulary are facts and console-style procedure, and no listed mission or planned engine practises them directly.

lessons.plain: Google Kubernetes Engine, or GKE, is a service that runs your containers, which are packaged copies of an application, on a group of machines. You do not have to install or patch the system that coordinates those machines. This objective is about choosing how that group is set up when you create it. You pick a management style that decides who handles the machines, a location that decides how many places the group is spread across, and a network style that decides whether the machines can be reached from the internet. Each choice trades effort, cost, and resilience against one another, and an engineer needs to know which one fits a given job.
