lessons.guessPrompt: A team runs its web app on a container cluster where every machine sits in one data centre zone. That zone loses power for an hour. What happens to the app, and what single change to where the cluster is placed would have protected it?
lessons.teach:
A GKE cluster is a group of machines managed by Kubernetes, the open system that runs containers. The control plane is the coordinating part: it stores the desired state of the cluster and decides which container runs on which machine. The nodes are the worker machines that actually run the containers. Three choices shape a cluster when you create it. The first is the mode. Autopilot means the platform manages the nodes for you, and you pay for the CPU, memory, and storage your containers request. Standard means you choose and manage the machine groups yourself. The second is the location. A zonal cluster keeps its control plane and nodes in one zone, while a regional cluster spreads them across several zones in one region. The third is networking. A private cluster gives its nodes internal addresses only, so they cannot be reached directly from the internet. Those nodes still need a route out, usually through Cloud NAT, a service that lets private machines make outbound connections, so they can pull container images and call outside services.

Why it works: Autopilot removes machine sizing, because the platform places your containers on nodes it runs. A regional cluster survives a zone failure because copies of the control plane and nodes exist in other zones and keep serving.

Worked example: A team needs a production cluster that survives a zone outage and keeps its nodes off the public internet. Step 1: choose Autopilot so nobody sizes node groups. Step 2: choose a regional location so the cluster spans several zones. Step 3: enable private nodes so each node gets only an internal address. Step 4: confirm a Cloud NAT gateway exists in the same network so nodes can still reach external image registries. The result is a cluster that tolerates one zone failure without exposing any node to direct inbound internet traffic.

Common mistake: engineers create a private cluster and forget the outbound route. The nodes then cannot pull images, new containers never start, and the deployment appears to hang with no obvious error.

Consequence: a zonal cluster in a single zone goes dark along with that zone, so the whole application is down until the zone recovers.

questions.prompt: A games studio runs a leaderboard service that must keep answering if one zone in its region fails. The team does not want to size node groups, and it wants nodes that have no public address. Their plan has three steps. Step 1: create the cluster in Autopilot mode, so the platform manages the nodes and the team pays for the CPU, memory, and storage its containers request. Step 2: choose a regional location, so the control plane and nodes are spread across several zones in one region. Step 3: enable private nodes, so each node gets only an internal address. Step 4 is not shown yet. Which completion is the correct next step?
choices: Give every node a public IP address so the nodes can pull container images directly.
Switch the cluster to Standard mode so the team can choose its own machine groups.
Move the cluster to a single zone to reduce cost, since the leaderboard can tolerate a zone outage.
Confirm that a Cloud NAT gateway exists in the same network, so the private nodes can make outbound connections to image registries and outside services.
questions.why: A private cluster's nodes have only internal addresses, so they need a Cloud NAT gateway in the same network to make outbound calls such as pulling images, and this is the remaining step that keeps the design working.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does enabling private nodes on a GKE cluster change about the nodes?
choices: The nodes get internal addresses only, so they cannot be reached directly from the internet.
The nodes stop running containers until a Cloud NAT gateway is attached to them.
The nodes run only in one zone, which keeps their traffic inside that zone.
The nodes are managed by the team instead of the platform, so the team sizes machine groups itself.
questions.why: A private cluster gives its nodes internal addresses only, which blocks direct inbound internet access, while the nodes can still reach out through a route such as Cloud NAT.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm created a private GKE cluster with no Cloud NAT gateway in its network. Its deployment pods stay in a waiting state, and the events show no clear error. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The control plane is zonal, so the pods cannot be scheduled while one zone is busy.
The nodes have no outbound route, so they cannot pull container images and new containers never start.
Autopilot is billing the pods for too much memory, which blocks their startup.
The cluster is in Standard mode, so the platform refuses to place containers on nodes.
questions.why: Private nodes without an outbound route cannot pull images, so containers never start and the deployment appears to hang, which matches the symptom described.

questions.prompt: A data team runs a GKE Autopilot cluster with 12 containers that each request 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of memory. What does Autopilot charge for?
choices: The CPU, memory, and storage that the containers request, not the empty space on nodes the platform runs.
The number of nodes the team configures, because Autopilot requires the team to size each node.
Only the number of zones the cluster spans, since regional clusters are billed per zone.
A fixed fee for each node machine, regardless of what the containers request.
questions.why: In Autopilot the cost follows the CPU, memory, and storage that containers request, because the platform manages the nodes and the team does not size them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used GKE the difference between Autopilot and Standard mode, and the main tradeoff of making a cluster private. Name at least one limit or cost of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Autopilot is the mode where Google manages the nodes, so you do not size or patch machine groups, and you pay for the CPU, memory, and storage your containers request. The limit is less control: you cannot pick arbitrary machine setups the way you can in Standard, where you manage the node groups yourself and take on that operational work. A private cluster gives nodes only internal addresses, which reduces exposure because nothing on the internet can reach them directly. The tradeoff is that they can no longer make outbound connections on their own, so you must provide a route out such as Cloud NAT before they can pull images or call external services. Without it, new containers quietly fail to start. Regional placement adds resilience against a zone outage but costs more than a single zonal cluster, because more machines and control plane copies run.
rubricPoints: Autopilot means Google manages the nodes and billing follows requested resources, while Standard means the team manages node groups.
A regional cluster spreads the control plane and nodes across several zones so a single zone failure does not stop the cluster.
A private cluster gives nodes only internal addresses, which reduces direct internet exposure.
Private nodes need an outbound route such as Cloud NAT, or they cannot pull images or reach external services.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a mode, location, and network style is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario with competing constraints, which no current or planned hands-on mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: A container packages an application together with everything it needs to run, such as its libraries and settings, into one sealed unit that behaves the same on any machine that can run containers. Google Kubernetes Engine, called GKE, is Google's managed service for running many of these containers across a group of machines called a cluster. Deploying a containerized app means putting a built package where the cluster can reach it, telling the cluster how many copies to run, and letting it start them and replace them safely when you ship a new version. Think of it like hiring a team of identical workers from a template, with a manager who keeps the right number on shift and swaps them out without closing the shop.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs fine in a single container on your laptop. You now ask a cluster to run three copies of it, then ask for a new version to replace the old one. What do you think happens to the old copies while the new ones start, and what could go wrong for users if nothing else is set up?
lessons.teach:
An image is a frozen, versioned copy of a container's files and startup instructions. A registry is a storage service that holds images under a name and a tag, and the cluster pulls images from it. A node is a machine in the cluster that runs containers. A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that share network and storage, usually running one copy of your app. A Deployment is a Kubernetes object that declares the desired state: which image, how many pod replicas, and how updates should roll out. A Service gives a stable address and routes traffic to whichever healthy pods carry its matching label. GKE runs the cluster's control machinery and node management for you, but you still write the Deployment and Service.

Why it works: you declare what you want, and a controller keeps comparing that declaration with reality. If a pod dies, a replacement starts. When you change the image tag in the Deployment, the controller creates new pods, waits until they report ready, then removes old pods, within limits on how many may be unavailable or extra at once.

Worked example: you build shop-api version 1.4.2, push it to a registry, and apply a Deployment asking for three replicas. (1) The scheduler finds nodes with spare CPU and memory. (2) Each node pulls the image. (3) Each pod starts and passes its readiness check. (4) The Service sends requests to pods labelled app=shop-api. (5) You change the tag to 1.4.3. The controller starts one new pod, waits for it to be ready, removes one old pod, and repeats until all three run 1.4.3.

Common mistake: using the tag latest, or reusing a tag that gets overwritten, so you cannot tell what is running or return to a known version. Another frequent error is skipping the readiness check, so traffic reaches a pod that has started but cannot yet serve.

Consequence: if the new image crashes on startup and no readiness check exists, traffic may be sent to broken pods while the rollout looks healthy. With a correct check, the rollout stalls and the old pods keep serving. Pin an immutable version tag, declare readiness, and let the Deployment roll out.

questions.prompt: A ticketing team runs the image ticket-web at tag 2.0.7 in a Deployment with four replicas and a readiness check. They want to ship 2.0.8. Here is their rollout, with one step missing. (1) They build ticket-web 2.0.8 and push it to their registry under that tag. (2) They edit the Deployment so the image tag reads 2.0.8. (3) The controller creates one new pod running 2.0.8. (4) ??? (5) The controller removes one old pod running 2.0.7, then repeats until all four pods run 2.0.8. Which step fills the gap?
choices: The Service label is changed so traffic goes to the new pod before it starts.
The controller deletes an old pod right away to free capacity for the new one.
The controller waits until the new pod reports ready before removing any old pod.
The team re-tags the 2.0.8 image as latest so every node pulls it.
questions.why: The readiness check is what tells the controller a new pod can serve, so the controller only removes an old pod after the new one reports ready.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a pod in Kubernetes, as described in the GKE teaching text?
choices: A saved copy of a container's files and startup instructions kept in a registry.
One or more containers that share network and storage and usually run one copy of an app.
A machine in the cluster whose only job is to store the desired state of the cluster.
A stable network address that routes requests to healthy machines in the cluster.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a pod as the smallest schedulable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage, usually one copy of the app.

questions.prompt: A university runs its timetable app from a Deployment with no readiness check. The team pushes a new image that crashes on startup, then starts the rollout. What is the most likely result for students?
choices: The controller deletes the new pods on its own and no traffic is affected.
The registry blocks the image because it failed to start, so no pods are created.
Requests may be sent to pods that have started but cannot serve, while the rollout looks healthy.
The rollout stalls and the old pods keep serving every request.
questions.why: Without a readiness check, the controller treats started pods as usable, so broken pods can receive traffic while the rollout appears successful.

questions.prompt: A Service has the label selector app=orders-web. The cluster has three pods labelled app=orders-web, all ready, and one pod labelled app=orders-worker, also ready. Which pods can the Service send requests to?
choices: None of them until the labels are changed to match the Service name.
Only the one app=orders-worker pod, since it was the most recently started.
All four pods, because the Service routes to every pod on the same node.
The three app=orders-web pods, because the Service routes to healthy pods that carry its matching label.
questions.why: A Service routes traffic to healthy pods whose labels match its selector, so the three ready app=orders-web pods are the only valid targets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a containerized app goes from a built image to running pods on GKE, and name one limit or tradeoff of a rolling update.
lessons.modelAnswer: The image is built, tagged with a specific version, and pushed to a registry the cluster can read. A Deployment names that image and a replica count, and the cluster's controller schedules pods onto nodes, which pull the image and start the containers. A Service then routes traffic to pods that pass their readiness check. For an update, the Deployment changes the image tag and replaces pods gradually, so some capacity stays up. The tradeoff is that old and new versions run side by side during the rollout, so the app must tolerate both, and a bad image can cause a stall or slow failure that only a readiness check and monitoring will reveal. Rolling back means pointing the Deployment at the previous pinned tag.
rubricPoints: Explains image, registry, pod, and Deployment, or the path from build to running pods
Describes how a Service routes traffic only to ready pods
Names a rolling update tradeoff such as mixed versions during rollout
Mentions pinning a specific version tag so rollback is possible

suggested.rationale: The deploy-shift engine would let learners practise how gradual replacement of instances behaves during a version change, which is the core operational skill here.

lessons.plain: Serverless compute means you give a provider a small piece of code, and it runs that code only when something asks for it, without you managing any servers. An event is a short message saying that something happened, such as a file being uploaded or a message being posted to a queue. Processing events this way means your code wakes up for each event, does its job, and goes back to sleep. The hard part is not starting the code but making sure it behaves correctly when the same event shows up more than once.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo app saves each upload to a storage bucket and wants a resize function to run for every new photo, without keeping a server running all day. If the resize function fails halfway through one photo, what do you expect the platform to do with that event?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small message saying that something happened, such as a file being uploaded to a Cloud Storage bucket (a container for files) or a message being published to a Pub/Sub topic (a named channel that holds messages for subscribers). Serverless compute runs your code only when it is asked to, and you do not manage the machines underneath. Cloud Run runs containers that answer HTTP requests, and Cloud Run functions runs single functions. Either one can be the target that receives events.

There are three common ways events reach your code. A Pub/Sub subscription (a named reader attached to a topic) can push each message to an HTTPS endpoint. A Cloud Storage notification is a bucket setting that publishes an event to a Pub/Sub topic whenever an object is created or deleted. Eventarc is a managed routing service: you create a trigger that says which event source should be delivered to which Cloud Run service, and Eventarc handles the delivery.

Worked example: a bucket named photos-raw has a notification sending events to a topic called new-photos. A push subscription on that topic calls a resize service at its HTTPS address. Step 1: a user uploads cat.jpg. Step 2: the bucket publishes an object-created event. Step 3: the subscription pushes that event to the service. Step 4: the service writes a thumbnail and returns a success code. If the service returns an error or times out, the subscription sends the same message again later.

Common mistake: assuming each event arrives exactly once. Delivery is at least once, so the same event can arrive twice, and events can arrive out of order. A handler that charges a card or sends an email on every delivery will do it twice after a retry. The handler must record which event IDs it has already handled and skip repeats.

Consequence in a running system: a slow handler that times out causes redelivery, so duplicate work grows during an incident instead of shrinking. Event-driven serverless code is reliable only when each handler can safely be run more than once.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain, Crumb & Co, stores delivery receipts in a bucket named receipts-eu. Its team wants a Cloud Run service named receipt-indexer to run whenever a new receipt file is added. They create an Eventarc trigger that names receipts-eu as the event source and receipt-indexer as the target. Step 1: a driver uploads route-88.pdf to the bucket. Step 2: the bucket produces an object-created event. Step 3 is the one left blank for you to fill in. Step 4: receipt-indexer records the event ID, adds the receipt to the index, and returns a success code.
choices: The bucket sends the event straight to receipt-indexer with no routing step in between.
Eventarc delivers the object-created event to receipt-indexer because the trigger routes that source to that target.
Eventarc holds the event until an hourly batch runs, then sends all uploads together.
The driver's upload is copied into a second bucket before any service is contacted.
questions.why: An Eventarc trigger is the routing rule that tells Eventarc which event source should be delivered to which Cloud Run service, so Eventarc handles that delivery as step 3.

questions.prompt: In this course's terms, what is a Cloud Storage notification?
choices: A container that holds files and sends a message each time a file is read.
A managed service that runs single functions only when they are called.
A named reader attached to a Pub/Sub topic that pushes each message to an HTTPS address.
A bucket setting that publishes an event to a Pub/Sub topic when an object is created or deleted.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a Cloud Storage notification as a bucket setting that publishes an event to a Pub/Sub topic when an object is created or deleted.

questions.prompt: A Pub/Sub push subscription calls a Cloud Run service that sends invoice emails. During a traffic spike the handler takes 40 seconds, exceeds the timeout, and the subscription retries. What is the most accurate description of the result and the fix?
choices: The timeout makes the subscription drop the message permanently, so only one email is ever sent.
Redelivery sends the same message again, so duplicate emails can grow during the incident; the handler should record handled event IDs and skip repeats.
Events arrive in order, so the handler only needs to remember the newest timestamp it has seen.
Pub/Sub guarantees exactly-once delivery, so the retries cannot produce duplicate emails.
questions.why: A slow handler that times out causes redelivery, and because delivery is at least once the handler must be safe to run more than once by recording processed event IDs.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot sends a restock event to a Cloud Run service through a Pub/Sub subscription. The service adds 20 units to a shelf count on every delivery. A duplicate delivery occurs. Which change is correct?
choices: Add a longer retry delay so that duplicates never happen.
Record each handled event ID and skip any event whose ID is already recorded before adding units.
Ignore duplicates, because the first addition is the only one that matters.
Have the subscription push to a second endpoint so each event is handled twice on purpose.
questions.why: Delivery is at least once, so the handler must check its record of event IDs and skip repeats rather than assume each event arrives only once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an upload to a storage bucket can trigger a serverless function, and name one limit or tradeoff of this design that they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a file lands in a bucket, the bucket publishes an event to a Pub/Sub topic, or Eventarc routes that event to a Cloud Run service. The service starts only for those events, so we pay per use and do not run servers all day. The main tradeoff is delivery semantics: events are delivered at least once, so the same event can arrive twice and can arrive out of order. That means the handler must be idempotent, which means it can run again on the same event without doing the work twice, for example by recording processed event IDs. We also have to watch timeouts, because a slow handler causes redelivery and extra load during a spike. Without these safeguards, a retry could duplicate a charge or a notification.
rubricPoints: Describes the path from a bucket or source event through a topic or Eventarc trigger to a serverless target
States that events are delivered at least once, so duplicates and reordering can happen
Explains that the handler must be idempotent, for example by tracking processed event IDs
Names a tradeoff such as timeouts causing redelivery or cost and load spikes under bursts

suggested.rationale: The mission makes the learner write an event handler that stays correct when the same event is delivered more than once, which is the central risk of this objective.

lessons.plain: A GPU and a TPU are two kinds of chips built to do huge amounts of arithmetic at the same time, which is the heavy lifting behind machine learning. Think of an ordinary processor as one skilled chef, and these chips as large kitchens where many cooks handle many simple steps together. A GPU, short for graphics processing unit, began in video and is flexible enough for many kinds of parallel work. A TPU, short for tensor processing unit, is Google's own chip designed mainly for the matrix maths that neural networks rely on. Choosing between them comes down to how well your work fits the chip and how tied you are willing to be to a particular software style.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team trains a neural network and already has custom code written specifically for GPU programming. Would you lean toward a GPU or a TPU for training, and what would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach: An accelerator is a specialized chip that does one kind of work much faster than a general-purpose processor. Two families matter here. A GPU, or graphics processing unit, runs thousands of small calculations in parallel and is programmed through general tools, so it accepts many kinds of code and many frameworks. A TPU, or tensor processing unit, is an application-specific chip that Google designed around the large matrix multiplications at the heart of neural networks. A framework is the library, such as PyTorch, TensorFlow or JAX, that a team uses to write its model. TPUs get their speed from a compiler called XLA, which converts the framework's computation into the chip's own instructions, so the model must be written in a form that compiler accepts. A TPU is very efficient when the work is large, regular, and made of matrix operations with fixed input shapes, because every change in tensor shape can trigger a fresh compilation that costs time. A GPU tolerates irregular work and code written against GPU-specific libraries, which is why custom low-level kernels often stay on GPUs. Worked example: a team trains a recommendation model in JAX. Step one, the model is mostly large matrix multiplications with fixed batch sizes, and JAX supports TPUs through XLA. Step two, the team checks for custom GPU-only kernels and finds none. Step three, they check whether the chip is available in the region they need and what it costs per training hour. Step four, they choose a TPU for training and keep the code portable enough to fall back to GPUs. Common mistake: treating a TPU as a faster GPU you can swap in unchanged. Code that depends on GPU-only libraries will fail on a TPU, and dynamic shapes cause repeated recompilation. In a running system this appears as a training job that stalls at startup, or an inference service whose latency spikes each time a new input size arrives. Whichever chip you choose, the host machine that feeds it data must also be sized to keep the accelerator busy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company trains a demand-forecasting network in PyTorch. Every training batch has exactly 128 sequences, each padded to 96 time steps, and the model uses only standard matrix operations. The team converts the model so the XLA compiler can accept it. The team's work so far: Step 1, the workload is large, regular matrix work with fixed shapes, which suits a TPU. Step 2, they search for custom GPU-only kernels and find none. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, they choose a TPU for training and keep the code portable enough to run on GPUs if needed. Which action best fills Step 3?
choices: Rewrite the batch so its size changes every step, letting the compiler adapt on the fly
Check that TPUs are offered in the region where the training data is stored, and compare the per-hour cost against the GPU option
Convert the whole training loop to a GPU-only library so it can run on any accelerator
Buy the accelerator with the most parallel units, since cost does not matter for training speed
questions.why: Step 3 in the method is checking regional availability and the per-training-hour cost, which is the practical check before committing to a chip.

questions.prompt: A team's PyTorch model runs on a TPU only after its computation is passed through XLA. What is XLA's job?
choices: It converts the framework's computation into the chip's own instructions
It picks the cheapest region for each training job
It measures how much memory the host machine has free
It stores the training dataset physically close to the chip
questions.why: XLA is the compiler that translates the framework's computation into the instructions the TPU runs, which is why the model must be written in a form it accepts.

questions.prompt: A team wrote custom kernels against a GPU-only library and wants to run the same training job on a TPU without changing the code. What is the most likely result?
choices: It speeds up automatically, because TPUs are simply faster GPUs
It fails, because GPU-only library code cannot run on a TPU
Nothing changes, because the compiler ignores library calls
It runs unchanged but costs more per hour
questions.why: Code that depends on GPU-only libraries will not run on a TPU, so a TPU is not a drop-in replacement for a GPU.

questions.prompt: An inference service on a TPU receives requests with different input lengths. Each time a new length arrives, latency spikes. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The model has too many layers for a TPU, so remove layers
The GPU driver is outdated, so move the service to a GPU
The data bucket is in the wrong region, so move the bucket
Varying input shapes force repeated recompilation, so use fixed input shapes
questions.why: Changes in tensor shape trigger fresh compilation on a TPU, and fixed input shapes avoid the repeated compile cost that causes the spikes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a GPU and a TPU for a new training job. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the code is written in and whether it depends on anything GPU-specific. If the model uses a framework that compiles through XLA, such as JAX or TensorFlow on TPU-supported paths, and the work is mostly large matrix operations with stable input shapes, a TPU is a strong candidate and can be efficient for training. If the team has custom GPU kernels or needs many different framework and library combinations, a GPU is the safer fit. The tradeoff with a TPU is portability: code tuned for it may need changes to run elsewhere, and changing input shapes can cause slow recompilation. The tradeoff with a GPU is that you may pay more per unit of matrix work for very large, regular training runs. I would also check regional availability and the cost of the host machine, because the accelerator is only part of the total cost.
rubricPoints: A GPU is a flexible parallel processor that supports many frameworks and custom low-level code.
A TPU is a specialized chip built for matrix-heavy neural network work, usually through a compiler such as XLA.
Choosing a TPU depends on framework compatibility, stable input shapes, and the absence of GPU-only code.
Tradeoffs include portability, recompilation cost, regional availability, and total cost including the host machine.

suggested.rationale: A scenario asking which accelerator fits a given model and codebase adds the most, because the decision depends on weighing several workload features at once.

lessons.plain: Google Cloud offers several managed databases and data services, each built for a different shape of data and way of using it. Choosing one is like choosing a vehicle: a van, a freight train and a bicycle all move things, but each suits different loads, distances and speeds. Some products store rows that must stay consistent, some answer huge analytical questions over years of data, some pass messages between systems, and some keep data in memory for speed. Your job is to read the workload's shape (how much data, how it is read and written, how fast, and where users are) and pick the product that fits, rather than the most familiar one. This lesson walks through that reasoning.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app stores customer orders and must never show a half-finished order, and it also needs a nightly report that scans five years of sales. Would one database be the right fit for both jobs, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Start with four questions about the workload: what shape the data has (linked rows, flexible documents, huge key-value records, or a stream of events), how it is accessed (many small reads and writes, or a few large scans), how much consistency and scale it needs, and whether it serves a live application or analysis. Then map the answers to products.

Cloud SQL is a managed relational database for MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Relational means data sits in tables linked by keys and changed in transactions, where a group of writes either all happen or none do. Google handles patching and backups while you keep familiar SQL. AlloyDB is a PostgreSQL-compatible database built for heavier transactional and analytical mixes. Spanner is a relational database that spreads data across many machines and regions while keeping strong consistency, meaning every reader sees the same committed state. BigQuery is a serverless analytics warehouse: you run SQL over very large datasets and pay for queries and storage, not servers. Firestore is a document database for app data with flexible fields. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store for very high throughput and fast lookups by key, such as time series. Memorystore is a managed in-memory cache for hot data that must be read in under a millisecond. Pub/Sub is managed messaging: publishers send messages to a topic and subscribers receive them asynchronously. Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs Kafka, a streaming log, for teams already using Kafka. Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines that transform streams or batches of data.

Worked example: an order system needs transactions across order and payment rows, about 2 TB of data, in one region. Step 1: it needs transactions, so choose a relational product. Step 2: the size and single region fit Cloud SQL. Step 3: if it later must write consistently across continents, Spanner becomes the candidate. Step 4: the nightly sales report scans years of history, which is analytics, so export the data to BigQuery instead of running the report on the order database.

Common mistake: choosing the product you know best, such as running heavy analytics on the transactional database. In a running system, the report's large scans compete with live checkout writes, causing slow pages and timeouts at peak hours. Pub/Sub or Kafka can sit between the order service and downstream consumers so each consumer works at its own pace.

Pick by workload shape first, and the product name follows from it.

questions.prompt: A parking-garage operator collects sensor pings from 40,000 gates across the country. Pings must be accepted even when a downstream system is slow, so each ping goes into a messaging topic first. Step 1: the pings need a buffer that absorbs bursts and lets other systems read at their own pace, so use Pub/Sub. Step 2: the pings must be cleaned and counted per gate in a continuous pipeline, so run Dataflow. Step 3: (missing) choose the product that stores the cleaned counts for month-long trend reports that analysts run with SQL. Step 4: the live gate-status screen needs sub-millisecond lookups of each gate's current state, so Memorystore holds that hot copy. What belongs in step 3?
choices: BigQuery, because analysts run SQL over months of history and pay for queries rather than servers
Memorystore, because it keeps the counts in memory
Firestore, because each gate's counts are flexible documents
Cloud SQL, because the counts are relational rows that need transactions
questions.why: Month-long analytical scans over large history are the warehouse workload that BigQuery serves, while the other options fit live lookups, transactional rows, or flexible app documents rather than analysis.

questions.prompt: A payroll startup with about 200 GB of employees, pay runs and tax rows, all in one region, needs each pay run to either fully commit or fully roll back. Which product fits best?
choices: Cloud SQL, because it is a managed relational database with transactions across linked tables
BigQuery, because it stores large volumes cheaply
Bigtable, because it handles very high write throughput by key
Pub/Sub, because pay runs arrive as messages
questions.why: Linked tables changed in all-or-nothing transactions at this size in one region match a managed relational database, which Cloud SQL provides.

questions.prompt: A team runs a nightly marketing report that scans three years of click history on the same database that handles live checkout writes. At peak hours checkout pages time out. What is the most sound change?
choices: Move the checkout writes into Memorystore so they are cached
Switch the checkout database to Bigtable to speed up scans
Export the click history to BigQuery and run the report there, keeping checkout on the transactional database
Add more checkout web servers so requests are spread wider
questions.why: The timeouts come from large analytical scans competing with live writes, so moving the analysis to BigQuery separates the two workloads.

questions.prompt: A mobile game must look up each player's current session data in under a millisecond, and this data is read far more often than it is written. Which product fits this access pattern?
choices: Spanner, because it offers strong consistency across regions
Memorystore, because it is a managed in-memory cache for hot data read in under a millisecond
Dataflow, because it transforms data as it is read
AlloyDB, because it is a PostgreSQL-compatible database
questions.why: Sub-millisecond reads of hot data are the purpose of an in-memory cache, which is what Memorystore provides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Cloud SQL, Spanner and BigQuery for a new service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking whether the data serves live transactions in the application or analysis by people. If it is live transactions with rows linked by relationships, I would pick Cloud SQL for a single region of moderate size, because it is a managed relational database with familiar SQL and transactions. The tradeoff is that it scales a single primary instance rather than spreading writes across regions, so write throughput and geographic reach have a ceiling. If the requirement later becomes globally consistent writes at large scale, Spanner is the step up, but it costs more and adds design complexity. BigQuery is not the live store; it answers analytical questions over large history, so I would export data to it rather than run reports on the order database. My first pick is Cloud SQL, and I would state clearly that its limit is single-region scale.
rubricPoints: Start from the workload's shape: transactional, analytical, document, wide key-value, stream, or cache.
Cloud SQL or AlloyDB fits relational transactions at moderate scale using familiar SQL.
Spanner fits relational data needing strong consistency across regions and horizontal scale.
BigQuery is for analytics over large datasets, not live transactional traffic.
Name a real tradeoff, such as Spanner's higher cost and complexity or Cloud SQL's single-region scaling limit.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a product from a described workload is an exam-style reasoning task, so a short situation to reason through teaches it better than a list of facts.

lessons.plain: Cloud Storage keeps files as objects inside containers called buckets. Each bucket, or each object, has a storage class, which is a setting that trades storage price against access cost. Think of an office filing system: papers you pull out every day stay at your desk, while old records go to a basement archive where they cost less to keep but take a trip and a fee to fetch. Choosing a class means accepting a lower monthly storage cost in exchange for minimum storage periods and retrieval charges. The four classes are Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive, ordered from data you touch most often to data you almost never touch.
lessons.guessPrompt: If the cheapest storage class charges the least per month to hold a file, why might it still be a poor choice for files you open a few times a year? Name one reason you would guess.
lessons.teach:
An object is one stored file plus its metadata, and a bucket is the named container that holds objects. A storage class is the pricing and access tier set for a bucket or an object. Standard has the highest monthly storage price and no minimum storage period or retrieval fee. Nearline, Coldline, and Archive each have a lower monthly storage price, but they add two costs: a minimum storage duration (the shortest period you are billed for, even if you delete the object sooner) and a retrieval fee charged per gigabyte you read. The minimum durations are 30 days for Nearline, 90 days for Coldline, and 365 days for Archive. Deleting early triggers an early deletion charge covering the rest of the minimum period.

Why it works: the provider prices holding data and reading data separately, so a cheap-to-keep class is expensive to read. Worked example: you store 2,000 GB of old backups in Archive and delete them after 100 days. The minimum is 365 days, so you are billed for the remaining 265 days of storage as an early deletion charge, even though the data is gone. Had the same backups sat in Standard, there would be no minimum, but the monthly storage price would be higher.

Common mistake: putting data that is read every week into Coldline because its storage price looks low. Retrieval fees for repeated reads can exceed the savings, and the bill arrives as a surprise. Consequence in a running system: a nightly job that scans archived logs turns a cheap storage line into a large access charge. Lifecycle rules can move objects to colder classes automatically as they age, so the class follows the actual access pattern.

questions.prompt: A media company uploads 800 GB of raw event recordings into a Coldline bucket on day 0 and deletes every object on day 60. Coldline has a 90-day minimum storage duration. Step 1: identify the minimum for Coldline, which is 90 days. Step 2: count how many days the recordings were actually stored before deletion, which is 60 days. Missing step: work out how many days of storage the company is still billed for as an early deletion charge.
choices: 90 days, the full minimum, because any early deletion bills the whole minimum period
30 days, the minimum minus the days already stored
0 days, because deleted objects are not billed after removal
60 days, the time the recordings were actually stored before deletion
questions.why: The early deletion charge covers the rest of the minimum period, so 90 minus 60 leaves 30 days billed, which is the remaining part of the minimum.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps medical imaging files that its staff open several times a week. Which Cloud Storage class has no minimum storage duration and no retrieval fee?
choices: Standard
Nearline
Coldline
Archive
questions.why: Standard is the class with the highest monthly storage price but no minimum storage period and no per-gigabyte retrieval fee, which suits frequently read data.

questions.prompt: A records office stores 1,200 GB of compliance documents in an Archive bucket and deletes them after 200 days. How many days of early deletion charge apply?
choices: 365 days, the full Archive minimum
200 days, the time the documents were stored
0 days, because the data was deleted before any charge applies
165 days, the Archive minimum minus the 200 days already stored
questions.why: Archive has a 365-day minimum, so 365 minus 200 leaves 165 days billed as an early deletion charge even though the documents are gone.

questions.prompt: A reporting team reads 300 GB of data stored in Nearline every day to build dashboards. They chose Nearline because its storage price is lower than Standard. What is the main risk to the bill?
choices: Nearline charges a higher monthly storage price than Standard for any daily reads
Nearline has no retrieval fee, so the daily reads are free
Retrieval fees on every daily read can add up to more than the storage saving
Nearline deletes objects that are read too often
questions.why: Nearline is cheap to keep but charges a retrieval fee per gigabyte read, so frequent daily reads can cost more than Standard would have.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why choosing the cheapest Cloud Storage class for a bucket of rarely read files is not always the lowest total cost. Name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: The cheapest class per month is Archive, but it charges retrieval fees and has a 365-day minimum storage period. If we delete an object earlier, we still pay for the rest of that minimum, which is an early deletion charge. So for data we might delete within a year or read more than occasionally, Archive can cost more than Standard. Standard has a higher monthly storage price but no minimum period and no retrieval fee, so it suits data we read often or may remove soon. Nearline and Coldline sit in between, with shorter minimums and smaller retrieval fees. My rule is to match the class to how often we expect to read the data and how long we will keep it, then add lifecycle rules so objects move to colder classes as their access drops. I would check the expected reads and retention before choosing.
rubricPoints: Explains that colder classes have lower storage prices but add retrieval fees
Names the minimum storage durations and what early deletion costs
Connects the class choice to expected access frequency and retention time
Mentions that lifecycle rules can move data between classes as it ages

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a set of facts and pricing rules about classes, which is best learned by reading and comparing the four tiers.

lessons.plain: Getting data into the cloud means copying files or records from where they live now into cloud storage, where other services can read them. There are three common routes. You can push files yourself from a terminal, which suits a few files you control. You can point a data service at files already sitting in a storage bucket, which is a named container for files, so the service reads them directly. For large or recurring copies from other places, such as another cloud or a local file server, a managed copy service can run the job on a schedule and retry what fails. The right route depends on how much data there is, where it starts, and whether the copy happens once or repeatedly.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to move 40 terabytes of log archives from a data center file server into a cloud storage bucket, then repeat the copy every night. Would you run a copy command from your laptop each night, or use a service built for scheduled bulk transfers? Why?
lessons.teach: A bucket is a named container in Cloud Storage, Google's object storage, where each file is stored as an object. A command-line upload is a copy you start yourself from a terminal, using the gcloud command-line tool. Storage Transfer Service is a managed service that copies data in bulk from a source such as another bucket, another cloud, or an on-premises server into a bucket, once or on a repeating schedule, and retries files that fail.  Why these routes exist: a copy is limited by the machine and connection doing it. A laptop uploading tens of terabytes is slow, fragile, and tied to your session. A managed service runs close to the data, works on many files in parallel, skips what already arrived, and keeps going after temporary errors. Loading from Cloud Storage is different: some data services can read files already in a bucket, so the data is loaded where it sits without a separate copy step.  Worked example: a team has 300 GB of CSV exports on a local server and must refresh them weekly. Step one, the files sit on a server the team controls and the job repeats, so a one-off laptop upload is the wrong fit. Step two, a transfer job is set up with the local server as source, the bucket as destination, and a weekly schedule. Step three, the first run copies everything, later runs copy only changed files, and failed files are retried. Step four, the analytics service loads the bucket contents directly from storage.  Common mistake: treating every copy as a manual upload, then finding that a nightly script silently stopped when a laptop went to sleep. Another is assuming a copy finished because the command started; check object counts and sizes at the destination.  Consequence: a partial load that looks complete can feed wrong totals into reports, so verify counts and sizes after every bulk load. The route changes who does the work and how reliably it finishes, not the stored object itself.

questions.prompt: A small architecture studio has 8 TB of project renders on a file server in its own office and needs a one-time copy into a Cloud Storage bucket for archiving. Step 1: the source is a server the studio controls, and the copy is large and bulk, so a laptop upload is the wrong fit and Storage Transfer Service is the right route. Step 2: a one-time transfer job is created with the office server as source and the archive bucket as destination. Step 3 is missing and is what you must supply. Step 4: before the archive is marked complete, the team compares object counts and total sizes at the destination against the source. What belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: Let the transfer job run until it reports finished, since it retries files that failed along the way.
Convert every render to a different file format before the job copies it, so the archive is consistent.
Start a second manual gcloud upload of the same folders in parallel to make the copy faster.
Delete the source renders as soon as the job starts so the office server frees disk space.
questions.why: The managed job retries failed files on its own, so the correct missing step is to let it run to a finished state before checking the destination.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a bucket in Cloud Storage?
choices: A scheduled job that copies files from one cloud to another and retries failures.
A command-line tool that starts an upload from a terminal session.
A named container in which each file is stored as an object.
A query service that reads data directly from files without copying them.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a bucket as a named container in Cloud Storage where each file is stored as an object.

questions.prompt: A retail chain keeps 40 TB of product images in a bucket on another cloud and wants a copy in a Google Cloud bucket refreshed every week, skipping files that have not changed. Which route fits best?
choices: Loading the images directly into a data analytics service without copying them.
Storage Transfer Service with the other cloud's bucket as source and a weekly schedule.
A gcloud upload typed by hand each Monday from an engineer's workstation.
A single gcloud upload run once and left to repeat on the workstation's own schedule.
questions.why: Storage Transfer Service copies bulk data from another cloud on a repeating schedule, and later runs copy only changed files, which matches the weekly refresh need.

questions.prompt: An engineer uploads 2 TB from a laptop with a gcloud copy command. The terminal returns to the prompt, and the engineer reports the load as complete without checking anything else. What is the main flaw?
choices: Command-line uploads cannot be used for any amount of data above one terabyte.
The upload should have been done through an analytics service instead of a bucket.
The command returning does not prove the copy finished, so object counts and sizes at the destination should be checked.
The bucket should have been created in a different region before any copy started.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a copy can look finished when the command starts or returns, so counts and sizes at the destination must be verified after a bulk load.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a command-line upload, loading from Cloud Storage, and Storage Transfer Service for a new data set. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with two questions: where the data is now, and whether the copy happens once or repeats. If it is a handful of files on my own machine, a command-line upload is fine and quick to check. If the files are already in a bucket and the target service reads storage directly, I would not copy them again; I would point the service at the bucket. If the data sits on another cloud or a local server, or the copy must run every night, I would use Storage Transfer Service, because it runs the job, retries failed files, and moves only changes after the first run. The tradeoff to flag is that a managed transfer needs setup and permissions, which is overkill for one small file. After any bulk load I would also check object counts and sizes at the destination, because a job reporting progress is not the same as a complete copy.
rubricPoints: Choose the route based on where the data starts and whether the copy repeats.
A command-line upload suits small, one-off copies that a person runs and checks.
Loading from Cloud Storage reads files already in a bucket without copying them again.
Storage Transfer Service handles large, scheduled, or cross-source copies with retries, but needs setup and permissions.

suggested.rationale: Picking the right load route from a described situation is reasoning under constraints, which an exam-style scenario practises better than reading a list.

lessons.plain: Multi-region redundancy means keeping copies of your data in more than one geographic region, so that if one region has an outage, the data still exists somewhere else and the service can keep working. Think of keeping the master copy of a recipe book in two kitchens across town rather than one: a fire in one kitchen does not destroy the recipes. For data solutions this is a set of choices: where the copies live, how fresh they must be, and how quickly you can switch to a copy when the main site fails. Redundancy is not the same as backup. Copies also repeat mistakes, so an accidental delete can spread to every copy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an order database lives in only one region, and that region loses power for a full day. What happens to the stored orders and to the customers trying to use the app, and what single change would reduce that damage?
lessons.teach:
A region is a large geographic area that contains several zones, which are independent data centers. A replica is a copy of data kept on another machine or in another location. Replication is the ongoing process of sending writes from the primary copy to replicas. Synchronous replication waits until the replica confirms a write before the write counts as done, so the replica is never behind, but every write is slower because it waits across distance. Asynchronous replication confirms the write locally and sends it to the replica afterward, which is faster but means the replica can lag. Two terms describe the gap you accept. Recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service can be down. Multi-region setups spread copies across a wide area, and dual-region setups use two named regions.

Worked example: an orders database has a primary in region A and an asynchronous replica in region B. The replica usually lags by about 20 seconds. Region A fails at 10:00:00. The last write the replica received was at 09:59:40, so 20 seconds of orders are missing. Staff promote region B, which takes about 5 minutes. The RPO achieved is 20 seconds and the RTO is 5 minutes.

Common mistake: assuming that multi-region copies protect against deletion or corruption. A delete or bad write is replicated to every region, so you still need backups with point-in-time recovery.

In a running system, the choice of replication mode sets the data you can lose and the downtime you can tolerate. Multi-region redundancy only helps when the team has tested the failover path.

questions.prompt: A freight company keeps shipment tracking records in a primary copy in region europe-west1. An asynchronous replica in europe-north1 usually lags by 45 seconds. At 14:20:00 the primary becomes unreachable. The last write the replica received is stamped 14:19:15. Staff then promote the replica, which takes 12 minutes. Work through it. Step 1: the failure time is 14:20:00. Step 2: the last write the replica received is 14:19:15. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the recovery time is the 12-minute promotion. Which choice correctly fills step 3 and gives the recovery point objective (RPO) achieved?
choices: Add the 12-minute promotion time to the 45-second lag to get the RPO.
Treat the typical 45-second lag as the recovery time, because lag and downtime are the same measure.
Subtract 14:19:15 from 14:20:00 to get 45 seconds of lost writes, which is the RPO.
Compare 12 minutes with 45 seconds and take the larger number as the RPO.
questions.why: The RPO is the amount of recent data lost, which is the gap between the failure time and the last write that reached the replica: 14:20:00 minus 14:19:15 is 45 seconds.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which replication mode guarantees the replica is never behind the primary, at the cost of slower writes?
choices: Multi-region replication, because copies are spread over a wide area.
Backup replication, because a separate snapshot is taken each night.
Synchronous replication, because each write waits for the replica to confirm it.
Asynchronous replication, because it confirms writes locally first.
questions.why: Synchronous replication holds each write until the replica confirms it, so the replica cannot lag, but every write takes longer.

questions.prompt: A retail app uses an asynchronous replica in another region. The replica typically trails the primary by 8 seconds. The primary fails during a busy checkout period. Which statement best describes the data at risk?
choices: The full day's orders are at risk, because the replica only syncs at midnight.
The orders are at risk only if the promotion of the replica takes longer than 8 seconds.
No orders are at risk, because asynchronous replicas always hold every write.
Roughly the last 8 seconds of writes may be missing from the replica, which sets the recovery point objective.
questions.why: With asynchronous replication the replica can lag, so writes from the last few seconds before the failure may never have reached it, and that lag is the data you accept losing.

questions.prompt: A team runs a multi-region database with synchronous replication. A developer accidentally deletes a production table. What happens after the team fails over to the other region?
choices: The table is still missing in the new region, because the delete was replicated like any other write, so backups with point-in-time recovery are needed.
The table is restored automatically, because the second region holds a separate older copy.
The table is restored, because failover always rolls the data back to the last backup.
The table reappears after the replica catches up, because replicas undo deletes they did not receive.
questions.why: Replication copies every write, including a delete or a bad write, to every region, so multi-region copies do not protect against deletion or corruption and you still need backups with point-in-time recovery.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why keeping data in two regions does not automatically mean we are safe during a regional outage. Name one tradeoff of choosing synchronous over asynchronous replication across regions.
lessons.modelAnswer: Having two copies only helps if the second copy is current and we can switch to it quickly. If replication is asynchronous, the replica can be seconds or minutes behind, so a sudden regional failure loses the most recent writes. Promoting the replica also takes time, and someone has to decide to do it, and the application must point at the new location. A bad delete or corrupted write would be copied to both regions, so the copies do not protect against that. Synchronous replication closes the freshness gap, but every write must wait for the remote region to confirm, which adds latency to each request and can make writes fail if the link between regions is slow or down. So the choice is between slower writes and possible data loss. We should set RPO and RTO targets first, then choose the replication mode and test the failover.
rubricPoints: Redundant copies only help if they are current and reachable when the primary fails.
Asynchronous replication can lose the most recent writes, which is the RPO gap.
Synchronous replication adds write latency across regions and can block writes when the link is slow.
Multi-region copies do not protect against deletes or corruption, which need backups.

suggested.rationale: The dr-planner engine would let the learner work through RPO, RTO and failover choices for a specific workload, which is the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A cloud network is a private space where your servers talk to each other using private addresses. In Google Cloud that space is called a VPC network. Inside it you carve out smaller address ranges called subnets, each tied to one region. You can let the cloud create those subnets for you, or choose every range yourself, which is custom mode. Sometimes one team owns the network and shares it with other teams' projects, which is Shared VPC. Sometimes two separate networks need to reach each other directly, which is peering. This lesson covers how to choose among these three setups.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two teams each run a separate app in their own cloud project, and both need their servers to talk over private addresses without going over the public internet. Before reading on, what would you need to check about the address ranges each team uses, and why?
lessons.teach: A VPC network (virtual private cloud, a private software network inside the cloud provider) is the container for your private addresses. A VPC network is global, but the subnets inside it are regional: each subnet is one block of IP addresses, written like 10.10.0.0/20, that lives in one region. In auto mode, the platform creates one subnet in every region using ranges it picks. In custom mode, no subnets appear until you create them, and you choose each region and range. Custom mode is the usual choice when addresses must fit an existing plan or avoid clashing with other networks. Auto mode can be converted to custom later, but custom cannot go back to auto. Shared VPC lets a host project own one network while service projects create resources in its subnets. A central networking team keeps control of routes and firewalls while application teams deploy into those shared subnets. Peering is different: two separate VPC networks, possibly owned by different projects or organizations, exchange routes so their private addresses can reach each other. Peering is not transitive, so if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Worked example: network A has subnet 10.10.0.0/20. A partner's network B has subnet 10.10.0.0/16. Step 1: you request a peering. Step 2: the platform compares the ranges. They overlap inside 10.10, so the peering cannot route correctly until one side is re-addressed. Common mistake: treating peering as a shortcut that connects every network to every other network. The consequence is that a planned chain of peerings fails, and an application in one network times out reaching a service two hops away while no firewall rule is at fault. Choose the model by asking who owns the network, whether the address ranges must align, and whether traffic must pass through another network.

questions.prompt: Network M belongs to a payments team and has one subnet, 192.168.20.0/24. Network N belongs to a reporting team and has one subnet, 192.168.21.0/24. Network N also peers with network R, which has subnet 10.50.0.0/16. The payments team wants M to reach R. Step 1: the payments team requests a peering between M and N. Step 2: the platform compares the ranges, finds that 192.168.20.0/24 and 192.168.21.0/24 do not overlap, and the M-N peering becomes active. Step 3: M and N exchange routes. Step 4 is missing: the platform decides whether M can reach R through N. Which completion of Step 4 is correct?
choices: Yes, but only after the address check is repeated for R, which blocks the traffic.
Yes, because N already holds a route to R, so traffic from M passes through N to R.
Yes, automatically, because every peered network shares all of its routes with the others.
No, peering is not transitive, so M needs a direct link to R or another model.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so a route that exists between M and N and between N and R does not give M a path to R through N.

questions.prompt: A team creates a network in custom mode. Which statement about its subnets is correct?
choices: The platform creates one subnet in every region automatically, using ranges it selects.
No subnets exist until the team creates them, choosing each region and address range.
The network can later be switched back to auto mode at any time without losing subnets.
Subnets are created as soon as the first virtual machine is deployed to the network.
questions.why: In custom mode no subnets appear until you create them, and you pick each region and range; the reverse switch to auto is not possible.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses Shared VPC. Its host project owns the network, and an application team's service project deploys virtual machines into a subnet of that network. Who keeps control of the firewall rules and routes for that subnet?
choices: Nobody, because firewall rules are removed when a service project joins.
Each service project separately, through its own copy of the network.
The central networking team that manages the host project.
The application team, because its project hosts the virtual machines.
questions.why: In Shared VPC the host project's central networking team keeps control of routes and firewalls while service projects deploy into the shared subnets.

questions.prompt: Network Q has subnet 172.31.0.0/18 and network S has subnet 172.31.32.0/19. An engineer requests a peering between Q and S, and the peering cannot route correctly. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Their address ranges overlap inside 172.31.32 to 172.31.63, so one side must be re-addressed.
A firewall rule on one network is blocking the peering request.
Both networks must be in auto mode before peering is allowed.
Shared VPC must be enabled first, because peering only works inside one organisation.
questions.why: The two ranges share addresses from 172.31.32.0 to 172.31.63.255, so routes would conflict and one network must change its addressing before peering routes correctly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a custom-mode VPC, Shared VPC, and VPC Network Peering for a company with two business units. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking who owns the network and whether both sides need one shared network or two. If one platform team should control routing and firewalls while several app projects deploy into it, I would use Shared VPC, where one host project holds the network and the service projects attach to it. If the two business units already run separate networks and only need private connectivity, I would use peering, because each network stays independently managed. I would create networks in custom mode so I choose the ranges myself, and I would confirm that no subnet ranges overlap before peering, since overlapping ranges cannot route. The tradeoff with peering is that it is not transitive: if unit A must reach unit C through unit B, that path needs its own peering or a different design. The tradeoff with Shared VPC is that the central team becomes a dependency for network changes.
rubricPoints: Custom mode lets you choose each subnet's region and address range, while auto mode creates predefined subnets.
Shared VPC places one network in a host project that service projects use, with central control of networking.
VPC Network Peering connects two separate networks so private addresses route between them.
Peered networks must not have overlapping subnet ranges.
Peering is not transitive, so traffic does not pass through a middle network to reach a third.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner follow traffic across subnets, shared networks, and peerings, which is the hands-on skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network traffic may reach a machine and which may leave it. On Google Cloud you write rules that say: when traffic of this kind comes from here and is headed for these machines on this port, allow it or block it. VPC firewall rules apply inside your virtual network, and Cloud NGFW policies are a newer way to group similar rules so they can be shared across many projects. This lesson explains the parts every rule is made of, so you can read one and predict what it will do before it touches a real server.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server should accept visitors on port 443 from anywhere, but it should refuse SSH on port 22 from anywhere. If you wrote two rules for that, what would each one need to say, and which one would you expect to be checked first if both matched the same connection?
lessons.teach:
A firewall rule is a single statement made of a direction, a priority, an action, a source or destination, a set of targets, and a protocol with optional ports. Direction says whether the rule judges traffic coming into a machine (ingress) or leaving it (egress). Action is either allow or deny. Priority is a number from 0 to 65535, and a lower number is checked first. The first rule that matches decides the outcome. Source (for ingress) and destination (for egress) are IP address ranges, network tags, or service accounts that describe the other end of the connection. Targets are the machines the rule applies to: all instances in the network, instances carrying a given network tag, or instances running as a given service account. Protocol is tcp, udp, icmp, or all, and ports narrow tcp and udp to specific numbers. Every network also has implied rules at the lowest priority: deny inbound, allow outbound.

Why it works: rules are checked where traffic meets the machine, and they are stateful. When a connection is allowed in, the replies are allowed back out without a separate rule.

Worked example: rule A has priority 500, action deny, direction ingress, source 0.0.0.0/0, target tag web, protocol tcp, port 22. Rule B has priority 1000, action allow, direction ingress, source 0.0.0.0/0, target tag web, protocol tcp, port 443. A visitor connects to a web-tagged VM on port 22. Step 1: the engine checks rule A first because 500 is lower than 1000. Step 2: rule A matches on source, target, protocol and port. Step 3: the action is deny, so the connection is dropped and rule B is never reached.

Common mistake: assuming that a rule written later, or a more specific-looking rule, wins. Only the priority number decides order. Another mistake is tagging the wrong machines, so a rule meant for one server quietly applies to none of them or to many.

Consequence: a single broad allow on port 22 from anywhere exposes an admin login to the internet on every machine carrying that tag.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has a database VM tagged db inside its VPC network. Rule P has priority 300, action deny, direction ingress, source 10.20.0.0/16, target tag db, protocol tcp, port 5432. Rule Q has priority 200, action allow, direction ingress, source 10.20.5.0/24, target tag db, protocol tcp, port 5432. A host at 10.20.7.9 opens a connection to the db VM on tcp port 5432. Step 1: the engine checks rule Q first because 200 is lower than 300. Step 2: rule Q does not match, because 10.20.7.9 is outside 10.20.5.0/24. Step 3: the engine checks rule P, which matches on source, target, protocol and port. Step 4 is missing: what does the engine do with the connection?
choices: Allow it, because rule Q was checked first and its allow action takes precedence over later rules
Deny it, because rule P matched and its action is deny, so the connection is dropped
Allow it, because replies from the database are stateful and the port is well known
Hand it to the implied inbound deny rule, since no allow rule matched
questions.why: The first matching rule in priority order decides the outcome, and rule P matches with a deny action, so the connection is dropped.

questions.prompt: In a VPC firewall rule, what does the priority number control?
choices: How the rule is ordered against others: a lower number is checked first, and the first matching rule decides
The size of the address range in the source field, so higher numbers mean broader ranges
Which machines the rule is applied to, with lower numbers reserved for instances with more tags
How many ports the rule can cover, with higher numbers allowing wider port ranges
questions.why: Priority is a number from 0 to 65535 where a lower value is checked first, and the first rule that matches decides the outcome.

questions.prompt: A batch worker VM in a different company's VPC carries the network tag batch. Two egress rules exist. Rule E1 has priority 100, action deny, destination 203.0.113.0/24, target tag batch, protocol all. Rule E2 has priority 900, action allow, destination 0.0.0.0/0, target tag batch, protocol tcp, port 443. The worker opens a tcp port 443 connection to 203.0.113.40. What happens?
choices: The connection succeeds, because the allow rule for port 443 is more specific than the deny rule
The connection succeeds, because egress traffic is always allowed by default in every network
The connection is blocked by E1 at priority 100, because E1 is checked first and matches the destination, target and protocol
The connection is blocked by the implied outbound rule, which runs before any custom rule
questions.why: E1 has the lower priority number so it is checked first, matches the destination range, target tag and protocol, and its deny action drops the connection.

questions.prompt: A team wants only their analytics VM to accept SSH on tcp port 22 from their office range 198.51.100.0/24. They create an ingress allow rule with source 198.51.100.0/24, target tag analytics-vm, protocol tcp, port 22. However, the VM actually carries the tag analytics-vm-2, and no other rule allows SSH. What happens when someone in the office connects?
choices: The connection is blocked, because the new rule matches no machine and the implied inbound deny rule applies
The connection is blocked, but only until the VM is restarted, when the tag is re-read
The connection succeeds, because allow rules override the implied rules regardless of targets
The connection succeeds, because the rule still applies to the VM through a partial tag match
questions.why: Targets must match exactly, so the rule does not apply to the VM, and with no matching allow rule the implied inbound deny blocks the SSH connection.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that if we add a deny rule for port 22 after the existing allow rule, SSH will be blocked. Explain to them how Google Cloud firewall rules decide which one applies, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing targets by network tag.
lessons.modelAnswer: Rules are not read top to bottom in the order we wrote them. Each rule has a priority number, and the engine checks rules from the lowest number upward. The first match decides. So a deny at priority 500 blocks SSH even if an allow sits at 1000, and a deny added later with a higher number changes nothing. A new deny only works if its priority number is lower than the allow it must beat. On the tradeoff: targeting by network tag is flexible, because any new VM with the right tag inherits the rules, but a tag is just a label that someone can add or remove. A mistyped or accidentally added tag can expose a machine or cut it off, and the rule itself does not reveal that. Targeting by service account ties the rule to an identity, which is harder to change by accident.
rubricPoints: Rules are evaluated by priority number, lowest first, and the first match decides.
A deny only overrides an allow if its priority number is lower.
Network tags are flexible, so any VM given the tag inherits the rule.
Tags can be added or removed by mistake, changing exposure without editing the rule.
Service accounts give a firmer target tied to identity.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which of several ordered rules applies to a request is the same kind of first-match reasoning the planned authorization policy evaluator would require the learner to work through.

lessons.plain: A firewall rule decides which network traffic is allowed in or out of your machines. People often write these rules by listing IP addresses, but machines get new addresses and the list goes stale fast. This objective is about a better approach: label each machine with a tag, or name the identity the machine runs as, and write the rule against that label. The rule then follows the workload wherever its address changes. It is like telling a bouncer to let in anyone wearing a staff badge, rather than keeping a list of every staff member's home address.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you have 40 web servers whose IP addresses change every time they are rebuilt, what goes wrong when a firewall rule lists their current IP addresses, and what could the rule match on instead?
lessons.teach: A Cloud NGFW policy is a set of firewall rules that Google Cloud checks against traffic entering or leaving your network. Each rule has an action (allow, deny, or pass the decision to a later policy), a direction (ingress for incoming traffic, egress for outgoing), a priority (a number where lower values are checked first, and the first matching rule wins), and a match. The match has two sides: sources or destinations that the traffic comes from or goes to, and targets, which are the resources the rule applies to. Instead of IP addresses, a rule can match on two kinds of identity. A secure tag is a key and value pair attached to a resource and governed by permissions, for example role equals web. A service account is the identity a virtual machine runs as. Matching on a tag or service account means the rule follows the workload: a new machine carrying the tag is covered automatically, even with a new IP address. Do not confuse secure tags with the older network tags used in VPC firewall rules. Worked example: an ingress rule with priority 100, action allow, target secure tag role equals web, source secure tag role equals loadbalancer, and TCP port 443. A new server is created and tagged role equals web. Traffic arrives on port 443 from a load balancer tagged role equals loadbalancer. The rule is checked at priority 100, the target matches because the server carries the tag, the source matches, the port matches, and the action allows the traffic. No IP address was edited. Common mistake: the tag exists on the resource but the rule names a slightly different value, or several workloads share one service account and the rule is assumed to single out one role. The new server then falls through to a later rule or to the default ingress deny, and its traffic is blocked without any error on the server itself. In a running system, this means a deploy can look healthy while real requests quietly never arrive.

questions.prompt: A team at a logistics company, Northwind Parcels, writes a Cloud NGFW ingress rule with priority 50, action allow, target service account billing-api, source secure tag tier equals gateway, and TCP port 8443. A new VM is started and runs as the service account billing-api. A gateway VM carrying the secure tag tier equals gateway sends a request to the new VM on port 8443. Trace the check: Step 1, the rule is checked first because 50 is lower than any other priority in the policy. Step 2, the target matches because the VM runs as billing-api.
