Step 3, this step is missing and you must supply it. Step 4, the port matches because the request uses 8443. Step 5, the action is allow, so the request is delivered. Which sentence correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The source is checked against the secure tag tier equals gateway, and because the gateway VM carries that tag, the source matches.
Because several VMs could run as billing-api, the rule must also confirm a second service account before the source can match.
The rule compares the gateway VM's older network tag against the source, so the match depends on that network tag existing on the gateway.
The rule compares the gateway VM's IP address with its own address list, and the request only matches if those two addresses are the same.
questions.why: A source that is a secure tag matches when the sending resource carries that exact key and value, which the gateway VM does here.

questions.prompt: In Cloud NGFW, why would a rule match a secure tag such as tier equals api instead of a list of IP addresses?
choices: Because the tag follows the workload, so a new machine carrying the tag is covered without editing the rule, even if its IP address is new.
Because IP addresses cannot be used in Cloud NGFW rules at all, so tags are the only option available for any match.
Because a tag makes the rule check priority first, which means it is always evaluated before any rule with a lower number.
Because a tag removes the need for an action, so the rule allows traffic automatically whenever a tagged resource is present.
questions.why: A secure tag is attached to the resource, so the rule keeps applying to any machine carrying it regardless of its address.

questions.prompt: A team runs five batch VMs, all running as the service account reports-sa. They want an ingress rule that allows only one of those five VMs to receive traffic on port 9000. What is the problem with matching on the service account as the target?
choices: The rule would apply to all five VMs, because every VM running as reports-sa matches the same target.
The rule would apply to none of them until each VM is given its own separate IP address in the rule.
Service accounts cannot be used as targets, so the rule would be rejected when saved to the policy.
The rule would apply only to the most recently created VM, because a service account always points to one machine.
questions.why: Several workloads sharing one service account all match the same target, so the rule cannot single out one of them.

questions.prompt: A developer tags a new VM with the secure tag role equals gateways, with an s on the end. The ingress rule that should allow traffic to it names role equals gateway, without an s, and the VM is otherwise correctly placed. What happens to traffic sent to that VM on the allowed port?
choices: The VM refuses the connection itself and logs an error, because a mismatched tag stops the VM from accepting traffic.
The rule is automatically corrected to the new value, so the traffic is allowed after the next policy refresh.
The rule matches anyway, because Cloud NGFW ignores the value of a tag and only checks the key role.
The rule does not match, so the traffic reaches a later rule or the default ingress deny, and the VM shows no error of its own.
questions.why: A tag match needs the exact key and value, so a near-miss value leaves the rule unmatched and the traffic is blocked silently by a later rule or the default deny.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a Cloud NGFW rule that targets a secure tag is easier to maintain than one that lists IP addresses, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on tags or service accounts.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rule that targets a secure tag describes the role of a machine rather than its address. When the autoscaler or a rebuild gives a new server a new IP, the server carries the same tag, so the rule still covers it without anyone editing the policy. A rule that lists IPs has to be updated every time addresses change, and it breaks silently when someone forgets. The tradeoff is that the protection is only as good as the tagging. If a server is created without the tag, or the tag value in the rule does not match exactly, the rule will not cover it, and traffic may be blocked or, worse, not filtered at all. Shared service accounts add a related risk: one identity used by several workloads means a rule can apply to more machines than intended. So I would check tag attachment as part of deployment and keep service accounts dedicated per role.
rubricPoints: Tags or service accounts describe a workload's role, so rules keep working when IP addresses change.
Rules are evaluated in priority order, and the first match decides the action.
A tag or service account that is missing or misspelled means the rule silently does not apply.
Shared service accounts can make a rule cover more machines than intended.

suggested.rationale: The priority-ordered, first-match evaluation of identity-based rules is what the planned authorization policy evaluator would let a learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: A cloud network is a private space you build inside a provider's data centres, but your office, your own data centre, or another cloud sits somewhere else, so you need a link between them. This objective covers three ways to make that link. Cloud VPN sends encrypted traffic across the ordinary internet. VPC Network Peering joins two cloud networks so they talk privately without touching the internet. Cloud Interconnect is a dedicated, high-capacity private line into Google's network. Each option trades off cost, speed, privacy, and setup effort, and choosing among them is a common decision in exam-style scenarios.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network and your cloud network must exchange large amounts of sensitive data every day. Without looking anything up, which would you guess fits better: encrypted traffic over the public internet, or a dedicated private physical line, and what would make you choose one over the other?
lessons.teach:
Some terms first. A VPC network (virtual private cloud) is your private network inside Google Cloud, divided into subnets, where each subnet is a range of IP addresses. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol two networks use to automatically share which address ranges they can reach. In Google Cloud, a Cloud Router handles BGP for you.

Cloud VPN creates IPsec tunnels, which are encrypted pipes running over the public internet. HA VPN, the recommended form, uses two interfaces and two tunnels so that one failure does not stop traffic. It is quick to set up and cheap, but the internet path varies in speed and each tunnel has a bandwidth ceiling.

VPC Network Peering connects two VPC networks directly over Google's network, with no VPN devices and no internet hop. Peered networks exchange subnet routes, and their subnet ranges must not overlap. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Each side creates its own peering, and firewall rules still apply on both sides.

Cloud Interconnect provides a private physical link into Google's edge. Dedicated Interconnect uses your own circuits to a colocation facility, with 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps links. Partner Interconnect rents capacity through a service provider when you cannot reach a facility directly. The traffic is private but not encrypted by default, so add encryption, such as HA VPN over Interconnect, if policy requires it.

Worked example: an on-premises network at 10.20.0.0/16 must reach a VPC at 10.0.0.0/16 and needs about 20 Gbps of steady replication traffic. Step one: the ranges do not overlap, so routing works. Step two: that sustained rate is more than a single VPN tunnel should carry, so VPN is a poor fit. Step three: Dedicated Interconnect with multiple 10 Gbps links across two facilities gives capacity and redundancy.

Common mistake: choosing VPC Network Peering to reach an on-premises network. Peering only joins cloud VPCs, so it cannot reach your data centre.

The right link is the one that matches the workload's bandwidth, privacy, and redundancy needs, not simply the cheapest one.

questions.prompt: A company has a production VPC at 10.60.0.0/16 and an analytics VPC at 10.70.0.0/16. It wants the two networks to talk privately, with no VPN devices and no internet hop. The team works through it this way. Step one: the ranges do not overlap, so routes can be exchanged. Step two: [missing]. Step three: each network creates its own peering, so the connection is active on both ends. Which step two completes the reasoning?
choices: Confirm the analytics network can reach an on-premises office through the production network, since peering passes traffic onward.
Switch to Cloud VPN so the link is encrypted, since peering offers no encryption.
Check that firewall rules on both networks permit the intended traffic, because they still apply to peered traffic.
Order a Dedicated Interconnect circuit of 10 Gbps, since peering has a bandwidth ceiling.
questions.why: Peered networks still apply firewall rules on both sides, so the permitted traffic must be checked on each network after the routes are shared.

questions.prompt: A bank has a branch office network that is not in a colocation facility. It needs a private connection to its Google Cloud VPC for about 200 Mbps of traffic, and its policy requires the traffic to be encrypted. Which option fits best?
choices: Dedicated Interconnect with two 100 Gbps links
Partner Interconnect with no encryption added
HA VPN with two tunnels over the internet
VPC Network Peering between the branch office and the VPC
questions.why: HA VPN gives encrypted IPsec tunnels over the internet, which suits modest bandwidth and an office that cannot reach a facility, while peering cannot reach an office at all.

questions.prompt: A startup peers network Alpha with network Beta, and separately peers Beta with network Gamma. A virtual machine in Alpha cannot reach a service in Gamma. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Peering is not transitive, so Alpha needs its own peering with Gamma
Beta's Cloud Router must copy Gamma's routes into Alpha manually
Peering requires a VPN tunnel between Alpha and Gamma before traffic can pass
Gamma's subnets are too large for Alpha to route to
questions.why: Peering only connects the two networks named in each peering, so traffic cannot pass through Beta to reach Gamma, and Alpha needs a direct peering with Gamma.

questions.prompt: A retailer's on-premises network uses 192.168.0.0/22, and its planned VPC subnet also uses 192.168.2.0/24, which falls inside that range. The team wants to connect them with Cloud VPN. What is the main problem and the right response?
choices: Peering is the fix, because it lets overlapping ranges coexist on the same link
Traffic is encrypted automatically, so the overlap is harmless and can be left as it is
Overlap only matters for Dedicated Interconnect, so VPN handles it without changes
Routing becomes ambiguous, so one range must change before the networks are connected
questions.why: Overlapping address ranges make it unclear which network a destination belongs to, so one side must be renumbered before routes can be shared reliably.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Cloud VPN, VPC Network Peering, and Cloud Interconnect for a new connection, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would be least willing to use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking where the other end is and how much traffic must flow. If the other network is another VPC in Google Cloud, peering is usually the simplest choice, since it is private and sends traffic over Google's network. But I have to check that the subnet ranges do not overlap, and remember that peering is not transitive, so a chain of peerings will not let traffic pass through the middle network. If the other end is an office or data centre and volume is modest, HA VPN is quick to set up and encrypted by default, though its internet path varies and each tunnel has a bandwidth limit. For sustained high volume with predictable latency, I would consider Dedicated or Partner Interconnect, but it takes longer to provision and is not encrypted unless I add encryption on top. The option I would be least willing to use for a large steady transfer is a single VPN tunnel, because it can become the bottleneck.
rubricPoints: Peering connects cloud VPCs privately, requires non-overlapping subnet ranges, and is not transitive.
Cloud VPN runs encrypted IPsec tunnels over the internet and suits moderate traffic with quick setup.
Cloud Interconnect offers a private, high-bandwidth physical link but is not encrypted by default and takes longer to set up.
A named limit, such as a single tunnel's bandwidth ceiling or peering's inability to reach on-premises networks.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among three connectivity products from a workload's shape is best practised through exam-style scenarios that require reasoning about bandwidth, privacy, and topology.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a front door that spreads incoming requests across several copies of a service, so no single copy gets overwhelmed and a broken copy stops receiving traffic. On Google Cloud you choose among several kinds, mainly depending on whether the traffic is web requests or raw connections, whether users are on the public internet or inside your private network, and whether the service runs in one region or several. Picking the wrong kind is a common and expensive mistake, because each kind sees different details of the request and offers different features.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website runs on three identical servers in one city. If you put one public address in front of them and one server crashes, what should happen to the requests that would have gone to it, and how would the front door know that server is broken?
lessons.teach:
A load balancer is a managed front door: clients send traffic to one stable address, and the balancer forwards each request to a backend, meaning one of the running copies of your application. A health check is a periodic probe the balancer sends to each backend; a backend that fails the probe is taken out of rotation until it passes again. A forwarding rule holds the public or private IP address and port that clients use. A backend service groups the backends together and sets how traffic is spread among them.

The main decision is the layer and the reach. Application Load Balancers work at layer 7, the HTTP and HTTPS level, so they can route by host name or URL path and terminate TLS, the encryption wrapper around web traffic. Network Load Balancers work at layer 4, forwarding TCP or UDP connections without reading their contents; the passthrough kind keeps the client's original IP address and is regional. Choose by protocol first, then by whether you need path-based routing, then by whether users are public or private, then by how many regions you serve.

Worked example: a public API runs in two regions, and users in Europe and North America all reach one global IP address. Step 1: the request arrives at a global external Application Load Balancer at the Google edge nearest the user. Step 2: the balancer reads the URL path, so requests to /api go to the API backend service. Step 3: it picks a healthy backend in the closest region that has capacity. Step 4: if that region's backends fail their health checks, new requests move to the other region.

Common mistake: choosing a regional balancer for a multi-region audience, or writing a health check against a path the application does not really serve, so a healthy server is marked down or a broken one stays in rotation.

Consequence: when every backend is marked unhealthy, the balancer returns errors to clients even though the machines are still running, so health check design directly controls availability.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs an internal reporting tool in a single region, us-central1. Only employees on the corporate network use it. The tool has two services: /reports for dashboards and /exports for file downloads. Step 1: the team needs routing by URL path, so it chooses a layer 7 balancer. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the balancer sends /exports requests to the export backend service and /reports requests to the reports backend service. Step 4: each backend is probed through its own health check path, so a failing export server leaves rotation without affecting the dashboards.
choices: Use a global external Application Load Balancer, so the single regional deployment is reachable from anywhere on the internet
Use a passthrough Network Load Balancer, because it can read URL paths and route by them
Use an internal Application Load Balancer, since the users are private and the service runs in one region
Skip the balancer and attach the health check directly to each virtual machine so the clients connect to them
questions.why: Choosing by reach comes after choosing by protocol and path routing, and private users in a single region call for an internal Application Load Balancer.

questions.prompt: In a load balancer, what is a backend service?
choices: The periodic probe that tests whether each server is alive
The encryption certificate the balancer uses to terminate TLS
A group of backends together with the rule for spreading traffic among them
The stable IP address and port that clients connect to
questions.why: A backend service groups the backends and sets how traffic is spread among them, while the forwarding rule holds the address and the health check is the probe.

questions.prompt: A team configures its health check to request /ping, but the application only serves /healthz, so every backend fails the probe. The servers are running normally. What happens to client requests?
choices: The balancer removes the backends from rotation, so clients receive errors even though the machines are up
The balancer automatically rewrites the probe path to match the application
The balancer keeps sending requests to all backends because they are running
The balancer routes requests to the health check path instead of the application
questions.why: A backend that fails its health check is taken out of rotation, and when all backends are marked unhealthy the balancer returns errors even though the machines still run.

questions.prompt: A game studio runs a UDP game server in one region on port 7777. The server needs to see each player's original IP address, and all players connect from within that region. Which balancer fits best?
choices: A regional internal Application Load Balancer
A global external Application Load Balancer with path-based routing
A global external Application Load Balancer
A regional passthrough Network Load Balancer
questions.why: UDP is a layer 4 protocol, so a Network Load Balancer is needed; the passthrough kind keeps the client's original IP and is regional, which fits a single-region game.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to deploy a service how you would choose between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer for it, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the protocol. If the service speaks HTTP or HTTPS and I need to route by URL path, or I want the balancer to handle TLS, an Application Load Balancer fits, because it works at layer 7 and reads the request. If the service uses raw TCP or UDP, or I need to keep the client's original IP address with minimal processing, a Network Load Balancer fits better, since it works at layer 4 and does not look inside the traffic. Then I check reach: public users or private internal callers, and one region or several. The tradeoff I would name is that the Application Load Balancer adds processing on every request and costs more, while the passthrough Network Load Balancer is regional and cannot do path routing, so a multi-region public service would need a different design. I would also make sure the health check hits a real endpoint, because a wrong check silently removes healthy backends from service.
rubricPoints: Chooses the balancer type by protocol and layer, such as HTTP routing versus raw TCP or UDP
Considers whether traffic is public or internal and whether the service spans regions
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as cost, added processing, regional scope, or lack of path routing
Explains that health checks decide which backends receive traffic and must test a real endpoint

suggested.rationale: Choosing a load balancer from a workload's shape is a scenario decision best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When your application is reachable from the internet, the network path its traffic takes matters. Google Cloud offers two network service tiers, which are two different routes for traffic moving between your resources and users. Premium Tier carries traffic on Google's own private global backbone for most of its journey, so it enters the network close to the user and rides a fast, consistent path. Standard Tier hands traffic to ordinary internet providers sooner, which costs less but can be slower and less predictable. Think of it like choosing between a private highway with tolls and a cheaper public road. Picking a tier is a trade between speed, reliability, and price.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two routes carry the same web request, which would you expect to be steadier for users spread across the world: a route that stays on one company's private network for most of the trip, or one that hands off to many public networks early? Why?
lessons.teach:
A network service tier is a setting that decides which path traffic takes between a Google Cloud resource and the outside world. Premium Tier is the default. It carries traffic across Google's global backbone, meaning the high-capacity private network Google runs between its data centers and its edge locations, which are points of presence close to end users. Standard Tier sends traffic onto the public internet sooner, through transit providers, so traffic leaves Google's network closer to its destination.

Why it works: a longer ride on a network you control tends to have fewer hops, steadier latency, and less congestion. That is why Premium suits user-facing services with a global audience. Standard trades some of that consistency for a lower price on outbound data transfer, and it fits regional, latency-tolerant, or cost-sensitive workloads.

Each tier also limits what you can build. Standard Tier external IP addresses are regional, and global external load balancing is not available on Standard. A regional external load balancer can still serve traffic on Standard.

Worked example: a team serves a website from one region to users on several continents. Step one, a user in Tokyo sends a request. Step two, on Premium, the request enters Google's network at a nearby edge location and travels the backbone to the backend. Step three, on Standard, the request leaves Google's network earlier and crosses public internet links to reach the region. Step four, the team compares outbound data costs and the latency users actually see before choosing.

Common mistake: treating Standard as a cheaper copy of Premium with no downside, or choosing it for a global service and then wondering why global load balancing is missing.

Consequence in a running system: changing a tier generally means a new external IP address and possibly a different load balancer, so the tier should be decided before the public address is published in DNS and given to users.

questions.prompt: Harbor Pay runs a card-payment API in one region, europe-west3, and its customers are only in Germany and Austria. The engineers want one global external load balancer with a single public IP address. Step 1: they note that the design requires global external load balancing. Step 2: they check which network service tiers support that feature. Step 3 is missing: they must decide whether the Standard Tier can be used. Step 4: they keep Premium and publish the address in DNS only after the tier is fixed. What is the missing step 3?
choices: Conclude that Standard cannot be used, because global external load balancing is not available on Standard
Add a second regional IP address on Standard so that the global balancer is not needed
Enable a private link that moves the API onto Premium's backbone without changing the tier
Switch to Standard to cut outbound costs, since a regional customer base makes global balancing irrelevant
questions.why: Global external load balancing is not available on Standard, so a design that requires it rules that tier out, which is the conclusion step 3 must state.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new external IP address for a service and does not specify a network service tier. Which tier applies?
choices: Standard, because regional services default to it
Premium, because it is the default tier and carries traffic on Google's global backbone
Transit, because public internet links are the default path
Regional, because the tier follows the region of the resource
questions.why: Premium is the default tier, so an address created without a choice uses Google's backbone.

questions.prompt: Pixelrun serves a leaderboard API to players in Southeast Asia from one region. The service is latency tolerant, sends a large volume of outbound data, and does not need global load balancing. Which tier fits best?
choices: Premium, because a regional service must cross the backbone to reach any user
Premium, because it is the only tier that can serve players in more than one country
Standard, because it lowers outbound transfer cost and suits a regional, latency-tolerant, cost-sensitive service
Standard, because it removes the need for any external IP address
questions.why: Standard trades some consistency for lower outbound data cost, which matches a regional, latency-tolerant workload that does not need global balancing.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Analytics runs a regional service on the Standard Tier with a published external IP address in DNS. Later it wants to use global external load balancing. What is the consequence to plan for?
choices: Nothing changes; the tier can be switched while the address and DNS record stay the same
Changing tier generally means a new external IP address and possibly a different load balancer, so DNS must be updated
Only a firewall rule edit is needed, because the backbone path is unchanged
Premium will automatically convert the existing Standard address into a global anycast address
questions.why: Changing tiers generally requires a new external IP and possibly a different load balancer, which is why the tier should be decided before the address is published.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how Premium Tier and Standard Tier differ, and name one limit or tradeoff you would weigh before choosing Standard for a public-facing service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Premium Tier is the default. It moves traffic across Google's private global backbone for most of the path, entering close to the user, so latency tends to be steadier and global features such as global external load balancing are available. Standard Tier hands traffic to public internet providers sooner, so it usually costs less for outbound data but the path is less predictable and external addresses are regional. The main tradeoff for a public service is that Standard saves money at the cost of consistency and global reach. Before choosing it, I would measure what users in each region actually experience, check whether we need a global load balancer, and remember that changing tiers later usually means new external addresses, so the decision should be made before DNS points to the service.
rubricPoints: Premium Tier uses Google's global backbone for most of the path and is the default.
Standard Tier exits to public internet providers sooner and usually costs less for outbound data.
Standard limits features such as regional-only external addresses and no global external load balancing.
Changing tiers later typically changes external addresses, so the choice should be made deliberately up front.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and a price-versus-path tradeoff that OpsForge's planned engines do not cover directly, so reading the tier comparison is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing your cloud setup, such as networks, virtual machines, storage and permissions, in text files instead of clicking through a web console. The files can be stored, reviewed and run again to rebuild the same setup. Four tools cover this topic from different angles. Terraform builds cloud resources from a description. Config Connector lets you manage Google Cloud resources through the same interface you use for Kubernetes. Helm packages and installs applications onto Kubernetes. Fabric FAST is a ready-made, opinionated set of Terraform blueprints for setting up an organization's foundations. Knowing which tool fits which job is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team needs to recreate the same network, firewall rules and virtual machines in a second project next month. Which would be more reliable: following a written list of console clicks, or running a text file that describes the finished result? Why?
lessons.teach:
Declarative means you write down the end state you want, not the steps to reach it. The tool compares that description with what currently exists and makes the difference. Terraform works this way. You write configuration files naming resources such as a network, a subnet and a virtual machine. Terraform keeps a state file, a record of what it has created and the identifiers it uses. A plan step shows the changes it would make, for example three resources to add and none to remove. An apply step carries them out. Because the state file records ownership, you can apply the same files again and only the difference is changed. Terraform reaches Google Cloud through a provider, a plugin that translates resource descriptions into API calls. A module is a reusable group of resources. Fabric FAST is a set of Terraform modules arranged as an organization foundation: folders, projects, access grants and network layout, applied in ordered stages.

Config Connector applies the same declarative idea inside a Kubernetes cluster. You create a custom resource, an object that extends the Kubernetes interface, describing a Google Cloud resource such as a storage bucket. A controller watches these objects and reconciles continuously: if the real resource drifts from the description, the controller pushes it back.

Helm solves a different problem. It packages a Kubernetes application as a chart, which is a set of templated manifests plus a values file of settings. A release is one installed instance of a chart. Helm can upgrade or roll back a release. It does not manage cloud networks or buckets.

Worked example: you need a bucket with versioning turned on. In Terraform you declare the bucket and its versioning setting, run plan, which reports one addition, then apply. Next month you change the setting and apply again; the plan shows one in-place change and nothing else.

Common mistake: editing a resource by hand in the console while Terraform or Config Connector manages it. The recorded state no longer matches reality, so the next plan shows a change you did not expect, and an apply may silently revert your fix. In a running system, a hand-edited firewall rule can be overwritten during a routine deploy.

questions.prompt: A payments team keeps a Terraform configuration that created a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription on it. Both are recorded in the state file. Later, the team deletes the subscription block from the .tf files and leaves the topic block alone. Step 1: they run a plan. The plan reports ___. Step 2: they run apply, which removes the subscription. Fill in the missing plan result.
choices: One resource to add and none to remove, because the topic is still declared
Two resources to destroy, the topic and the subscription, because deleting any block removes everything
One resource to destroy and none to add, because the state records the subscription but the files no longer declare it
No changes, because the state file only changes when someone edits it by hand
questions.why: Terraform compares the files with the state file, so a recorded resource that is no longer declared shows up in the plan as a removal, while the still-declared topic is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Config Connector?
choices: It packages Kubernetes manifests with a values file and tracks installed releases
It is a plugin that runs inside a Terraform plan and translates changes into Kubernetes API calls
It is a Terraform module that groups folders, projects and access grants into ordered stages
It lets you describe Google Cloud resources as custom objects inside a Kubernetes cluster, and a controller keeps the real resources matching those objects
questions.why: Config Connector stores resource descriptions as custom Kubernetes objects and a controller continuously reconciles the real resources to match them.

questions.prompt: An engineer changes a firewall rule by hand in the console. The rule is managed by Terraform, and the next routine deploy runs apply. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Terraform keeps the console change because the state file is updated automatically when the console is used
The apply quietly fails and the console change stays in place until someone deletes the state file
Terraform detects the manual edit, asks the engineer to confirm, and keeps the change
The recorded state no longer matches reality, so the apply may revert the hand edit without warning
questions.why: Hand edits leave the state file out of date, and an apply can overwrite the change, which is why manual edits to managed resources are risky.

questions.prompt: A team wants to create a Cloud Storage bucket with versioning turned on and keep that setting in a reviewable file. Which choice fits, and why does Helm not fit?
choices: Helm, because a Kubernetes chart can describe any Google Cloud resource
Helm, because a values file can hold the bucket name and versioning flag
Config Connector, because it can declare the bucket as a custom object and Helm can only package Kubernetes applications
Helm, because it installs releases and can roll back a bucket setting
questions.why: Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts and does not manage cloud resources such as buckets, so a declarative tool like Terraform or Config Connector is the right fit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud work when you would reach for Terraform, when you would reach for Config Connector, and when you would reach for Helm. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: Terraform is my default for building cloud infrastructure such as networks, machines and permissions. I write files describing the end state, run a plan to see what would change, then apply it. Terraform keeps a state file of what it owns, so the same files can be rerun safely. Config Connector fits when the team already runs everything through Kubernetes and wants a controller to keep Google Cloud resources matching the files all the time. Helm is for packaging and installing an application onto Kubernetes, with upgrades and rollbacks per release. It does not build networks or buckets. The main limit of Terraform is that the state file must be stored safely and only one person should apply at a time, or changes can collide. For Config Connector, the limit is that it depends on a healthy cluster, so cluster problems can block infrastructure changes. Fabric FAST saves time but is opinionated, so heavy customization takes real effort.
rubricPoints: Terraform describes a desired end state, shows a plan, then applies it, tracked by a state file
Config Connector expresses Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes objects that a controller keeps reconciled
Helm packages and installs Kubernetes applications as charts and releases, not cloud infrastructure
Each tool has a limit, such as state file handling, cluster dependency, or opinionated structure

suggested.rationale: Choosing among these four tools and explaining the tradeoff back is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: These are Google Cloud's AI helpers for planning and building cloud systems. Some run in your terminal and can read your project files and propose commands, asking before they act. Some sit inside a code editor and can plan and carry out multi-step coding tasks. One lives in the cloud console and helps explain what is happening in a project when something breaks. One is a visual canvas where you lay out the parts of an application before building it. The core idea is that these tools draft plans and changes quickly, but a person still has to check them, because a fluent suggestion can be wrong, costly, or too permissive.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an AI assistant writes a configuration file that would create a database and open it to the whole internet, what should you do before running it, and why?
lessons.teach:
Start with the definitions. An AI-assisted tool is software that uses a large language model, a program trained to produce text, to read context and propose actions. Gemini CLI is a command-line agent: you type a request in a terminal, it reads files and can suggest commands, and it asks before acting on your machine. Google Antigravity is an agent-first development environment, an editor where an AI agent can plan a task, edit several files, and run checks. Gemini Cloud Assist is an assistant inside the Google Cloud console that can summarize logs, explain errors, and suggest fixes for a project that already runs. Application Design Center is a visual design tool for assembling an application's components, such as compute, storage, and networking, from templates. It can help turn a design into infrastructure-as-code, which means configuration files that describe resources so they can be created the same way every time.

Why this works: each tool gives an AI model context, such as your files, your logs, or your diagram, plus a way to propose actions. The model is good at drafting and spotting patterns, but it does not know your budget, your security rules, or what your organization has approved. So the workflow is to ask, read the proposal, check it against your constraints, and only then apply it.

Worked example: a team needs a small web service with a database on a private network. Step 1: sketch the parts in Application Design Center. Step 2: export the design as configuration files. Step 3: read the generated file and confirm the database is not reachable from the whole internet and the machine size fits the budget. Step 4: review the plan that shows what would be created or changed, and apply it only after that check.

Common mistake: accepting a generated plan because it looks complete, then finding it created a public address, an oversized machine, or a service account with broad permissions. In a running system, a quietly widened permission or an always-on oversized resource can persist for weeks, adding cost and exposure until someone reviews it. AI tools speed up the drafting, but the review step is where the engineer's responsibility stays.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm wants a nightly job that reads invoice files from one private storage bucket and writes a daily total to a second bucket. Its engineer uses Gemini CLI to draft the setup, then follows these steps. Step 1: she asks Gemini CLI for a draft of the job's configuration files. Step 2: she reads the draft line by line and notes which account the job runs as and whether either bucket allows public access. Step 3: she has not yet written down. Step 4: she reviews the plan showing what would be created, and applies it only after that review. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: She asks Gemini CLI to rate its own draft and accepts the rating as the safety check.
She runs the draft directly in the live accounting system to see whether it works.
She skips any further checks, because Gemini CLI asks for permission before it changes anything on her machine.
She checks the draft's account permissions, public access settings, and cost against the firm's approved rules before going further.
questions.why: The AI model does not know the firm's budget or approved rules, so the engineer must check the draft against those constraints before applying it.

questions.prompt: Which Google Cloud AI-assisted tool is an agent-first development environment, meaning an editor where an AI agent can plan a task, edit several files, and run checks?
choices: Gemini Cloud Assist
Application Design Center
Gemini CLI
Google Antigravity
questions.why: Google Antigravity is described as an agent-first editor where an agent plans, edits several files, and runs checks, while the other three tools have different roles.

questions.prompt: A project has been running for months, and its error logs have started showing repeated timeouts. The team wants an assistant inside the Google Cloud console that can summarize those logs and suggest a fix. Which tool fits best?
choices: Gemini CLI
Gemini Cloud Assist
Google Antigravity
Application Design Center
questions.why: Gemini Cloud Assist is the console assistant that summarizes logs, explains errors, and suggests fixes for a project that already runs.

questions.prompt: An engineer accepts an AI-generated plan because it looks complete, and the plan later turns out to give a database a public address and a service account broad permissions. What is the core mistake?
choices: Using an AI tool to draft a plan at all, instead of writing every configuration by hand.
Trusting Gemini CLI because it asks before acting on the machine.
Skipping the review step that checks the plan against constraints the AI model does not know, such as security rules and budget.
Using Application Design Center to build the diagram before exporting configuration files.
questions.why: The model does not know the organization's security rules or budget, so the review against those constraints is the engineer's responsibility and was skipped here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Gemini CLI, Google Antigravity, Gemini Cloud Assist, and Application Design Center each do, and name one limit or risk of letting an AI tool make infrastructure changes.
lessons.modelAnswer: Gemini CLI is a terminal agent: I describe a task, it reads files and proposes commands, and it asks before running them. Antigravity is an agent-first editor that can plan and edit several files and run checks for a coding task. Gemini Cloud Assist lives in the cloud console and helps me investigate errors and logs in a project that already exists. Application Design Center is a canvas where I lay out an application's parts from templates and can generate infrastructure-as-code from the design. The main limit is that these tools work from the context they can see and a model's best guess about it. They do not know our budget, compliance rules, or which permissions are acceptable. So I review every proposed change, read the plan that shows what would be created or changed, and get a second person to check anything touching IAM, networking, or spend before we apply it.
rubricPoints: Names each of the four tools with its generic role: terminal agent, agent-first editor, console troubleshooting assistant, and visual design canvas.
Explains that AI output is a proposal built from limited context, not a verified fact.
Says changes should be reviewed through a plan or diff before they are applied.
Names a specific risk such as overly broad permissions, public exposure, or unexpected cost.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right AI tool for a described situation and then checking its output is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, which exam-style situations do most effectively.

lessons.plain: Connecting remotely to a Compute Engine instance means opening a command-line session on a virtual machine that runs in Google's data centre, from your own laptop or a browser, as if you were sitting at its keyboard. Compute Engine is the service that provides virtual machines on demand. The usual way in is a secure shell, a protocol that encrypts traffic and proves who you are with a key pair rather than a shared password. Engineers use it to read logs, restart a service, or fix a broken setting when a server misbehaves. The hard part is rarely the typing. It is making sure the right people can reach the machine and nobody else can.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server runs in the cloud but has no public IP address, and you need to read its logs from your laptop. What would have to be true for a secure shell session to reach it, and who should be allowed to start one?
lessons.teach:
Some terms first. A secure shell session (SSH) is an encrypted connection that gives you a text prompt on a remote machine. An instance is one running virtual machine. A key pair is two linked files: a private key you keep secret, and a public key you place on the machine. The machine accepts you only if you can prove you hold the matching private key. A firewall rule allows or blocks traffic to a network port; SSH normally uses TCP port 22. An identity-aware proxy is a relay that checks your cloud identity and then forwards your connection to a machine that has no public address.

Why it works: the machine does not rely on a password someone could guess. Access is the result of three checks that must all pass. First, your account must hold a permission that allows logging in. Second, the machine must trust the key you present, or accept your identity. Third, a network path must be open, meaning a firewall rule permits traffic on port 22 from where you are connecting.

Worked example. Instance web-1 has only an internal address. Step 1: an engineer's account is granted the role that lets them log in. Step 2: a firewall rule allows TCP port 22 from the address range the relay uses. Step 3: the engineer runs a command on their laptop that opens a tunnel through the relay and starts an SSH session. Step 4: the machine checks the engineer's identity and key, grants a shell, and the engineer reads the log file.

Common mistake: opening port 22 to every address on the internet so that 'it just works'. Automated scanners then try password guesses against the machine all day, and each attempt appears in the system authentication log.

Consequence: a running service is only as safe as its remote access. An overly broad firewall rule turns a maintenance door into a public one.

questions.prompt: A bookshop's point-of-sale team needs to reach an instance named till-sync-07, which has a public address. Their connection follows three checks, and the steps are listed below. Step 1: the engineer Marta's account is granted the permission that allows logging in to the instance. Step 2: this step is not shown and must be filled in. Step 3: Marta's public key is placed on the instance. Step 4: Marta connects from the office using her matching private key, and the instance grants her a shell. Which step 2 completes the sequence so that all three checks are covered?
choices: Add a firewall rule that admits TCP port 22 from the office's address range
Generate a fresh key pair on the instance itself and email the private key to Marta
Restart the instance so that the newly placed public key takes effect on the next boot
Open TCP port 22 to every address on the internet so the office range can never be blocked
questions.why: The three checks are permission, trusted key, and an open network path, and the network path is provided by a firewall rule admitting TCP port 22 from the office range, which is the only option that does this without opening the port to everyone.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the public half of a key pair do on a machine that you want to log in to over SSH?
choices: It lets the machine check that whoever connects holds the matching private key, without a password
It is sent to the firewall so the firewall can decrypt your traffic on port 22
It is shared with the scanners so they can verify the machine is safe to probe
It replaces your cloud login permission so that you no longer need an identity
questions.why: The public key sits on the machine and is used to verify that the connecting party holds the matching private key, which is why no password is needed.

questions.prompt: An engineer has the correct login permission and the right private key for an instance named db-eu-4, which has only an internal address and is reached through the identity-aware relay. The connection still fails before any login prompt appears. Which of the three checks is the most likely gap?
choices: The machine has not been told the engineer's name, so it refuses to start a shell
The engineer's private key must be copied to the instance's public address to be accepted
The network path is not open, because no firewall rule permits TCP port 22 from the relay's address range
The login permission must be granted on the firewall instead of on the account
questions.why: Since the permission and key checks are described as already passing, the remaining required check is the network path, which needs a firewall rule allowing TCP port 22 from the relay's range.

questions.prompt: A team opens TCP port 22 on their public web server to every address on the internet so that anyone on any network can connect for maintenance. What is the most direct consequence to expect?
choices: The instance is automatically moved behind an identity-aware relay so that no outside address can reach it
The key pair is revoked, so the team's own engineers can no longer log in until the rule is removed
Automated scanners attempt password guesses against the machine continuously, and each attempt is recorded in the system authentication log
The web server's traffic on port 80 slows down because the firewall must inspect more packets
questions.why: Opening port 22 to everyone makes the maintenance door public, and scanners then try password guesses all day, with each attempt showing up in the system authentication log.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that if we put our SSH keys on every instance, we are covered. Explain to them how remote access to a Compute Engine instance is actually decided, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would prefer instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Access is decided by three things together: the person's account must have a permission to log in, the machine must accept the identity or key presented, and a firewall rule must allow the connection path. Copying keys onto each machine works, but it is hard to audit and easy to forget. When someone leaves, you have to find and remove their key from every server. I would prefer tying logins to the cloud identity, using the OS Login approach so access is granted and removed centrally with one permission change. The tradeoff is that it depends on the identity service and on the right roles being assigned, so a misconfigured role can lock people out. For instances without public addresses, the identity-aware proxy adds a relay that must also be allowed by a firewall rule, which adds a moving part to troubleshoot.
rubricPoints: Access requires a login permission, an accepted key or identity, and an open firewall path together
Instances without public IPs are reached through a relay such as the identity-aware proxy
Centralised identity-based login makes revoking access a single change instead of many key removals
Each approach has a tradeoff, such as more moving parts to troubleshoot or dependence on correct role assignment

suggested.rationale: Once connected, navigating an unfamiliar server to find logs and config is the day-2 skill this objective leads into, and that mission practices it directly.

lessons.plain: A Compute Engine instance is a virtual computer that Google runs for you in its data centers. Looking at currently running instances means getting an up-to-date list of the ones you own, with each machine's name, location, state, and network addresses. It is usually the first check when someone asks whether a server is up. Think of it like a register of parked vehicles: it tells you which ones exist, where they are, and whether their engines are on, but not whether the driver is actually getting anywhere. Reading that list quickly and filtering it is a basic day-two skill for anyone looking after a cloud system.
lessons.guessPrompt: A colleague says the reporting server is up. Name two things you would check, and say which one tells you more about whether it is actually doing its job.
lessons.teach:
A Compute Engine instance is a virtual machine: a computer that runs as software inside Google's data centers, rented by the second instead of bought as hardware. Viewing running instances means getting a current inventory of those machines in one project, with each one's name, zone, status, and internal and external IP addresses. A project is the container that groups your resources and billing. A zone is one physical location inside a region. Status is the lifecycle state of an instance. RUNNING means the machine is booted and accruing compute charges. TERMINATED means it is powered off; it still exists, keeps its disks, and those disks still cost storage money. PROVISIONING and STOPPING are transitional states showing work in progress.

Why it works: the list is a live read of the control plane, the service that tracks every resource you own. It is scoped, so it shows only instances in the selected project and, unless you ask for all zones, only the zone you pick. You can read the same data in the console's VM instances page or with the command-line tool's instances list command, and filter by name or status.

Worked example: a team reports the reporting server is down. Step 1: open the instances list for the production project. Step 2: filter for names containing reporting. Step 3: read the status column; one copy in zone us-central1-a says TERMINATED. Step 4: check the other zone; a second copy in us-central1-b says RUNNING. Step 5: before starting anything, find out whether the terminated copy was stopped on purpose.

Common mistake: assuming an instance that appears as RUNNING is serving traffic. The list shows the control plane's view of the machine, not whether the application inside answers. Consequence: a healthy-looking RUNNING status can hide a crashed service, so pair this inventory with monitoring metrics and logs before declaring an outage over.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps its nightly batch workers in the project freight-ops-dev. An engineer lists instances across all zones and sees two batch workers with status TERMINATED: batch-7 in europe-north1-a and batch-9 in europe-north1-b. Step 1: list instances in freight-ops-dev with the all-zones option so no zone is hidden. Step 2: note that batch-7 and batch-9 both read TERMINATED. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: only if the stop was unplanned, start the instance and then confirm the application answers, not just that the status reads RUNNING. Which action best fills Step 3?
choices: Find out whether someone stopped batch-7 and batch-9 on purpose, for example through the audit log or the team's change notes.
Switch the list to show only RUNNING instances so the TERMINATED ones disappear from view.
Rename both instances so the name filter matches them more easily.
Delete batch-7 and batch-9 so their disks stop costing storage money.
questions.why: A TERMINATED instance may have been stopped deliberately, so confirming intent comes before any start or delete action, and deleting or hiding entries skips that check.

questions.prompt: A payments VM named ledger-03 shows TERMINATED in the instances list. Which statement correctly describes what that status means for the instance and its disks?
choices: The instance has been deleted, and its disks were removed with it.
The instance is powered off but still exists, and its attached disks still incur storage charges.
The instance is booting and will be RUNNING shortly.
The instance is running but has lost its external IP address.
questions.why: TERMINATED means the machine is powered off; it still exists and its disks keep costing storage money.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a media startup sees that the instance cdn-edge-12 reads RUNNING in the instances list. A customer reports that pages from it load slowly. What is the most accurate reading of the RUNNING status here?
choices: The instance is serving the expected traffic at full capacity.
The application on cdn-edge-12 is confirmed healthy, so the slowdown must be on the customer's network.
The instance has been restarted recently, which is why the status changed.
The machine is booted and billed, but the list does not show whether the application is answering, so metrics and logs are needed.
questions.why: The list reflects the control plane's view of the machine, not whether the application inside works, so monitoring metrics and logs must be checked alongside it.

questions.prompt: A team lists instances with the command-line instances list command against project sales-analytics-prod and gets 4 results. A console view of the same project shows 6 instances. The team has not changed any filters. What is the most likely cause of the difference?
choices: The list command returned instances from a deleted project that still has cached entries.
The list was scoped to a single zone, and the other instances sit in zones the command did not include.
The command-line tool cannot read instances whose names contain numbers.
The console shows instances from other projects that are linked to the same billing account.
questions.why: The list is scoped to the selected zone unless all zones are requested, so instances in other zones of the same project will not appear.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would confirm which Compute Engine instances are actually running for a given service, and name one limit of the instance list that they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing instances in the right project and filtering by name, because the list is scoped to one project and, by default, to the zone I select. Then I would read the status column: RUNNING means the machine is booted and billing for compute, while TERMINATED means it is powered off but still exists with its disks. I would also note the zone, since the same service can have copies in several zones. The limit to remember is that the list only reports the state of the virtual machine, not whether the application on it works. A RUNNING instance can still have a crashed service, so I would confirm health with monitoring metrics and logs before saying the service is up.
rubricPoints: Names the project and zone scope of the instance list and how to filter it
Explains that RUNNING and TERMINATED differ in billing and whether the instance exists
Notes that a RUNNING status does not prove the application is healthy
Points to monitoring metrics or logs as the way to confirm service health

suggested.rationale: No listed mission has the learner browse Compute Engine inventory, so this is console and command facts best absorbed by reading.

lessons.plain: A snapshot is a saved copy of a storage disk as it looked at one moment, so you can recover data if something goes wrong. An image is a reusable starting template, usually for building new machines that already have the right operating system and software. A schedule runs snapshots automatically at set times and removes old copies after a chosen period, so nobody has to remember to do it. Think of it like a photo of a whiteboard: you can look at it later, copy it onto a fresh board, or throw it away when it is no longer needed.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you copy a disk every day and then delete the oldest copy, do you lose data that the newer copies still need? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A disk is the storage volume a virtual machine uses for its operating system and data. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk, taken without shutting the machine down. An image is a reusable boot template, built from a disk or a snapshot, that new machines can start from. A snapshot schedule is a policy attached to disks that creates snapshots at set times and keeps each one for a retention period.

Why it works: the first snapshot copies all the data. Later snapshots are usually incremental, meaning they store only the blocks that changed since the previous one. Each snapshot still looks complete to you, yet shared blocks are kept only once. Deleting an older snapshot does not break newer ones, because the system carries forward any data they still depend on.

Worked example: a database disk is snapshotted daily at 02:00 with a retention of seven days. On day eight, the oldest snapshot becomes eligible for removal. Blocks that newer snapshots still reference are kept, and only blocks no longer needed are freed. To restore, you create a new disk from the chosen snapshot and then attach that disk to a machine.

Common mistake: treating a snapshot taken while an application is writing as a guaranteed clean backup. The copy captures what was on disk at that instant, so data held in memory or half-written may be inconsistent. Pause writes or run the application's own flush step first.

Consequence: restoring from a snapshot produces a new disk, so the machine must be pointed at it, and any data written after the snapshot time is not in the restored copy.

questions.prompt: A team keeps a reporting disk on a machine in a staging project. Their snapshot schedule takes one snapshot every six hours and keeps each one for three days. An engineer wants to roll the reporting data back to an earlier state. Steps so far: (1) she picks the snapshot taken at 06:00 on Thursday; (2) she creates a new disk from that snapshot. The third step is missing. Which action completes the restore?
choices: Create an image from the Thursday snapshot and resize the original disk to match it
Attach the new disk to the reporting machine so the machine uses the restored data
Delete the Thursday snapshot once the new disk exists, so the copy is not reused
Copy the snapshot's blocks back over the original disk while it is still mounted
questions.why: Restoring from a snapshot produces a new disk, so the machine has to be pointed at that disk by attaching it, and the original disk is not changed by the restore.

questions.prompt: A logistics platform engineer says a snapshot 'stops the machine' while it is taken. Which statement is accurate?
choices: A snapshot is a policy that creates copies of a disk at set times
A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk, taken without shutting the machine down
The machine must be paused and shut down so that the copy is consistent
A snapshot is a reusable boot template that new machines can start from
questions.why: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk taken without shutting the machine down; the boot template describes an image and the schedule describes a policy.

questions.prompt: A ledger database writes transactions to its disk, and a snapshot is taken at 23:59 while writes are still happening. Which risk matters most for that snapshot?
choices: The snapshot is a guaranteed clean backup because it was taken at a fixed time
The snapshot stores every block again, so it is as large as the disk each time
Deleting the snapshot later will corrupt the live disk that the database is using
Data held in memory or half-written at that instant may be inconsistent in the copy
questions.why: A snapshot captures what was on the disk at that instant, so in-memory or half-written data can leave the copy inconsistent unless writes are paused or the application flushes first.

questions.prompt: A reporting disk has daily snapshots with a retention of ten days. An engineer deletes the oldest snapshot, which was taken on day one. What happens to the newer snapshots?
choices: They must be re-taken, because each newer snapshot depends wholly on the first one
They stay restorable, because the system carries forward any data they still depend on
They are deleted too, because snapshots form a chain that breaks when one link is removed
They become images automatically, so they can still be used to start machines
questions.why: Incremental snapshots keep shared blocks only once, and deleting an older snapshot does not break newer ones because the system carries forward any data they still need.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a snapshot, an image, and a snapshot schedule, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on snapshots as your only backup.
lessons.modelAnswer: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of one disk, used to recover that disk's data. An image is a reusable template that new machines can start from, so it is about building machines, not recovering data. A schedule is a policy that creates snapshots automatically and deletes them after a retention period. The main limit is consistency: a snapshot captures what was on disk at that instant, so an application mid-write may restore to a state it cannot cleanly resume from. Also, a snapshot covers only the disks you attached it to, not the machine's configuration, other services, or data written after the snapshot time. So I would pair snapshots with an application-level flush and a tested restore procedure.
rubricPoints: Defines a snapshot as a point-in-time copy of a disk used for recovery
Distinguishes an image as a reusable template for creating new machines
Explains a schedule as automatic creation plus retention-based deletion
Names a real limit, such as application consistency or data written after the snapshot

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine asks the learner to create, view, or schedule cloud snapshots, so reading the console concepts and locating them in the console is the fit.

lessons.plain: A Kubernetes cluster is a group of machines that run your containerized apps. Viewing its inventory means taking a list of what is actually running: the machines (nodes), the small units of work that hold your app's containers (Pods), and the stable addresses that route traffic to those units (Services). On Google Cloud, GKE, the managed version of this system, shows the same picture in the console and in a command-line tool. Knowing where to look turns a vague worry like 'is the app up?' into a few concrete checks.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a website running on a group of machines suddenly responds slowly, what would you check first: the machines themselves, the individual copies of the app, or the address users connect to? Why that order?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A node is a worker machine, here a Compute Engine virtual machine, that the cluster uses to run workloads. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that share a network address and run together. A Service is a stable name and address that forwards traffic to a changing set of Pods, chosen by matching labels, which are key-value tags attached to Pods. Pods are replaced often, so clients should talk to the Service, not to a Pod directly. A namespace is a named grouping inside a cluster that keeps workloads separate.

Why it works. Kubernetes stores a record of the state you asked for and keeps comparing it with what really exists. An inventory view is a read of that record and of live status. Nodes show the capacity the cluster has and whether each machine is Ready. Pods show where each piece of work is scheduled and whether it is restarting. Services show which Pods they send traffic to.

Worked example. The checkout app is slow. Step 1: list the nodes and confirm they are all Ready. Step 2: list the Pods in the checkout namespace and see that two of four are restarting. Step 3: list the Services and check that the checkout Service's label selector matches the healthy Pods. The restarting Pods are the lead to follow. In the console, the same data sits under Kubernetes Engine, then Clusters, Workloads, and Services and Ingress. From a terminal you read it with kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods in the namespace, and kubectl get services, after fetching cluster credentials once.

Common mistake. Checking only that the Service exists and assuming the app is fine. A Service with no matching Pods has nowhere to send traffic, so requests fail even though the Service and the nodes look healthy.

Consequence. When a Service's Pod list is empty or stale, users see errors while the node view still looks green, so you must read all three layers together.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a booking API in a GKE cluster named booking-east. Users see intermittent 503 errors from the bookings Service. Trace so far: Step 1, list the nodes: all three are Ready. Step 2, list the Pods in the bookings namespace: all four are Running with zero restarts. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it. Step 4: the bookings Service has no Pods to send traffic to, so requests fail. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Rename the bookings Service so the cluster rebuilds its traffic routes from scratch.
Add more nodes to the pool so the Service has more capacity to route to.
Check that the bookings Service's label selector matches the labels on the healthy bookings Pods.
Review the project billing report for a spending cap that could be cutting off requests.
questions.why: Step 4 says the Service has no Pods to send traffic to, and the label selector is the rule that decides which Pods a Service picks, so checking that rule is the step that shows the mismatch.

questions.prompt: A new team member asks what a Pod is in their GKE cluster. Which answer is correct?
choices: A Compute Engine virtual machine that the cluster uses to run workloads.
A stable name and address that forwards traffic to whichever Pods match its labels.
The smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: containers sharing one network address.
A named grouping inside a cluster that keeps one team's workloads apart.
questions.why: A Pod is the smallest schedulable unit, made of one or more containers that share a network address; the other options describe a node, a namespace, and a Service.

questions.prompt: A retail team's cart-svc Service selects Pods labelled app=cart-v2. After a rollout, the running Pods are labelled app=cart-v3. The nodes are Ready and the Pods are Running. What does the inventory view most likely show, and why do customers see errors?
choices: The nodes are likely NotReady, which would explain the failing requests.
The Service is healthy because it appears in the namespace listing next to the Pods.
The Service matches no Pods, so requests fail while nodes and Pods look healthy.
The Service relabels the Pods on its own once the rollout completes, so traffic recovers.
questions.why: A Service sends traffic only to Pods that match its label selector, so with no matching Pods it has nowhere to send requests even though the nodes and Pods look healthy.

questions.prompt: On an engineer's laptop with cluster credentials already fetched, which command shows whether each node in the media-prod cluster is Ready?
choices: kubectl get services
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get namespaces
questions.why: Nodes are listed with kubectl get nodes, which shows each machine's Ready status; the other commands list Services, Pods, or namespaces instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take a quick inventory of a GKE cluster to find out why an app is unreachable, and name one limit of what that inventory tells you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with nodes, to confirm the machines are Ready and have capacity. Then I would list the Pods for that app's namespace, looking for Pods that are restarting, pending, or missing. Last, I would list the Services and check that the Service's label selector matches a set of running Pods, because a Service with no matching Pods sends traffic nowhere. The limit is that this is a snapshot of state, not a history. It shows that a Pod is restarting now but not why it crashed, so for the cause I would move to the Pod's logs and the cluster's monitoring data in Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring. A healthy-looking inventory does not prove the app answers correctly, only that the pieces are in place.
rubricPoints: Nodes, Pods and Services are each checked and what each one tells you
A Service depends on matching Pods through labels, so an empty match means failure
Inventory is a point-in-time snapshot, not a record of why something failed
Logs and monitoring are needed to find the cause

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console locations and command names, which a reading lesson with the terms defined covers better than an existing mission.

lessons.plain: When a cluster runs a container, it first has to download the packaged app from a storage place called Artifact Registry. Downloads from that storage are locked unless the downloader proves who it is and has been given permission to read. Configuring access means giving the right identity permission to read that storage, so the cluster can fetch the app whenever it starts a new copy. Without that permission the app never starts, even though the rest of the setup looks correct. A useful picture: the cluster is a kitchen, the registry is the pantry, and access configuration is the key card that lets the kitchen staff into the pantry.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer pushes a new container image to Artifact Registry successfully, then a Kubernetes cluster refuses to start a Pod using that image. Before reading further, what is the first thing you would suspect is missing, and why might the developer's own permission not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Artifact Registry is Google Cloud's managed store for container images and other packages. A container image is a bundle containing an application and everything it needs to run. GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) is the managed Kubernetes service that runs those containers inside Pods, the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules. A node is a virtual machine in the cluster that hosts Pods. Before a Pod can start, the node must pull the image from the registry, and that pull is an authenticated request. So configuring access means making sure the identity making the pull has permission to read the repository. Two identities matter. The first is the node's identity: each node VM runs as a service account, which is a non-human identity, and by default that account often performs the pulls for every Pod on the node. Granting it the Artifact Registry Reader role on the repository lets pulls succeed. The second is a Pod-level identity, where a Kubernetes service account is linked to a Google service account through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. That approach is more precise because only the workloads you choose receive read access.

Worked example: a Deployment references an image at a regional repository path. Step 1: the kubelet on node n1 asks to pull the image. Step 2: the request carries the node service account. Step 3: Artifact Registry checks that account against the repository's IAM policy. Step 4: no reader role exists, so the pull is denied. Step 5: the Pod shows ErrImagePull, then ImagePullBackOff, and kubectl describe pod lists a denied event. Step 6: granting the reader role to the node service account lets the next retry succeed.

Common mistake: granting the role to your own user account and assuming the cluster inherits it. Cluster pulls never use your login.

Consequence in a running system: a rollout stalls, new Pods never become ready while old ones keep serving, and the failure appears in Pod events and workload logs rather than in the registry itself. Image access is a runtime dependency, so a missing grant blocks every future Pod start, including those created by scaling events.

questions.prompt: Lumen Labs runs a GKE cluster in europe-west1. A Deployment called ledger-api references an image in the regional repository payments in project lumen-prod, and its Pods sit in ImagePullBackOff. Here is the trace so far. Step 1: the kubelet on node n7 asks to pull the image. Step 2: the request carries the node service account used by the batch-pool node pool. Step 3: Artifact Registry checks that account against the repository's IAM policy. Step 4: the policy has no reader grant for that account, so the pull is denied. Step 5 is missing. What should the operator do so that the next retry can succeed?
choices: Grant Artifact Registry Reader on the payments repository to the personal login of the engineer who wrote ledger-api, because the cluster inherits that login's rights.
Make the payments repository publicly readable by allUsers so every node can pull without any account.
Grant Artifact Registry Reader on payments to batch-pool's node service account.
Change the image tag to latest so the node reuses a copy it already has cached.
questions.why: The pull is authenticated as the node service account, so giving that account the reader role on the repository is the grant that lets the retry succeed, while the other options either target the wrong identity or do not address the denied check.

questions.prompt: In GKE, which identity does a node most often use by default when it pulls an image from Artifact Registry for the Pods it hosts?
choices: The Artifact Registry service agent acting on its own behalf without any caller identity attached
The name of the Deployment object that requested the Pod, since Kubernetes passes it along with the image path
The node's Google service account, which is a non-human identity the node VM runs as
The Kubernetes service account of the Pod, which is always used for every registry request
questions.why: The teaching text says each node VM runs as a service account and that this account often performs the pulls for every Pod on the node by default.

questions.prompt: A team in a different organisation granted Artifact Registry Reader on their repository to a developer's own user account. A new Deployment on their cluster then shows ImagePullBackOff, and kubectl describe lists a denied pull event. What best explains this?
choices: The developer's account must hold the Owner role on the whole project before the cluster can pull images for any Pod
The tag in the image path uses uppercase letters, which Artifact Registry rejects before it checks any identity at all
The registry is unavailable for the region, so every pull request fails regardless of the grants that exist on the repository
The node's service account, which makes the pull, has no reader grant on the repository, and the developer's grant is not used for cluster pulls
questions.why: Cluster pulls are authenticated by the node service account, not by a person's login, so a grant to the developer does not allow the pull to succeed.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants only the Pods of one Deployment to be able to read images from a repository, and not every workload that happens to run on the same node. Which mechanism fits this need best?
