choices: Grant Artifact Registry Reader to the node service account, since every Pod on the node will then be able to pull the images it needs
Make the repository public to all users, which avoids the need to choose which workloads may read the images
Grant Artifact Registry Reader to the user who created the cluster, so that the cluster can use that person's permissions for pulls
Link a Kubernetes service account used by that Deployment to a Google service account through Workload Identity Federation for GKE, then grant reader access to that Google service account only
questions.why: Workload Identity Federation for GKE links a Pod-level Kubernetes identity to a Google service account, so only the chosen workloads receive read access, which is more precise than a node-wide grant.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a new GKE deployment is stuck pulling its image from Artifact Registry. Say which identity you would check first, and name one tradeoff between granting access at the node level and granting it at the Pod level.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Pods are failing at image pull, so the first thing I'd check is which identity the pull actually uses. On GKE that's usually the node's service account, not the account I log in with. I'd confirm that account has a reader role on the repository, and look at the Pod events for a denied message to confirm it's a permission problem and not a wrong image path or tag. If the fix is a grant, the tradeoff is scope. Granting the reader role to the node service account is simple and covers every Pod on those nodes, which is convenient but broader than needed. Linking a specific Pod's Kubernetes service account to a Google service account through Workload Identity Federation for GKE is more precise, but it needs more setup and must be right for each workload. For a small team with one cluster, node-level access is often acceptable, but I'd say so explicitly so nobody mistakes it for a least-privilege design.
rubricPoints: Identifies the node or Pod identity that performs the image pull, not the human developer.
Names the Artifact Registry Reader role or an equivalent read permission on the repository.
Explains how to confirm the cause from Pod events, such as a denied pull or ImagePullBackOff status.
States a tradeoff between broad node-level access and narrower Pod-level access via Workload Identity Federation for GKE.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a stalled rollout with the pull identity, role, and Pod events adds the most beyond reading the definitions.

lessons.plain: A Kubernetes cluster runs your containers on a set of machines called nodes. On Google Cloud, GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) groups nodes that share the same size and settings into a node pool. Day to day you may need to add a new group of machines, change an existing group, remove one you no longer need, or let the number of machines grow and shrink with load. This lesson explains what each of those actions does to the work already running on those machines.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your cluster has one node pool of three machines, and all of them are full during a traffic peak. Before reading on, what would you expect to happen if you turned on autoscaling for that pool with a maximum of six machines, and what would you worry about before deleting the pool entirely?
lessons.teach:
A node is one virtual machine that runs your containers. A node pool is a group of nodes in one cluster that share the same machine type and settings. Each pool can be changed on its own, which is why it is the unit you add, edit, or remove. Adding a pool creates new machines and gives workloads a place to run. Editing a pool changes its settings, such as machine type or autoscaling limits. Removing a pool deletes its machines.

Autoscaling lets the cluster change a pool's node count with demand. You set a minimum and a maximum number of nodes for the pool. When a Pod cannot be scheduled because no node has enough free CPU or memory for it, the autoscaler adds nodes, up to the maximum. When nodes sit mostly empty, it moves their Pods to other nodes and removes the empty machines, never going below the minimum.

Worked example: a pool called web-pool has a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 6 nodes. Traffic rises, and new Pods show Pending because no node has spare capacity. The autoscaler adds nodes one at a time until the pool reaches 6 or the Pods fit. Traffic later falls. A node stays underused for a while, its Pods are moved to other nodes, and the node is removed. The count settles at 2, never lower.

Common mistake: deleting a pool, or changing a machine's size, without first draining its nodes. Draining means moving Pods off a node gracefully before it goes away. Skipping it can interrupt running work immediately.

Consequence: when the maximum is too low, Pods remain Pending in the workload view, and users see slow or failed requests. Node count changes show up in Cloud Monitoring metrics for the cluster, and the related operations appear in Cloud Logging audit records.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a cluster with a node pool called batch-pool. Its maximum is 8 nodes, and during a nightly job some Pods show Pending because no node has enough free memory. The team decides to raise the pool's maximum to 12 without adding a new pool. Step 1: confirm in the workload view that the Pods are Pending for lack of memory. Step 2: edit batch-pool and set its maximum to 12. Step 3 is missing: it is the check that the change took effect, done in Cloud Monitoring by looking at the cluster's node count. Which completion of step 3 is correct?
choices: Look at the cluster's node count metric in Cloud Monitoring to see whether it rises above 8 as the autoscaler adds nodes.
Set the pool's minimum to 12 so the autoscaler starts at the new size.
Restart every node in batch-pool so the scheduler re-reads the new maximum.
Delete batch-pool and recreate it with a maximum of 12, so the existing nodes are kept.
questions.why: Node count changes appear in Cloud Monitoring metrics for the cluster, so checking that metric shows whether the autoscaler is actually adding nodes beyond the old maximum of 8.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a node pool in a GKE cluster?
choices: A single virtual machine that runs one container and nothing else.
A group of nodes in one cluster that share the same machine type and settings, and can be changed as a unit.
A list of Pods waiting for a node with enough free CPU or memory.
A set of clusters that share one network and one billing account.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a node pool as a group of nodes in one cluster that share machine type and settings, which is why each pool can be edited, added, or removed on its own.

questions.prompt: A retailer's payments-pool has a minimum of 4 nodes and a maximum of 4 nodes. During a sale, Pods stay Pending for a long time while CPU is full. Why does the autoscaler not add nodes?
choices: The maximum is 4, so the autoscaler is not allowed to add nodes beyond 4 even though Pods are waiting.
The minimum of 4 forces the autoscaler to wait until the pool is idle before adding any nodes.
The autoscaler only acts on pools whose minimum is lower than their maximum, so this pool is skipped.
Pending Pods are never a trigger for scaling; only CPU usage on existing nodes is.
questions.why: Autoscaling adds nodes only up to the pool's maximum, so with a maximum of 4 the autoscaler has no room to add a fifth node and the Pods remain Pending.

questions.prompt: A fintech team has a pool of 6 nodes and wants to move the pool to a larger machine size. Which action should come first?
choices: Delete the whole pool now, so the new larger pool can be created without any overlap.
Restart all six nodes at the same moment to speed up the change.
Drain the nodes so their Pods move off gracefully before the machines change.
Set the pool's minimum to zero, so the autoscaler removes all nodes on its own.
questions.why: Draining moves Pods off a node gracefully before it is changed or removed, and skipping it can interrupt running work immediately.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we split the cluster into two node pools instead of one large pool, and whether autoscaling will keep our costs under control. Explain to them what a node pool is, what autoscaling changes and does not change, and one limit or tradeoff they should weigh before raising the maximum.
lessons.modelAnswer: A node pool is a set of machines in one cluster that share a machine type and settings, so we can change or remove one group without touching the others. Splitting into two pools lets us run, for example, general workloads on one size and memory-heavy jobs on another, though each pool adds some management overhead. Autoscaling adjusts the number of nodes in a pool between the minimum and maximum we set. It reacts to Pods that cannot be scheduled and to nodes that are underused, so it helps match capacity to load. It does not reduce cost on its own, though: a higher maximum means the cluster may run more machines and cost more during peaks. Before raising the maximum, we should check the budget impact and confirm that the cloud project has enough quota for that many machines, since scale-up can stall when quota runs out.
rubricPoints: A node pool groups nodes that share machine type and settings, so each group can be changed independently.
Autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled and removes underused nodes, within a minimum and maximum.
Autoscaling does not by itself lower cost; a higher maximum can increase spend during peaks.
Raising the maximum can be limited by project quota, so scale-up may stall even with a higher setting.

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly console and CLI steps plus knowing where their effects appear in monitoring and logs, which is best learned by reading the product steps and checking them in a sandbox project.

lessons.plain: Kubernetes runs your app as small units called Pods, and it adds a few extra pieces so the app stays reachable and keeps its identity when things go wrong. A Pod is one running copy of your app. It can be replaced at any time, and the replacement usually gets a new internal address. A Service is a stable name and address that sends requests to whichever healthy Pods currently match it, so callers never have to track the moving copies. A StatefulSet is for apps that need each copy to keep a fixed name and its own storage, such as a database cluster. Think of Pods as workers who can be swapped out, Services as the front desk that always knows who is on duty, and StatefulSets as a roster that gives each person a permanent badge and locker.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a copy of your web app crashes and the system starts a replacement with a different internal address, should the people calling your app need to learn the new address? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers, which are packaged processes, that share a network address and storage volumes. Pods run on nodes, which are the virtual machines in the cluster. Pods are disposable. If a node fails or a Pod crashes, the system starts a replacement, and the replacement usually gets a different internal IP address. This works because Kubernetes treats Pods as interchangeable, so you manage a desired count rather than individual machines. A Service solves the moving-address problem. It is a stable virtual address and DNS name, which is a human-readable name that resolves to an address. A Service selects Pods using labels, which are key-value tags attached to each Pod. It keeps a running list of endpoints, meaning the Pods that currently match its selector and are ready to take traffic. A StatefulSet is a controller for workloads that need stable identity. Its Pods get ordered names such as db-0, db-1 and db-2, start and stop in sequence, and each keeps its own PersistentVolumeClaim, a request for storage that follows that Pod when it is rescheduled.

Worked example: a Service named web selects Pods labelled app=web. Step one, three Pods exist at 10.0.1.4, 10.0.2.7 and 10.0.3.9. Step two, the Pod at 10.0.2.7 crashes, and a replacement appears at 10.0.2.12. Step three, the Service removes the old address from its endpoints and adds the new one. Callers using the name web never notice.

Common mistake: a label typo. If the Service selector says app=webapp but the Pods say app=web, the Service has zero endpoints and every request fails, even though the Pods are healthy. Check the endpoints first.

Consequence in a running system: an empty endpoint list shows up as errors or timeouts at the load balancer and in container logs. It is the first thing to check when a deploy looks healthy but traffic fails.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company runs a StatefulSet named ledger with three replicas. It produces Pods ledger-0, ledger-1 and ledger-2, and each has its own PersistentVolumeClaim named data-ledger-0, data-ledger-1 and data-ledger-2. Step one: an operator deletes ledger-1 by mistake. Step two: the controller creates a replacement Pod, also named ledger-1, on a different node. Step three is missing. Which statement completes the sequence?
choices: The replacement creates a new empty volume called data-ledger-3 so the replica count stays at four.
The Service named ledger removes its record of ledger-1 and waits for an operator to restore the volume by hand.
The replacement is attached to the existing data-ledger-1 claim, so it can read the data ledger-1 wrote before it was deleted.
The replacement receives a random name and a new claim, because only the first Pod in a StatefulSet keeps its storage.
questions.why: The PersistentVolumeClaim belongs to the Pod's stable identity and follows that Pod when it is rescheduled, so the replacement reattaches data-ledger-1 rather than getting new storage.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a Service's endpoint list?
choices: The list of PersistentVolumeClaims that the Service has reserved for its Pods.
The Pods that currently match the Service's label selector and are ready to take traffic.
The DNS names that were registered for the Service when it was first created.
The list of every node in the cluster that is running at least one container.
questions.why: The teaching text defines endpoints as the Pods that match the selector and are ready to take traffic, which is the running list a Service keeps.

questions.prompt: A retail company's Service selects Pods with the label tier=api. Its three Pods are running and passing their checks, but they are labelled tier=API with capital letters. What does a caller see when it sends a request to the Service name?
choices: The Pods receive the request, but only after the Service restarts them with lowercase labels.
The Service has zero endpoints, so the request fails with errors or timeouts even though the Pods are healthy.
The request is routed to the Pods by their IP addresses because the names are close enough.
Kubernetes ignores label case, so the request succeeds with no visible difference.
questions.why: A selector that does not match the Pod labels leaves the Service with no endpoints, so traffic fails even when the Pods themselves are healthy, as the teaching text describes for label typos.

questions.prompt: A StatefulSet named ledger runs Pod ledger-0 on a node that fails. The system reschedules ledger-0 onto a healthy node. What happens to the storage that ledger-0 was using?
choices: The storage stays attached to the failed node, and the new ledger-0 has no access to it.
The storage is deleted with the failed node, and the new ledger-0 starts with an empty disk.
Its PersistentVolumeClaim follows the Pod to the new node, so ledger-0 keeps the data it had.
A fresh volume is created for the new ledger-0, and the old data is kept in a separate backup.
questions.why: The teaching text states that each StatefulSet Pod keeps its own PersistentVolumeClaim and that the claim follows the Pod when it is rescheduled, so the data stays with that Pod.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used Kubernetes what a Pod, a Service and a StatefulSet each do, and name one limit or tradeoff of the StatefulSet approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Pod is one running group of containers, and it is disposable: when it is replaced, it usually gets a new internal IP address. A Service gives a stable name and virtual address in front of a set of Pods. It finds those Pods by label and sends traffic only to the ones that are ready, so callers never track individual Pods. The limit to watch is the selector. If the labels do not match, the Service has no endpoints and quietly routes nothing. A StatefulSet is for apps that need stable identity, such as databases. Its Pods get fixed names like db-0 and db-1, start in order, and keep their own storage claims across restarts. The tradeoff is that ordered startup makes rollouts slower and more careful, and it does not replace backups. Deleting a StatefulSet may leave its storage claims behind, so check them afterwards and make sure you are not paying for disks nobody uses.
rubricPoints: A Pod is a disposable running unit whose internal address can change when replaced
A Service gives a stable name and address and routes only to ready Pods that match its labels
A StatefulSet gives Pods stable ordered names and per-Pod storage that survives rescheduling
Names a concrete limit, such as label mismatches leaving a Service with no endpoints, or slower ordered rollouts and storage left behind after deletion

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly concepts and console locations, and no listed mission or planned engine has the learner work with Kubernetes Pods, Services or StatefulSets.

lessons.plain: Autoscaling means a system changes how much capacity it has without a person editing it each time. On Kubernetes, which runs an app as many small units called Pods, there are two kinds. Horizontal autoscaling adds or removes copies of a Pod, like opening more checkout lanes when the queue grows. Vertical autoscaling changes how much CPU and memory each Pod is allowed, like giving one checkout lane a bigger till. Both watch usage and react, but they change different things, and if they both act on the same signal they can work against each other. This lesson explains what each one changes and how to tell whether it is working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app's copies are all running close to their CPU allowance during a traffic spike. Would you rather give each copy a bigger CPU allowance or run more copies, and what would you watch to tell whether your choice worked?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs; it holds one or more containers. A replica is one running copy of a Pod. A resource request is the CPU or memory a Pod is promised and scheduled against. Utilization is actual usage divided by that request, shown as a percentage.

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of replicas. It compares observed utilization with a target and calculates desired replicas as current replicas multiplied by observed utilization divided by target, rounded up. It works because more copies share the same load, so each copy's utilization falls toward the target.

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes the requests themselves. It recommends or applies new CPU and memory values based on past usage. Applying a change usually restarts the Pod, so it is disruptive for a single-copy workload.

Worked example: two replicas each request 200 millicores of CPU, the target is 60 percent, and each replica uses 300 millicores. Utilization is 300 divided by 200, which is 150 percent. Desired replicas are ceil(2 x 150 / 60), which is ceil(5), so 5. When load falls to 60 millicores per replica, utilization is 30 percent and desired replicas become ceil(5 x 30 / 60), which is 3.

Common mistake: letting the horizontal and vertical scalers both act on CPU for the same workload. The vertical scaler changes the requests, which changes the denominator in the horizontal calculation, so the two keep chasing each other. Leaving requests unset is also a mistake, because then there is no utilization to measure.

Consequence in a running system: if requests are set too high, utilization looks low, the horizontal scaler does not add Pods during a real surge, and users see slow responses even though the nodes appear underused.

questions.prompt: A team runs an image-resizing service with 4 replicas. Each replica requests 500 millicores of CPU and uses 455 millicores on average. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler target is 70 percent. Step 1: utilization is 455 divided by 500, which is 91 percent. Step 2 is missing. It is the calculation of desired replicas from the current replica count, the observed utilization, and the target, rounded up to a whole number. What is the result of Step 2?
choices: 4 x 91 / 70 = 5.2, so the scaler adds 0.2 of a replica
ceil(4 x 70 / 91) = 4, because the target is divided by the observed utilization
ceil(4 x 91 / 70) = 6, because 4 x 91 / 70 is 5.2, which rounds up to 6
floor(4 x 91 / 70) = 5, because the result is rounded down to avoid over-scaling
questions.why: Desired replicas equal current replicas times observed utilization divided by target, rounded up, so 4 x 91 / 70 = 5.2 becomes 6.

questions.prompt: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is set to target 60 percent CPU utilization for a Deployment whose containers have no CPU resource request. Why can the autoscaler not do its job?
choices: It can only scale Pods that have a memory request, so it ignores CPU entirely
It waits for the Vertical Pod Autoscaler to set a request before it reads any metrics
It treats a missing request as 100 percent and scales the Deployment to its maximum replica count
Utilization is actual usage divided by the request, and with no request there is no denominator to compute a percentage from
questions.why: Utilization is defined as usage divided by the resource request, so without a request the autoscaler has no percentage to compare with its target.

questions.prompt: A single-replica payment worker has a Vertical Pod Autoscaler set to apply its recommendations automatically, and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that also targets CPU on the same worker. What is the main operational risk?
choices: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes requests, which shifts the utilization the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler measures, so the two can keep reacting to each other and applying a change restarts the only Pod
Nothing changes, because the Vertical Pod Autoscaler only affects memory and never touches CPU requests
Both autoscalers will double the replica count every minute until the cluster runs out of nodes
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler will refuse to start because two autoscalers exist for one workload
questions.why: Changing CPU requests alters the utilization denominator, so the two scalers can chase each other, and an applied vertical change restarts the single Pod, which is disruptive.

questions.prompt: A service runs 3 replicas. Each replica requests 250 millicores of CPU and currently uses 100 millicores. The horizontal target is 50 percent. Based only on the horizontal calculation, what should the replica count become?
choices: 1 replica, because each replica is only using 40 percent of its request
5 replicas, because the scaler doubles the count whenever utilization is below target
2 replicas, because 3 x 40 / 50 is 2.4 and the scaler always removes one replica when load is low
3 replicas, because ceil(3 x 40 / 50) is ceil(2.4), which is 3, so no change is needed
questions.why: Utilization is 100 divided by 250, which is 40 percent, and ceil(3 x 40 / 50) = ceil(2.4) = 3, so the count stays the same.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between horizontal and vertical Pod autoscaling, and name one limit or tradeoff you would keep in mind before turning both on for the same service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Horizontal autoscaling changes how many copies of a Pod are running. The autoscaler measures usage against the Pod's CPU or memory request and adds or removes replicas to bring average utilization near a target. Vertical autoscaling leaves the replica count alone and changes each Pod's requests, so each copy gets a bigger or smaller allowance. The tradeoff is that vertical changes usually restart Pods, which interrupts a single-copy service, and that changing requests shifts the utilization number the horizontal scaler relies on. So before enabling both on the same workload, I would keep them on different signals or use the vertical scaler only in recommend mode, and I would check scaling events and Pod restarts after any change.
rubricPoints: Horizontal autoscaling changes the number of Pod replicas, while vertical autoscaling changes each Pod's CPU and memory requests.
Horizontal scaling compares measured utilization against a target, and utilization is measured against the requests.
Applying vertical changes usually restarts Pods, which is a disruption to plan for.
Running both scalers on the same CPU signal can make them conflict, and a learner should name a way to avoid that.

suggested.rationale: The planned autoscale engine would let the learner set and observe scaling policies, which is the hands-on practice this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A Pod is the smallest unit a Kubernetes cluster runs: one or more containers that share a network address and storage. When you tell the cluster how much processor time and memory a Pod needs, that statement is its resource request. In GKE Autopilot, Google's managed Kubernetes mode where Google runs the machines for you, the request does real work: the platform uses it to decide how much capacity to provide and what you are billed for. Setting the number close to what your app really uses keeps it running smoothly without paying for capacity it never touches.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your app requests 256 MiB of memory but actually needs about 900 MiB under heavy traffic. What do you expect to happen as load rises, and how would your answer change if you requested 4 GiB instead?
lessons.teach:
A resource request is the amount of CPU and memory a container asks the cluster to reserve for it. A resource limit is a ceiling the container may not exceed. In GKE Autopilot, you do not manage the machines underneath, so the requests in your Pod spec drive both placement and billing: Autopilot provisions enough capacity to satisfy them and charges for the requested amounts. Autopilot also enforces minimum and maximum amounts per Pod, and it raises requests that fall below the minimum.

Worked example. A Deployment's container asks for 500 millicores of CPU and 1 GiB of memory. Step 1: Autopilot reads the requests and provisions capacity that fits them. Step 2: the scheduler places the Pod on that capacity. Step 3: under load the app's memory climbs toward 1 GiB. Step 4: if the container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel stops it, the status shows OOMKilled (out of memory killed), and the kubelet restarts it. Step 5: you see the restarts and the memory use in the workload's metrics and in kubectl describe pod.

Common mistake: assuming that setting only a limit is enough. In Autopilot, if you set a limit without a request, the request is set equal to the limit, so you pay for the full limit every hour even if the app idles. The consequence in a running system is clear: requests set too low cause restarts and throttling under load, while requests set far too high waste money and can make scaling look expensive. Changing requests in a Deployment rolls out new Pods with the new values.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a route-planning container in GKE Autopilot. Its Pod spec requests 200 millicores of CPU (a millicore is one thousandth of a CPU core) and 640 MiB of memory, and sets no limit. Step 1: the team applies the Deployment, and Autopilot reads the requests and provisions capacity that fits them. Step 2: the scheduler places the Pod on that capacity. Step 3: [blank]. Step 4: the new Pods run, and the billed memory drops to match the lower request. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Raise the memory limit to 4 GiB so that Autopilot shrinks the request to fit the limit automatically.
Set the CPU limit to zero so that Autopilot ignores the memory request altogether.
Lower the memory request in the Pod spec toward observed use and reapply the Deployment, which rolls out new Pods with the new values.
Delete the old Pods by hand, because Autopilot keeps the previous requests stored on the node.
questions.why: Requests are read from the Pod spec, and changing them and reapplying the Deployment rolls out new Pods carrying the new values, so the lowered request is what reduces billing.

questions.prompt: In GKE Autopilot, what is the main job of a container's resource request?
choices: It chooses the size of the disk attached to the node.
It sets the hard ceiling the container may not exceed.
It tells the cluster how much CPU and memory to reserve, which drives placement and billing.
It sets how many replicas the Deployment keeps running.
questions.why: A request is the amount of CPU and memory the cluster reserves for the container, and Autopilot both places the Pod and bills based on those requested amounts.

questions.prompt: A fintech team sets only a CPU limit of 1.5 cores on a container in Autopilot. The app sits idle most of the day, yet the bill reflects the full 1.5 cores every hour. What explains this?
choices: Autopilot charges for the limit whenever the container exceeds it, and the app briefly does.
Autopilot ignores limits for billing, so the charge comes from a separate default request of 1 core.
The scheduler reserved 1.5 cores by coincidence on a busy node.
With no request set, Autopilot sets the request equal to the limit, so the full 1.5 cores are billed.
questions.why: In Autopilot a limit with no request makes the request equal to the limit, so the full amount is billed even when the app is idle.

questions.prompt: A service has a memory request of 512 MiB and a memory limit of 1 GiB. Under a traffic spike its memory climbs to 1.2 GiB. What happens, and where would you see it?
choices: The container is stopped with an OOMKilled status and the kubelet restarts it; the restarts and memory use show in the workload's metrics and in kubectl describe pod.
The Pod is moved to a different node, and nothing is written to logs or metrics.
The memory request is lowered to 512 MiB automatically, and the container keeps running at the same speed.
Autopilot raises the request to 1.2 GiB, and the Pod keeps running with no visible change.
questions.why: Going above the memory limit causes the kernel to stop the container with OOMKilled, the kubelet restarts it, and the restarts and memory use appear in workload metrics and kubectl describe pod.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Pod resource request does in GKE Autopilot, then name one limit or tradeoff of setting requests too low and one of setting them too high.
lessons.modelAnswer: A resource request tells GKE Autopilot how much CPU and memory a Pod needs. Autopilot uses that number to provision capacity for the Pod and to bill for it, so it is not just a hint to the scheduler. If the request is too low, the app can be starved under load: memory overuse gets the container killed with OOMKilled, and CPU overuse gets it throttled. If the request is too high, the app runs fine but you pay for capacity it never uses. You also cannot rely on the limit alone, because in Autopilot a limit without a request makes the request equal to the limit. To check the choice, compare requested against actual usage in the workload's metrics over a normal traffic cycle before settling on a number.
rubricPoints: A resource request is the amount of CPU and memory the Pod is guaranteed and that Autopilot provisions and bills for.
Requests are distinct from limits, which cap what a container may use.
Too-low requests cause throttling or OOMKilled restarts under load.
Too-high requests waste money, and requests set without limits or with limits only behave differently in Autopilot.

suggested.rationale: A running-system scenario where a Pod restarts under load and the learner must choose between request and limit adds more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Once an application is running, the team often needs to ship a new version without breaking the people who depend on the old one. On Cloud Run, a service that runs containers answering web requests and scales them up and down for you, each deployment creates a revision: a frozen snapshot of the container image and its settings. Traffic splitting is the control that decides what share of incoming requests goes to each revision. You might send 5 percent to the new version, watch its errors and response times, then raise its share or send everything back to the old one. The same idea applies to the functions that run on the same platform and, in a more hand-built way, to applications on Kubernetes clusters.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run a web app that serves real users and want to test a new version on a small slice of live traffic before everyone gets it, what would the platform need to let you do, and what could go wrong if it could only switch every user to the new version at once?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A revision is an immutable version of a Cloud Run service: each deploy that changes the container image or configuration creates one, and it keeps its settings even after newer revisions exist. A service is the named endpoint clients call; it points at a set of revisions through its traffic configuration. Traffic configuration is a list of revisions, each with a percentage, and the percentages must add up to 100. A tag is a named address that reaches one specific revision directly, regardless of the split, which lets you test a new revision before any user sees it.

Why it works. Because old revisions stay alive and addressable, rolling back is a change of percentages, not a rebuild. The platform routes each incoming request according to the weights, so the split is roughly proportional over many requests, not a guarantee for any single user.

Worked example. A service called orders-api sends 100 percent of traffic to revision 007. You deploy revision 008 with no traffic, so it receives 0 percent. You tag it canary and check its logs through the canary address. Then you move 10 percent of traffic to 008. Error rate for 008 in Cloud Monitoring stays flat, so you raise it to 50, then to 100. Each step is one traffic update.

Common mistake. Deploying with the default behaviour, which sends 100 percent of traffic to the newest revision immediately, and then discovering the bug from user complaints. A second mistake is editing percentages and leaving the total at something other than 100.

Consequence. A bad split sends real customer requests to broken code. The fast fix is to shift weight back to the known-good revision, which takes effect within seconds, while the bad revision stays available for inspection. Cloud Run functions use the same revision model, so the same steps apply. On GKE there is no single built-in traffic switch on a Service; weighted routing is done by a routing layer such as a Gateway API route or a service mesh, or approximated by adjusting replica counts. Traffic splitting is a routing decision separate from the deploy itself, so a newly deployed revision can be held at zero percent until it earns traffic.

questions.prompt: A team runs a Cloud Run service called ledger-webhook. Revision rev-41 receives 100 percent of traffic. They deploy rev-42 with no traffic, tag it preview, and check its logs at the preview address, which shows no errors. They then set rev-41 to 70 and rev-42 to 30. Monitoring now shows rev-42 returning server errors on about a third of requests. The team wants users back on the known-good code within seconds, and the failing revision should remain available for inspection. Which single traffic change completes this recovery?
choices: Delete rev-42 and redeploy rev-41 from its source code so the service is rebuilt.
Rebuild the container image from the previous commit, then send 100 percent of traffic to that new build.
Set rev-42 to 100 percent and rev-41 to 0 percent so the new code takes over fully.
Set rev-41 to 100 percent and rev-42 to 0 percent, leaving rev-42 deployed for inspection.
questions.why: Shifting weight back to the known-good revision is the fast rollback, and because revisions are immutable and stay addressable, the failing revision can be kept for inspection while receiving no traffic.

questions.prompt: A pricing-engine service on Cloud Run has been deployed three times in a month. In the platform's terms, what is each of those deploys producing?
choices: A tag that points only at whichever revision received the most recent traffic.
A single endpoint name that clients call and that is updated in place each time.
A traffic percentage that is recalculated automatically each time the service is deployed.
An immutable revision that keeps its own settings even after newer revisions exist.
questions.why: Each deploy that changes the image or configuration creates a new revision, which is immutable and keeps its settings, while the service is the endpoint that points at revisions through its traffic configuration.

questions.prompt: An image-resize service on Cloud Run has two revisions. An operator sets revision A to 55 percent and revision B to 40 percent and saves. What happens?
choices: The platform rescales both values to 50 percent each so the total becomes 100.
All traffic goes to revision A because it holds the larger share.
The leftover 5 percent is sent automatically to the newest revision.
The configuration is rejected because the percentages must add up to 100.
questions.why: Traffic configuration requires the percentages to total exactly 100, so a total of 95 is an error that must be corrected rather than silently adjusted by the platform.

questions.prompt: A team running a checkout Deployment on GKE wants to send 90 percent of requests to version 2 and 10 percent to version 1. Which statement is accurate?
choices: A Deployment accepts a traffic annotation that the cluster reads directly to split requests.
GKE has no single built-in traffic switch on a Service, so a routing layer such as a Gateway API route or service mesh is needed, or replica counts can approximate the split.
Only Cloud Run functions support weighted splits, so the team must move the checkout to Cloud Run.
A GKE Service has a built-in weight field, so the team sets it to 90 and 10.
questions.why: On GKE, weighted routing is not a single built-in switch on a Service and instead requires a routing layer or an approximation through replica counts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how traffic splitting lets you release a new version of a Cloud Run service safely, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deploying a new version on Cloud Run creates a new revision, but it does not have to receive traffic straight away. I would deploy it with no traffic, check it through its tag address, then send a small percentage, such as 5 or 10 percent, to the new revision while the rest stays on the known-good one. I watch error rate and latency in Cloud Monitoring and logs for that revision. If it is healthy I raise the share step by step; if not, I set the old revision back to 100 percent, which takes effect in seconds. The main limit is that the split is proportional across many requests, not per user, so a small share may not expose a rare bug, and sessions can bounce between versions. Also, the old revision must still exist and be compatible with the database schema, or a rollback can fail.
rubricPoints: A new revision is created on deploy and can be sent zero traffic until it is checked.
Traffic percentages across revisions must total 100 and are adjusted in small steps while watching metrics and logs.
Rollback means shifting weight back to a known-good revision, which is fast because old revisions remain.
A tradeoff exists: splits are proportional over many requests, not guaranteed per user, and compatibility between versions still matters.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner roll back a bad release quickly and then fix it forward, which is the same day-2 reasoning this traffic-shifting objective needs.

lessons.plain: Cloud Run runs your application in small copies called instances, and autoscaling is the set of rules that decides how many copies exist at any moment. When requests arrive, Cloud Run adds instances, and when traffic drops, it removes them. You control the boundaries: a floor (the minimum number of instances), a ceiling (the maximum), and how many requests one copy handles at once. Getting these right means users rarely wait on a slow start, costs stay predictable, and a sudden spike cannot overwhelm the systems behind the app.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a web app suddenly receives ten times its normal traffic, what would you expect to happen to the number of running copies of the app, and what would you want to limit?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. An instance is one running copy of your container. Concurrency is how many requests a single instance handles at the same time; the default is 80 and it can be raised to 1000. Minimum instances is the number Cloud Run keeps running even with no traffic; keeping it above zero avoids cold starts, the delay while a new copy boots. Maximum instances is the ceiling on how many copies may run at once. Cloud Run is request-driven: it adds instances when in-flight requests exceed what existing instances can absorb, and removes idle ones after a period with no traffic. Why it works: scaling is largely arithmetic. If each instance handles 20 requests at once and 150 are in flight, roughly 150 divided by 20 instances are needed, rounded up. Raising concurrency means fewer instances for the same load, but only if the code is safe to run concurrently and each instance has enough CPU and memory. Worked example: a service with minimum 1, maximum 10 and concurrency 20 receives 150 concurrent requests. Required instances is 150 divided by 20, which is 7.5, rounded up to 8. Cloud Run scales to 8, inside the ceiling of 10. At 300 concurrent requests it would need 15 but stops at 10, so the excess requests are delayed and then rejected with errors. Common mistake: setting maximum instances as a cost guard without checking the database behind the app. Ten instances each opening 20 connections can exhaust a database's connection limit long before the bill becomes a problem. Consequence: when the ceiling is reached, latency rises and error responses appear, visible in the instance count and request latency metrics in Cloud Monitoring and in the request logs in Cloud Logging. Scaling settings are part of the service configuration, and changes apply to instances started after the change.

questions.prompt: A support dashboard service on Cloud Run has concurrency set to 40 and maximum instances set to 6. At peak, 260 requests are in flight at the same moment. Step 1: divide 260 by 40, which gives 6.5. Step 2: the number of instances needed is the first whole number at or above 6.5, which is ___. Step 3: because the ceiling is 6, Cloud Run runs 6 instances and the extra requests wait, then fail if they cannot be served.
choices: 7, because fractional instances round up to the next whole instance
8, because one spare instance is always added
6, because the fraction is dropped
6.5 instances, since Cloud Run can run partial copies
questions.why: Instance counts are whole numbers and the calculation rounds up, so 6.5 becomes 7 instances needed, which the ceiling of 6 then caps.

questions.prompt: A checkout service gets almost no traffic overnight, but the first customer request each morning is noticeably slow because a new container has to boot. Which setting should the team change so that some copies stay running even when no requests arrive?
choices: Concurrency, raised so each copy takes more requests
Minimum instances, set above zero so copies stay warm
Request timeout, lengthened so slow boots are not cut off
Maximum instances, raised so more copies can start in the morning
questions.why: Minimum instances is the count of copies Cloud Run keeps running with no traffic, and keeping it above zero avoids the boot delay that causes slow first requests.

questions.prompt: A report generator runs with concurrency 10 and maximum instances 20. Under a steady load of 90 requests in flight, the code is confirmed safe to run concurrently and each copy has ample memory. The team raises concurrency to 30 without changing the load. Roughly how many instances does Cloud Run now need for that load?
choices: 10 instances, which is the old concurrency value
3 instances, from 90 divided by 30
30 instances, one per concurrency slot
9 instances, the same as before the change
questions.why: Required instances is the in-flight request count divided by the concurrency per instance, so 90 divided by 30 gives 3, and raising concurrency reduces the instance count for the same load.

questions.prompt: A batch resize service has maximum instances set to 5 and starts returning error responses during a traffic spike. The team wants to confirm that the ceiling is the cause. Which place shows instance count flattening at 5 while request latency climbs, and where are the individual failed requests recorded?
choices: Instance count and request latency metrics in Cloud Monitoring, with the failed requests in Cloud Logging request logs
The monthly billing report, with the failed requests listed by project
The storage bucket size chart in Cloud Storage, with failures listed by object
The VPC firewall rule logs, which show every dropped request by service
questions.why: When the maximum instance ceiling is reached, the instance count metric stops rising while latency and errors increase, and those patterns appear in Cloud Monitoring metrics and Cloud Logging request logs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what minimum instances and maximum instances each control in a Cloud Run service, and name one tradeoff of setting the minimum above zero.
lessons.modelAnswer: Minimum instances is the floor: Cloud Run keeps that many copies running even when nobody is calling the service. Maximum instances is the ceiling: Cloud Run will never start more copies than that, no matter how much traffic arrives. The tradeoff of a minimum above zero is cost and idle capacity. You pay for those warm instances even at 3 a.m., but in exchange new requests avoid the cold-start delay while a container boots. The ceiling has its own tradeoff. It protects the budget and downstream systems like databases, but if it is set too low, traffic above the limit slows down or fails. So I would check the ceiling against the connection limits of whatever the app depends on, and watch instance count and error metrics in Cloud Monitoring after any change.
rubricPoints: Minimum instances sets the floor of running copies and reduces cold starts
Maximum instances sets the ceiling and protects cost and downstream systems
Setting minimum above zero trades idle cost for faster response to new requests
A low ceiling causes slowdowns or errors under load, so it must be checked against dependencies

suggested.rationale: Adjusting minimum, maximum and concurrency and then observing the effect on instance count is best practised in the planned autoscaling policies engine, since no current mission covers Cloud Run.

lessons.plain: Some programs, such as machine learning training and video processing, run much faster on specialised chips than on ordinary processors. A GPU (graphics processing unit) is one such chip. A TPU (tensor processing unit) is Google's own chip built for similar heavy maths. Cloud providers let you attach these chips to a virtual machine or to a cluster node instead of buying hardware. The hard part in day-2 work is that the workload is already live, so adding a chip means planning a restart, checking that drivers and quota are in place, and confirming the new hardware is actually being used.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service runs on a virtual machine that is serving users right now, and its team wants that machine to have a GPU. Would you expect to add the GPU with zero interruption, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
An accelerator is extra hardware, such as a GPU or TPU, that handles specific kinds of work faster than a general-purpose CPU. Attaching one means telling the cloud platform that a particular machine should have that hardware. A virtual machine (VM) is a computer that runs as software inside the provider's data centre. A quota is a per-region limit on how many of a resource you may use, and you can run out of accelerator quota even when a region offers the hardware. A driver is the software that lets the operating system talk to the chip; without it the hardware sits idle. Hardware attachment is usually a stop-and-edit operation: you stop the VM, change its accelerator setting, and start it again. Machines with GPUs generally cannot be live-migrated during host maintenance, so their maintenance behaviour is usually set to stop rather than move.

Worked example. A VM is running and serving traffic. Step 1: check that the zone has the GPU model and that the project has quota for it. Step 2: stop the VM, which ends the service. Step 3: edit the VM and add one GPU of the chosen model, with maintenance set to terminate. Step 4: start the VM. Step 5: confirm the driver is installed and that the chip is visible from inside the operating system. Step 6: watch GPU utilisation in Cloud Monitoring while the workload runs. If utilisation stays near zero, the application is not using the chip.

Common mistake: assuming an attached GPU speeds up the application by itself. The code must be written or configured to use the accelerator, and the driver must be present.

Consequence: the stop in step 2 is an outage for that machine. An external IP that was not reserved may also change when the VM restarts, so anything that depends on it can break.

Adding an accelerator to a running workload is a planned change with downtime, a quota check, a driver check, and a usage check.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs a nightly image-labelling job on a VM named labeler-7. The zone offers the T4 GPU model, and the lab's project already has quota for two T4s. At 22:00 the on-call engineer stopped labeler-7 after notifying the team, edited it to add two T4 GPUs with maintenance set to terminate, and started it at 22:15. The driver is installed and both GPUs appear inside the operating system. The engineer then launched the labelling job with its existing configuration, which was written for CPU only, and reported the change as complete because the VM started without errors. Which step is missing from this change?
choices: Re-check zone GPU availability after the VM restarts.
Confirm the job is set to use the GPUs, then check utilisation in Cloud Monitoring.
Reserve a static external IP before stopping the VM.
Set maintenance back to migrate for live moves.
questions.why: An attached GPU only helps if the application is configured to use it, and the utilisation chart in Cloud Monitoring is where you confirm the chip is actually doing work.

questions.prompt: A company's VM runs a video transcoding service that uses only the CPU. Its owner asks whether adding a GPU to that VM will, by itself, make transcoding faster. Which answer is correct?
choices: Yes, but only once the VM has been live-migrated to a new host.
No, a GPU must be ordered separately from the cloud provider before it can be attached.
No, the software must be set to use the accelerator, and the driver must be present.
Yes, the operating system uses an attached GPU automatically for all tasks.
questions.why: An accelerator is only used when the application is written or configured to use it and the driver is installed, so attaching hardware alone does not speed up a CPU-only program.

questions.prompt: A team in a project tries to add one GPU to a VM in a zone that offers that GPU model. The edit request is refused. Which cause should they check first?
choices: The VM's boot disk is too small to hold a GPU driver.
The project's accelerator quota for that model in that region is zero or used up.
The operating system image is missing a GPU driver, which blocks the edit.
The VM needs a live-migration policy set before any edit is allowed.
questions.why: Quota is a per-region limit on accelerator use, so a refused add in a zone that offers the model is most often caused by the project having no quota left for it.

questions.prompt: A web service runs on a VM whose external IP address was never reserved, and clients call that address directly. An engineer adds a GPU by stopping the VM, editing it, and starting it again. Afterwards the clients cannot connect. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The VM was live-migrated, which changes only its internal address.
The external IP may have changed when the VM restarted, because it was not reserved.
The GPU blocks incoming network traffic until a driver is installed.
The provider throttled the service because the GPU quota was used up.
questions.why: An unreserved external IP can change when a stopped VM starts again, so anything calling the old address breaks, which is a consequence of the stop-and-start step rather than of the GPU itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what is involved in giving an already running workload a GPU or TPU. Name the main interruption or tradeoff, and one thing you would verify after the change.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a single VM, you usually cannot add a GPU while it runs. You check that the zone offers that accelerator and that the project has quota, then stop the VM, edit the accelerator setting, and start it again. That means the service is down for the restart, and an external IP that was not reserved may change, so we should reserve it first. GPU machines typically cannot be live-migrated, so maintenance is set to stop rather than move. After the restart I would confirm the driver is installed and the chip is visible to the operating system. Then I would check GPU utilisation in Cloud Monitoring while real traffic runs, because an attached GPU that the application does not use is wasted money.
rubricPoints: Adding an accelerator to a VM usually requires stopping and restarting it, which causes downtime
Check zone availability and accelerator quota before starting
The driver must be installed and the chip must be visible to the operating system
Confirm actual use through utilisation metrics, since attachment alone does not speed up the application

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a live capacity request, with its downtime, quota and usage-check trade-offs, teaches the decision better than a list of console steps.

lessons.plain: An AI agent is a program that takes a goal, decides on its next steps, and calls tools such as databases or other services to get work done. Deploying an agent means placing its code onto a hosting service so other people or apps can reach it over the network, without anyone keeping a server running by hand. Agent Runtime is Google Cloud's managed place for running deployed agents: you hand over the agent code and its list of required libraries, the platform starts it, gives it an address, and handles scaling. Your job as the engineer is to get it deployed correctly, confirm it answers, and know where to look when it misbehaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you deploy an agent to a managed service instead of a server you run yourself, what do you think you no longer have to do, and what do you still have to get right?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. An agent is software that uses a language model to decide what to do next and calls tools to act on that decision. A runtime is the environment that executes code. A managed runtime is one where the cloud provider runs the machines, patches them, and scales them for you. A deployment is the act of placing a specific version of your agent into that runtime so it becomes live. An endpoint is the network address callers use to reach the running agent. A service account is the identity the running agent uses when it calls other Google Cloud services, and it needs its own permissions.

Why it works: you describe the agent in code, plus a dependency file listing the libraries it needs at specific versions. The platform packages a copy, starts instances, routes requests to them, and adds or removes instances as traffic changes. You are not logging into a host to install things by hand.

Worked example: a dispatch-support team has a small agent that reads a question and calls a shipment-status tool. Step 1: write the agent code and a dependency list with pinned versions. Step 2: choose a Google Cloud project and region. Step 3: run the deploy, which packages the code, builds it, and starts it. Step 4: record the resource identifier and endpoint the deployment returns. Step 5: send one test question and confirm the answer is sensible. Step 6: open the logs for that agent and find the request you just made, with its timestamp and any error.

Common mistake: leaving dependencies unpinned, so a library update released later breaks the build even though no code changed. Another is forgetting that the agent's service account lacks permission to read the tool's data source, so answers fail with permission errors.

Consequence: a permission problem shows up as errors in the agent's logs, and a rising error count in monitoring is usually the first sign. Treat each deployment as a version change, and keep a known-good version available until the new one passes its test.

questions.prompt: A claims-intake team at an insurance firm deploys an agent that answers questions about policy wording by calling a clause-search tool. Their dependency file pins every library version, and the deploy succeeds and returns a resource identifier and an endpoint. A test question then returns an error. The agent's logs for that request show a permission denial when the agent tries to read the clause-search data source. Steps already done: (1) they found the failing request in the logs using its timestamp; (2) they confirmed that the agent's service account is the identity making the call. Missing step: one action is still needed before the test is retried. Which step completes the fix?
choices: Grant the agent's service account permission to read the clause-search data source, then send the test question again
Create a new deployment in a different region, since regions control which data sources an agent may read
Turn off logging so the permission denial stops appearing and the endpoint returns a clean answer
Remove the version pins from the dependency file so the build pulls the newest libraries
questions.why: The agent's service account is its own identity and needs its own permissions, so granting it read access to the data source fixes the denial the logs already showed.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a managed runtime on Google Cloud, as the teaching text describes it?
choices: A runtime where you log into each host yourself to install libraries and patch the operating system
A runtime that only runs agents written in one programming language and cannot call tools
A runtime where the cloud provider runs the machines, patches them, and scales them for you
A runtime that stores the agent's logs but does not execute any of the agent's code
questions.why: The teaching text defines a managed runtime as one where the provider runs, patches, and scales the machines, so the team does not manage hosts by hand.

questions.prompt: A team's agent deploys cleanly for months. After a library it depends on releases a new version, the next deploy fails, although nobody changed the agent's code. Which explanation fits the teaching text best?
choices: The runtime switched from managed to self-hosted automatically, which always breaks builds
The endpoint address changed when the library was released, so callers can no longer reach the agent
The dependency list did not pin the library version, so the build picked up a newer release that broke it
The service account was deleted when the library was updated, removing the agent's identity
questions.why: Unpinned dependencies let a later library release change what gets built, which breaks the deploy even when the agent's own code is unchanged.

questions.prompt: After a new agent version is deployed, the error count in monitoring starts rising. Which action best follows the teaching text's advice for handling a deployment as a version change?
choices: Delete the previous version immediately so only one version exists and billing stays simple
Edit the new version in place without redeploying, so the endpoint stays the same and no record is kept
Keep the known-good version available until the new version passes its test, then decide whether to move traffic
Remove the service account so the new version cannot read the data source and fail more clearly
questions.why: The teaching text says to treat each deployment as a version change and keep a known-good version available until the new one passes its test.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what deploying an agent to Agent Runtime does, and name one limit or tradeoff you would check before calling the deployment ready for real users.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deploying to Agent Runtime means packaging the agent's code and pinned dependencies and running them on Google Cloud's managed infrastructure. We do not manage the servers, and the platform gives the agent an endpoint and scales it with traffic. The tradeoff is that we depend on the platform's runtime rules and on the agent's service account having exactly the permissions it needs, so I would check that before go-live. I would also confirm that the new version answers a test request and that its logs and error metrics look normal, since a deploy can succeed while the agent still fails when it calls a tool.
rubricPoints: Describes the deployment as packaging the agent code and dependencies onto a managed runtime
Notes that the platform handles servers, scaling, and the endpoint
Names a real limit, such as the service account needing correct permissions or dependency pinning
Says to verify with a test request and check logs or error metrics after deploying

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers deploying managed AI agents, so the learner should read the console and product facts and then check the logs.

lessons.plain: A notebook in this context is a web-based workspace where you write and run code in cells, usually Python, and see the results directly below each cell. Workbench runs that workspace on a managed cloud machine, so you do not install anything on your own laptop. Managing notebooks is the day-to-day upkeep: starting and stopping the machine, choosing its size, setting it to shut down when nobody is using it, keeping work saved somewhere safe, and removing what is no longer needed. BigQuery also has a notebook experience that runs queries against your data from the same kind of workspace. The core skill is noticing which machines are still running and costing money, and knowing what each action does to the work stored on them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A data scientist left a notebook server running over the weekend with a large accelerator attached, and nobody has used it since Friday. Before reading anything, what do you think is the cheapest safe action to take, and what would you worry about losing?
lessons.teach:
A notebook server is the virtual machine that actually runs your code. The notebook is the document you see in the browser; the server holds the Python environment, installed libraries, and the attached disk. Two states matter day to day. A running instance is powered on and billed for its processor and any accelerator. A stopped instance keeps its disk but is not billed for the processor. Deleting an instance removes the machine and its disk, so any work that exists only on that machine is gone.

Why this works: notebook servers separate compute from storage. You pay for the processor while it runs, and the disk persists across stops. The usual pattern is to stop an instance when idle, resize its machine type when you need more memory or an accelerator, and enable an idle-shutdown setting so an abandoned server stops itself after a set period without activity.

Worked example. A team has a notebook server with an accelerator. Step 1: in the Workbench instance list, the status column reads running. Step 2: usage metrics show no activity for three days. Step 3: confirm the notebook files are saved to a shared repository or a Cloud Storage bucket, not only on the local disk. Step 4: stop the instance. Its disk stays, and accelerator billing stops. Step 5: start it later to resume with the same environment.

Common mistake: treating stop and delete as the same action, or deleting a server before confirming its important files live somewhere durable.

Consequence: an idle accelerated server left running can cost far more per day than a small one, and the cost appears in billing rather than as an error. BigQuery notebook queries are billed by the data scanned or compute used, so a cell that rescans a large table repeatedly costs money even when the notebook looks quiet. Regular review of running instances and query activity is part of day-2 operations.

questions.prompt: A research group called Kestrel Bio runs its analysis from a notebook server. One notebook cell sends a BigQuery query against a 4 TB raw table inside a loop of 50 iterations, and the monthly BigQuery charges have jumped. Their fix has four steps. Step 1: open the job history and confirm each loop iteration scans the full raw table. Step 2: identify which columns and rows the analysis actually needs. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: point the loop at the new table and rerun one iteration to check the output matches the old result. Which action belongs in step 3?
choices: Stop the notebook server so the queries cannot run until the bill has been reviewed
Create a smaller intermediate table holding only the needed columns and rows, built once from the raw table
Enable idle-shutdown on the server so it stops after a set period without activity
Resize the notebook server to a larger machine type so each query finishes faster
questions.why: BigQuery charges follow the data scanned, so building one reduced table once lets every loop iteration scan a small table instead of the 4 TB raw table, while the other choices either change the processor or address a server that is not idle.

questions.prompt: A small team's notebook server has been stopped for three weeks. What is the state of its disk and its billing?
choices: The disk is deleted and the processor is not billed
The disk is kept but the machine is removed from the instance list
The disk is kept and the processor is not billed
The disk is kept and the processor is still billed at a reduced rate
questions.why: A stopped instance keeps its disk while the processor, which is what the instance is billed for while running, is not billed.

questions.prompt: An analyst at a logistics firm deletes a notebook server she no longer uses. Her Python notebook files were saved only on that server's local disk, and she never copied them anywhere else. What is the consequence?
choices: The files are kept for a grace period and can be restored from the instance list
The files are lost, because deleting the instance removes the machine and its disk
The files move automatically to the notebook's browser cache
Nothing is lost, because stopping and deleting an instance do the same thing
questions.why: Deleting an instance removes both the machine and its disk, so any work that existed only on that machine is gone, which is why important files should live somewhere durable first.

questions.prompt: A data team at a retail company has a notebook cell that queries a 900 GB sales table every 10 minutes from a scheduled loop, and the server's processor usage is low. Where should the team look first to understand the rising cost?
choices: The stop and start history of the instance, because frequent restarts are the usual cost driver
The instance's disk size, because a larger disk always raises BigQuery charges
The BigQuery query history for the data scanned per run, because query billing follows the data scanned or compute used
The server's processor utilisation graph, because low processor use means the cost is coming from the server
questions.why: BigQuery notebook queries are billed by the data scanned or compute used, so a cell that repeatedly rescans a large table costs money even when the notebook server itself looks quiet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between stopping and deleting a managed notebook instance, and name one tradeoff of turning on idle shutdown.
lessons.modelAnswer: Stopping a managed notebook instance powers off its processor and any accelerator, so billing for that compute stops, but the disk and its files remain, and the instance can be started later with the same environment. Deleting it removes the machine and its disk, so anything saved only on that machine is lost, and it cannot be recovered by starting it again. Before deleting, we check that notebooks and data live in a shared repository or bucket. Idle shutdown saves money because abandoned servers stop themselves, but the tradeoff is that a long-running job or a background process can be interrupted if it looks idle to the system. Teams should either exclude such work or schedule it deliberately, and they should confirm the idle timeout matches how people actually work.
rubricPoints: Stopping halts compute billing but keeps the disk and files
Deleting removes the machine and its disk permanently
Important work should live in durable storage before any deletion
Idle shutdown saves cost but can interrupt long-running background work

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an idle-server cost scenario, choosing between stop and delete, adds more than reading console steps alone, and no listed mission covers notebooks.

lessons.plain: A cloud workstation is a development computer that runs in the cloud instead of on your laptop. You reach it from a web browser or from your usual code editor, and it already has the compilers, libraries, and tools your team needs. Because the company defines that setup once, every engineer starts from the same place, and a new person can be productive on their first morning. The machine costs money while it runs, so the useful habits are letting idle machines shut themselves off and keeping your work in storage that survives a restart. Think of it as a shared, pre-built desk you can sit at from anywhere.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new engineer's laptop is slow, and every teammate has a slightly different Python version installed. What would you change so everyone works on the same setup without buying new laptops, and what new cost would you have to watch?
lessons.teach:
A cloud development environment is a remote machine that a developer uses to write and test code. Google Cloud calls its managed version Cloud Workstations. It has three layers you should keep separate. A workstation cluster is the group that workstations live in, and it controls which private network they can reach. A workstation configuration is the template: the machine size, the container image that holds the tools, the size of the persistent disk, and the timeouts. A workstation is one developer's actual machine, created from a configuration. Platform staff usually define clusters and configurations, while developers start, stop, and connect to their own workstation.

Why it works: the image is built once and reused, so the toolchain is identical for everyone. The persistent disk keeps the developer's home directory when the container restarts. The idle timeout stops a workstation after a period with no connection, and the running timeout caps how long it can stay on in total. Those two settings control most of the bill.

Worked example: a configuration sets an idle timeout of 30 minutes. Priya connects at 09:00 and codes until 12:00, then leaves for lunch with no open connection. At 12:30 the platform sees no activity for thirty minutes and stops the machine. Her code sits on the persistent disk, so when she returns at 13:00 and starts the workstation, her files are there. Compute is charged only while the machine ran.

Common mistake: saving work to a temporary location inside the container instead of the persistent home directory. A restart or rebuild then erases it. A second mistake is leaving the idle timeout unset, so a forgotten workstation runs all night with nobody using it.

In a running team, the effect shows up in billing and in the workstation's status. Checking whether cost comes from running compute or from a disk that stays allocated while the machine is stopped is a routine day-two habit.

questions.prompt: A university lab, Harbor Lab, sets a workstation configuration with a 20-minute idle timeout and a 6-hour running timeout. Its student Ravi starts his workstation at 08:00 and connects until 09:10, then closes his connection and does not come back. Step 1: the idle timeout counts 20 minutes of no connection after 09:10, so the platform stops the machine at 09:30 unless someone reconnects. Step 2 is missing. Which statement completes the reasoning for whether the workstation can stay on past 14:00 if Ravi reconnects at 13:50?
choices: The idle timeout is counted from the workstation's creation date, so it would already have stopped the machine before 08:00.
Reconnecting at 13:50 resets the 6-hour running timeout, so the machine can run until 19:50.
The persistent disk is billed only while the machine runs, so the 14:00 mark has no cost effect and does not matter.
The running timeout is counted from the workstation's start at 08:00, so the machine is stopped at 14:00 no matter when he reconnects.
questions.why: The running timeout is a total cap measured from start, so a reconnection cannot extend it, which is why 14:00 is the hard stop.

questions.prompt: In a cloud development environment, which layer defines which private network a developer's workstations are allowed to reach?
choices: The workstation itself, since each developer's machine chooses its own network at creation time.
The workstation cluster, which is the group the workstations live in and controls network reach.
The container image, because the tools inside it decide which networks are reachable.
The persistent disk, because the disk holds the network addresses used by the container.
questions.why: The teaching text says the cluster is the group workstations live in and it controls which private network they can reach.

questions.prompt: A developer on a team saves a build script in a temporary folder inside the workstation container, not in the persistent home directory. The next morning the workstation has been rebuilt from its configuration. What happens to the script?
choices: It is kept on the persistent disk because all folders inside the container are backed up on the disk.
It is lost, because the temporary location is erased on restart or rebuild and only the persistent home directory survives.
It moves to the workstation cluster, which stores files for every workstation in the group.
It is restored automatically from the configuration template, since templates keep copies of developer files.
questions.why: Temporary locations inside the container are erased on restart or rebuild, while the persistent home directory on the disk is kept.

questions.prompt: A team's workstations were stopped all weekend, yet the monthly bill still shows a storage charge for each one. Which explanation fits the cost behaviour described for stopped workstations?
choices: The persistent disk stays allocated while the machine is stopped, so its storage is still billed even though compute is not.
The configuration template was charged again because it was re-applied when the workstations stopped.
The idle timeout failed, so the machines kept running compute over the weekend without anyone connected.
The workstation cluster charges a fee for each stopped workstation it still holds in its network.
questions.why: Compute is charged only while the machine runs, but the persistent disk remains allocated and billed while the workstation is stopped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Cloud Workstations configuration is, how it differs from a single workstation, and one limit or tradeoff of using remote development environments.
lessons.modelAnswer: A configuration is the template. It fixes the machine size, the container image with the tools, the persistent disk size, and the timeouts. A workstation is one developer's running machine, created from that template, so changing the configuration does not change machines that already exist. The main tradeoff is that a remote environment depends on network connectivity and on the cloud bill. If the connection is poor, typing lags. If the idle and running timeouts are wrong, machines run unused and cost money. Work must also be kept on the persistent disk, because anything in the temporary container layer disappears on restart. Teams get consistency and fast onboarding in return, but they need someone watching the timeouts and the disk usage.
rubricPoints: A configuration is the reusable template covering machine, image, disk, and timeouts
A workstation is one developer's machine created from a configuration
Idle and running timeouts control when compute stops and therefore the cost
Work must be saved to the persistent home directory or it can be lost on restart

suggested.rationale: This is product-specific console and configuration knowledge that no listed mission or planned engine exercises directly, so reading the concepts is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Cloud Storage is a place to keep files, called objects, inside containers called buckets. Managing it well means deciding who may read or change those files, and making sure old files move to cheaper storage or get removed on a schedule instead of piling up forever. Think of a bucket as a filing cabinet with a rule card on the front. The card says things like after 30 days move this folder to the basement, and after 3 years shred it. Securing objects means checking who holds the keys to the cabinet, and guarding against an accidental shredding that cannot be undone.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company stores five years of application logs in one bucket, and almost nobody reads logs older than 30 days. Without anyone moving files by hand, what would you set up so the storage bill stops growing forever, and what risk would you check before turning on automatic deletion?
lessons.teach:
A bucket is a named container in Cloud Storage. Its name must be unique across all of Google Cloud, and it has a location and a default storage class. Storage classes trade price against access. Standard suits frequent access. Nearline, Coldline and Archive cost less to hold but charge more to read, and each has a minimum storage duration of 30, 90 and 365 days respectively.
