You pay for that minimum even if you delete earlier. An object is a stored file plus its metadata. Object names sit in a flat list, so a slash in a name only looks like a folder.

Access is controlled by IAM roles, which are permission bundles granted to people or service accounts on a bucket or project. A viewer role lets someone read objects. Uniform bucket-level access turns off per-object access lists, so IAM becomes the single rule set. Public access prevention blocks accidental public exposure.

A lifecycle management policy is a list of rules. Each rule has a condition, such as the object's age in days or its current storage class, and an action, such as changing the storage class or deleting the object. Cloud Storage checks the rules in the background, so an action can happen up to about a day after its condition is met. In the console, the rules live in the bucket's lifecycle settings.

Worked example: a logs bucket has Rule A, which sets the class to Nearline once an object is 30 days old, and Rule B, which deletes objects at 365 days. A log created on 1 March stays Standard until a background check after about 31 March moves it to Nearline. Around 1 March the following year, the check deletes it.

Common mistake: enabling object versioning and assuming lifecycle rules remove old versions automatically. Overwritten or deleted versions remain as noncurrent versions and keep costing money until a rule targets them.

Consequence: if a retention policy or object hold is set, a delete rule cannot remove the object until the hold ends, so the rule quietly does nothing and storage keeps growing.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic keeps x-ray images in a bucket. The bucket has Rule A, which changes the storage class to Coldline once an object is 60 days old, and Rule B, which deletes objects at 400 days. An x-ray is uploaded on 1 February 2025 and starts in Standard. Trace it: Step 1, the object is created in Standard on 1 February 2025. Step 2, Rule A's condition is met on about 2 April 2025, and a background check moves the object to Coldline up to about a day later. Step 3: [missing step, to be chosen]. Which choice correctly completes the trace?
choices: Rule B's 365-day condition is met on 1 February 2026, so the object is deleted that day.
Rule B's 400-day condition is met around 8 March 2026, and a background check deletes the object up to about a day later.
Rule B deletes the object instantly at the moment its 400-day condition is reached, at midnight on 8 March 2026.
Because Coldline has a 90-day minimum, Rule B is postponed until 2 July 2025 and the object cannot be deleted before then.
questions.why: Rule B's condition is object age of 400 days, which falls around 8 March 2026, and deletion is performed by the background check, so it can lag by up to about a day.

questions.prompt: A team stores nightly database backups in the Archive storage class and sets a lifecycle rule to delete each backup after 100 days. What is the most accurate description of the cost?
choices: They pay for at least 365 days of storage for each backup, even though the rule deletes it at 100 days.
They pay for 30 days, which is the minimum for every storage class.
They pay nothing extra, because Archive storage has no minimum duration.
They pay only for the 100 days, because the delete rule ends billing as soon as it fires.
questions.why: Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration, and you pay for that minimum even when you delete an object earlier.

questions.prompt: A bucket has object versioning turned on, and a lifecycle rule that deletes objects 30 days after creation. An application overwrites a file, and the old version is kept. What happens to the old version?
choices: It is kept as a noncurrent version and keeps costing money until a rule targets noncurrent versions.
It is moved to Archive automatically and costs nothing to hold.
The rule deletes it at 30 days, because lifecycle rules always remove every version.
It is removed as soon as the new version is written, so nothing is kept.
questions.why: Versioning keeps overwritten data as noncurrent versions, and lifecycle rules do not remove them unless a rule is written to target them.

questions.prompt: A bucket has a retention policy that keeps objects for two years. A lifecycle rule is set to delete objects at 180 days. What happens to objects at 180 days?
choices: They are moved to Archive and then deleted, so retention is bypassed.
They are deleted on time, because lifecycle rules override retention policies.
The bucket rejects the lifecycle rule when it is saved, so no objects are affected.
The delete rule has no effect until the retention period ends, and storage keeps growing.
questions.why: A retention policy or object hold stops a delete rule from removing the object until the hold ends, so the rule silently does nothing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how lifecycle rules and bucket access control keep a Cloud Storage bucket affordable and safe, and name one limit or tradeoff of automatic deletion.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lifecycle management is a set of rules on a bucket that run in the background. Each rule matches objects by a condition such as age or storage class, then moves them to a cheaper tier or deletes them. That keeps cost from growing with data nobody reads. For safety, access is set by IAM roles on the bucket, and uniform bucket-level access removes per-object lists so there is one place to check who can read or delete. The tradeoff with automatic deletion is that it is irreversible once it runs, and it is delayed rather than instant, sometimes by up to a day after the condition is met. Cheaper tiers also carry minimum storage durations and retrieval charges, so moving data too early can cost more. Before enabling delete rules, check versioning and retention settings, because those can keep old objects around or block removal.
rubricPoints: Lifecycle rules match objects by conditions like age or storage class and apply actions like changing class or deleting.
Actions run in the background and may lag the condition by up to about a day.
IAM roles on the bucket control who can read or delete, and uniform bucket-level access simplifies this.
Deletion is irreversible, and versioning or retention settings can keep objects from being removed as expected.
Cheaper storage classes have minimum durations and retrieval costs that can make early moves expensive.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers Cloud Storage, so an exam-style scenario asking the learner to choose lifecycle rules and access settings best builds the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Running a query means asking a database a question and getting back the matching data. Each Google Cloud database product takes questions in a different style. Some take SQL, the standard language for tables of rows. Others look up records by a key or by the fields inside a document. You can run a query from a built-in console editor, a command-line tool, or a program. An engineer has to pick the right way to ask, ask in a way that does not overload the live system, and read the answer correctly. This lesson covers how each of the six products is queried and the habit that keeps a query from hurting production.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table holds one million orders, and you want the orders for one customer. Without any index on the customer field, roughly how much work does the database do to find them, and how would that change if an index existed?
lessons.teach: A query is a request that reads data from a database. The database has to do work to find the answer, and the amount of work depends on how the data is organised and how much of it the query must scan. Cloud SQL and AlloyDB are managed relational databases. Cloud SQL runs MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server. AlloyDB is PostgreSQL-compatible. You connect to both with a standard client such as psql, through the Cloud SQL or AlloyDB connector or proxy, which handles encryption and identity for you. Spanner is a relational database spread across regions and also takes SQL, from the console's query editor or a command-line tool. BigQuery is a serverless analytics warehouse that takes SQL, run from the console or the bq command. You pay for the data a query scans, so reading a large table in full costs money. Bigtable is a wide-column store with no joins. You read by row key or a key range, using the cbt tool or a client library. Firestore is a document store. You query collections with filters on fields, and combining filters often needs a composite index first. Worked example: a table of ten million orders, filtered by customer_id equal to 42. Step one, the query names the field and value. Step two, with an index on customer_id, the database jumps to the few matching rows. Step three, without an index it reads all ten million rows to find them. The answer is identical; the work is very different. Common mistake: running an exploratory SELECT with no filter against a production Cloud SQL primary, where a full scan competes with customer writes and slows the application. Send heavy reads to a read replica or a copy, and always filter or limit while exploring. On a running system, a slow query shows up as rising database CPU and query latency in Cloud Monitoring, and in BigQuery as bytes billed on the job in the job history.

questions.prompt: A utility company stores smart meter readings in Bigtable. Each row key is written as meterID then a hash sign then the date as YYYYMMDD, for example M-207#20240315. A dashboard needs every reading for meter M-207 in March 2024, and the query asks for the key range from M-207#20240301 up to but not including M-207#20240401. Step one: the query names a key range that starts and ends on M-207 dates. Step two: Bigtable reads only the rows whose keys fall inside that contiguous range. Step three, which you must complete: explain what would happen to the same request if the row key had been written date first, as 20240315#M-207.
choices: Bigtable would reorder the rows by meter ID automatically at no extra cost.
The query would fail, because Bigtable only accepts row keys that begin with a meter ID.
The March readings for M-207 would be scattered across the whole keyspace, so the query would have to read far more rows than the requested range contains.
Bigtable would still find the rows quickly, because it builds an index on every column.
questions.why: Bigtable reads by row key or key range, so a key that does not place one meter's March rows next to each other forces a much wider read to find them.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs appointment booking on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL primary instance. The office manager wants a count of no-shows per doctor for the last ten years and plans to run an unfiltered SELECT in the console against that primary during opening hours. What is the most suitable action?
choices: Run it during opening hours, since Cloud SQL scales reads automatically without affecting bookings.
Run it against a read replica or a copy of the data, and add a date filter or limit while exploring.
Remove the appointments table indexes first so the query runs faster.
Run it on the primary but split it into one query per doctor so each one is small.
questions.why: Heavy reads should go to a read replica or copy, and exploratory queries should be filtered or limited, so the primary's writes are not slowed.

questions.prompt: A retailer keeps a BigQuery table of website clicks, about 3 TB in total, partitioned by day. An analyst needs the number of clicks for one day and wants to keep costs low. Which query approach reads the least data?
choices: SELECT with a WHERE clause on all columns but no date filter, so the engine can choose.
SELECT COUNT(*) with a WHERE clause on the partition date column, so only that day's partition is scanned.
SELECT * FROM the whole table, then count the rows in a spreadsheet.
SELECT COUNT(*) on the whole table and filter the result afterwards in the console.
questions.why: BigQuery bills for the data a query scans, and filtering on the partition column limits the scan to one day's data.

questions.prompt: A travel app stores flight records in Firestore. A developer runs a query that filters where origin equals LHR and status equals delayed, then orders by departure time, and Firestore returns an error saying a composite index is required. What is the correct fix?
choices: Rewrite the query to use SELECT * with no filters, then sort in the app.
Increase the Firestore instance size so the query can run without an index.
Create a composite index covering origin, status and departure time, then rerun the query.
Remove the status filter so only one field is filtered and no index is needed.
questions.why: Firestore needs a composite index when a query combines several filters with an ordering, and creating that index lets the same query run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would run a read-only query against a production database without risking the application. Name one tradeoff of each approach you would consider.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not run exploratory queries on the primary database that serves customers. For relational systems like Cloud SQL, AlloyDB or Spanner, I would use a read replica or a copy, so a scan cannot slow writes. I would always add a filter and a LIMIT first, and check the query plan so I know whether an index is being used. The tradeoff is that a replica can lag behind the primary, so the numbers may be a little old. For BigQuery, the main risk is cost rather than load: I would preview the bytes a query will scan, select only the columns I need, and filter on partitions. The tradeoff is that a narrow query may take a few extra minutes to write. For Bigtable and Firestore I would query by key or indexed field, because they do not support arbitrary joins, and a query that does not match the key design can become a slow scan.
rubricPoints: Avoid running heavy or unfiltered reads against the production primary; use a replica or a copy.
Filter and limit exploratory queries, and check whether an index is used.
BigQuery cost depends on bytes scanned, so select only needed columns and filter partitions.
Bigtable and Firestore are queried by key or indexed field, not by arbitrary joins.
Each approach has a tradeoff, such as replica lag or extra query time.

suggested.rationale: Writing and reading queries against small tables is best practised in a hands-on SQL lab, which the planned sql-lab engine would provide.

lessons.plain: Estimating storage cost means working out roughly what a pile of stored data will cost each month before the bill arrives. Cloud providers charge for how much data you keep, how long you keep it, how often you read or write it, and whether it leaves the cloud network. An estimate lets you compare options, such as moving rarely used files into a cheaper tier, and it warns you when a surprise bill is coming. The goal is a reasonable number with its assumptions written down, not a perfect figure.
lessons.guessPrompt: You store 2 TB of old photos that people open about once a year. Would you expect the cheapest storage tier to be the best choice for them, and what could make it cost more than you first think?
lessons.teach: A storage class (also called a tier) is a price and access profile for stored objects in Cloud Storage, Google Cloud's object storage service. Standard is for data read often, while Nearline, Coldline and Archive are cheaper to keep but cost more to read and have minimum storage durations. The main charge is the storage price per gigabyte per month. Operations are charges per batch of requests, such as reads, writes or list calls. Retrieval fees are per-gigabyte charges for reading from the colder classes. Egress means data leaving Google Cloud or moving between regions, and it is billed per gigabyte. A minimum storage duration is the shortest time you are billed for an object, even if you delete it earlier. The cheap rate only wins when data is rarely read. Worked example with illustrative rates, not current prices: keep 500 GB in Standard at 0.02 dollars per GB-month, which is 500 times 0.02, or 10 dollars per month. Now move it to a cold class at 0.004 dollars per GB-month, so storage is 2 dollars per month. If you read 200 GB each month at a 0.03 dollar retrieval rate, that adds 6 dollars, for 8 dollars total, still cheaper, but only just. A common mistake is comparing storage prices alone and ignoring retrieval, operations, egress and minimum durations. A nightly job that scans a cold bucket can turn a cheap archive into an expensive one within a single billing cycle. A good estimate always states how much data is read, how often, and how long it is kept.

questions.prompt: A photo archive keeps 2,000 GB in Coldline at an illustrative rate of 0.004 dollars per GB-month, so storage is 2,000 times 0.004, or 8 dollars per month. Each month the team reads 100 GB from that class at an illustrative retrieval rate of 0.03 dollars per GB, which is 100 times 0.03, or 3 dollars. Step three, which you must complete yourself, is the egress charge: 40 GB leaves Google Cloud each month at an illustrative 0.12 dollars per GB. What is the estimated monthly total?
choices: 11.00 dollars
19.80 dollars
12.80 dollars
15.80 dollars
questions.why: The egress line is 40 times 0.12, or 4.80 dollars, and adding it to the 8 dollars storage and 3 dollars retrieval gives 15.80 dollars.

questions.prompt: In a cost estimate for stored objects, which charge is billed per gigabyte when data leaves Google Cloud or moves between regions?
choices: Storage price per GB-month
Operations
Minimum storage duration
Egress
questions.why: Egress is defined in the teaching text as the per-gigabyte charge for data leaving Google Cloud or moving between regions.

questions.prompt: A team stores 300 GB in Standard at an illustrative 0.02 dollars per GB-month, or a cold class at an illustrative 0.004 dollars per GB-month. It reads 100 GB each month from the cold class at an illustrative 0.03 dollars per GB retrieval rate, and ignores operations and egress. Which option has the lower monthly estimate, and what is it?
choices: The cold class, at about 4.20 dollars, compared with 6.00 dollars for Standard
The cold class, at 1.20 dollars, because retrieval is free for data read once a month
Standard, at 6.00 dollars, because retrieval fees always exceed the storage savings
Both cost the same, 6.00 dollars, because the cold class price is offset by retrieval
questions.why: The cold class costs 300 times 0.004, or 1.20 dollars, plus 100 times 0.03, or 3.00 dollars, for 4.20 dollars, which is below the 6.00 dollars for Standard.

questions.prompt: A team puts daily dashboard log files, which a job reads every day, into a cold storage class because the storage price per GB-month is the lowest. Its estimate compares only storage prices. What is the most likely problem with that estimate?
choices: The estimate is too low because retrieval and operation charges, which the storage-only comparison left out, can make the bill higher than Standard
Cold classes charge nothing for reads, so the storage-only estimate is already complete
The daily job cannot read cold storage at all, so the reading cost is zero
Standard storage becomes free after the files have been stored for thirty days
questions.why: Cold classes charge per-gigabyte retrieval and per-batch operations, so frequent daily reads can push the total above Standard even when the storage price is lower.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to move our old log archive into the cheapest storage class to save money. Explain to them how you would estimate the real monthly cost of that move, and name one limit or tradeoff of your estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the total gigabytes we keep and multiply by the storage rate for each class per month. Then I would estimate how often we read those logs, because retrieval fees and any data leaving the cloud are billed per gigabyte on top of storage. I would also check the minimum storage duration for the cheaper class, since deleting objects early still bills the rest of that minimum period. Finally I would compare the total with our current Standard cost. The main limit is that the estimate depends on how often we really read the logs, which is an assumption. If an incident needs many archived logs quickly, the real cost can be higher than predicted. Prices also vary by region and change over time, so I would confirm them against the current price list and set a budget alert.
rubricPoints: Storage cost is gigabytes times the per-month rate for the chosen class.
Retrieval, operations and egress charges can dominate if the data is read often.
Minimum storage durations bill early deletions for the full period.
The estimate rests on access assumptions and should be checked against current prices and billing data.

suggested.rationale: Working through storage tiers with fictional credits lets the learner practise combining storage, retrieval and minimum-duration charges into one estimate.

lessons.plain: A backup is a saved copy of a database taken at a moment in time, kept somewhere safe so you can get your data back if the original is damaged, corrupted, or lost through a mistake. A restore is the act of using one of those copies to bring data back. In a managed cloud database, the provider often takes copies on a schedule for you, but you still have to decide how long to keep them, how far back you can go, and whether to restore over the broken database or build a fresh one beside it. Knowing those choices is what turns a backup from a file into a recovery plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer ran a command that deleted rows from a production customer table about an hour ago. The database has automatic daily backups turned on. Before any teaching, what would you check first to decide whether yesterday's backup is enough to recover, and what work might be lost?
lessons.teach:
A database backup is a copy of the data and its structure taken at a point in time. A managed database service such as Cloud SQL, the Google Cloud service that hosts MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server for you, can run automated backups on a schedule and keep them for a set number of days. You can also trigger an on-demand backup yourself before a risky change. A restore takes a backup and rebuilds data from it, either back into the original instance, which overwrites what is there, or into a new instance, which leaves the damaged one untouched so you can compare.

Point-in-time recovery, often shortened to PITR, lets you restore to any moment inside a window, not only to the moment a backup was taken. It works by keeping a continuous log of changes (binary logs in MySQL, write-ahead logs in PostgreSQL) alongside the scheduled copies. To recover, the service starts from the nearest earlier backup and replays the change log up to the timestamp you choose.

Worked example: backups run at 02:00 daily, PITR is on, and at 14:37 someone deletes a table. You restore to a new instance at 14:36. The service takes the 02:00 backup, replays changes from 02:00 up to 14:36, and produces a new instance with the table intact. You check the rows, then copy back the missing data or point the application at the new instance.

Common mistake: assuming recovery is possible because automated backups are enabled, without checking the retention period or whether PITR is on. Without PITR, the 02:00 backup is the newest point you can restore, so the afternoon's writes are lost.

Consequence: an in-place restore overwrites current data and usually causes downtime, and writes made after the restore point are discarded. A restore is therefore a deliberate data-loss decision, not a free undo. A backup you have never restored is only a hope, so test restores on a schedule.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic runs a Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance with automated daily backups at 01:00, point-in-time recovery (PITR) turned on, and 7 days of retention. At 09:20 an engineer runs an update with no WHERE clause, which changes the billing status of every patient row. The recovery plan is: Step 1: choose a restore timestamp of 09:19, just before the bad update. Step 2: [MISSING STEP]. Step 3: the service starts from the 01:00 backup and replays the write-ahead log up to 09:19. Step 4: the team checks the billing rows in the restored copy and copies back the correct values. Which action completes Step 2?
choices: Turn off PITR before restoring so the replay does not overwrite the clinic's current rows
Restore in place over the existing instance so the application sees corrected data straight away
Restore to a new instance so the damaged instance is left untouched for comparison
Run the restore against the 09:19 backup file, since point-in-time restores need a backup taken at that exact minute
questions.why: Restoring to a new instance leaves the damaged instance intact so the team can compare and copy back only what is needed, whereas an in-place restore overwrites current data.

questions.prompt: A managed PostgreSQL instance has a scheduled backup at 23:30 each night and PITR is enabled. Which statement correctly describes what PITR adds?
choices: Only the exact minute each nightly backup finished, with nothing in between
Only the instant the change log was last flushed to disk during the night
Any moment at all, even before the oldest retained backup, because the log never expires
Any moment in the window, built from the nearest earlier backup plus the change log
questions.why: PITR restores to any moment inside the recovery window by starting from the nearest earlier backup and replaying the continuous change log up to the chosen timestamp.

questions.prompt: A team takes backups at 00:30 every day, keeps them for 3 days, and has PITR switched off. A row is deleted at 17:05 on Tuesday. What is the newest point they can restore to?
choices: 00:30 Monday, because the newest backup is always a day old
Any time up to 17:05, since retention keeps every write made during the window
00:30 Tuesday, because that is the newest backup taken before the deletion
17:04 Tuesday, because the deletion is the last change in the log
questions.why: Without PITR the only restorable points are the backup times, so the 00:30 Tuesday backup is the newest one before the deletion and the afternoon's writes are lost.

questions.prompt: A team has automated backups enabled but has never tried restoring one. Which practice best matches what the lesson says about trusting a backup?
choices: Restore over the production instance once a year to prove that the backup works
Restore a backup to a new instance on a schedule and check the data it produces
Assume the backup is good because the backup schedule shows as successful
Increase the retention period, since a longer retention shows that restores will succeed
questions.why: A backup that has never been restored is only a hope, so restoring to a separate new instance on a schedule and checking the data tests recoverability without risking production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, the difference between restoring a scheduled backup and restoring to a point in time, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scheduled backup is a full copy taken at a set time, such as 02:00 each day, so restoring it brings the database back to exactly that moment, and anything written later is lost. Point-in-time recovery adds a continuous change log on top of those copies, so we can rebuild the database at nearly any second inside the retention window, for example just before a bad delete. The tradeoff is cost and setup: PITR needs the change log kept for the whole window, which costs storage, and it only reaches back as far as the retention period allows. Scheduled backups have their own limit, because the newest one may be many hours old. In either case I would restore to a new instance first, verify the data, and only then switch traffic over, since an in-place restore overwrites current data and causes downtime.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a scheduled backup, which restores the database to the moment it was taken.
Explains point-in-time recovery as a backup plus a change log replayed up to a chosen time.
Names a limit or tradeoff: retention window, storage cost, or data lost since the last backup.
Notes that restoring to a new instance is safer than overwriting the original in place.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a scheduled backup and a point-in-time restore during a live data-loss scenario is a judgement call that reasoning through a situation practises better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A data job is a program that reads a large amount of information, changes it, and writes the result somewhere else. Google Cloud runs two common kinds. Dataflow is a managed service that runs such pipelines in batch or streaming mode, and BigQuery is a data warehouse where queries, loads, and exports each run as a job. Reviewing job status means checking whether each job is still going, finished cleanly, or failed, and why. It is one of the first things you do on day two, when someone asks whether last night's data arrived. You read the job's state, its progress numbers, and its log messages, and then you act on what they say.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that loads yesterday's sales into a warehouse table reports no visible error, but the table is empty. Before you read anything else, what would you check first to tell whether the job actually finished and what it did?
lessons.teach:
A job is one unit of work that a managed service accepts, runs, and reports on. You rarely watch it execute step by step. Instead you read its status, which has two parts: its state, a label for where it is in its life, and its details, which explain what happened.

Dataflow runs pipelines, which are graphs of steps that read from sources, transform records, and write to sinks (the destinations). Each Dataflow job moves through states such as starting, running, and then a final state: done, failed, or cancelled. A streaming job, which processes data continuously, never reaches done on its own, so 'still running' is normal there. The job view shows the graph of steps with record counts flowing between them, and a count that stops growing points at the step where the trouble is. Errors from the workers, the machines doing the processing, appear in the job's logs.

BigQuery treats every query, load, copy, and export as a job with its own ID. A job is pending, running, or done. A done job can still carry an error result, so done does not mean succeeded. The job history for a project lists recent jobs, and the INFORMATION_SCHEMA views, which are built-in tables describing past activity, let you search that history with SQL.

Worked example, the empty table. Step 1: find the load job by its time and destination table. Step 2: read its state, which is done. Step 3: read its error result, which says the source file was not found. Step 4: conclude the job ran against nothing, so the empty table has a cause you can name.

Common mistake: treating the state done as proof of success, or reading only a summary screen and never the error details.

Consequence: a silent failed load means downstream reports show zeros, and the gap goes unnoticed until someone asks why the numbers are missing.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs a streaming Dataflow job called clickstream-enrich that reads website events, enriches them, and writes them to a warehouse table. The job state is running, which is normal for a streaming job. An engineer opens the job graph and sees that the record count leaving the parse step has stayed at 880,412 for the past 90 minutes, while the count entering that step keeps climbing. Step 1: confirm the job is streaming, so running is expected and not a problem by itself. Step 2: note that the count after parse has stopped growing, which points at the parse step or the step right after it. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: conclude the trouble is in the step that stopped, and name it.
choices: Cancel the job at once and resubmit it, since a stalled count always means a corrupt pipeline
Mark the job as done in the console, since a running streaming job is considered finished once its counts stall
Check the warehouse table's row count, since a full table means the job is healthy
Open the job's logs and read the errors reported by the worker machines for that step
questions.why: The graph shows where the count stopped, and the worker errors in the job logs explain why, so reading them is the step that turns a symptom into a named cause.

questions.prompt: A BigQuery job shows the state done. Which statement is accurate?
choices: It completed successfully and the output is ready to use
It is still waiting for resources and will start shortly
It was stopped by a user before any rows were written
Finished, but an error may be recorded, so check the result
questions.why: In BigQuery, done only means the job has finished; a done job can still carry an error result, so the outcome has to be checked rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: A Dataflow batch job moved from starting to running and then reached the cancelled state, and rows are missing downstream. What does the cancelled state tell you?
choices: The job is still running in the background and will finish later
It stopped before done, so output may be incomplete; read its details
The job failed in the first minute and no steps ran
All steps completed and the missing rows are only a display issue
questions.why: Cancelled is a final state reached without finishing, so the output is likely partial, and the job's details are where you find out how far it got and why it stopped.

questions.prompt: An analyst needs every load job into a sales table from the past day, along with the error details of any that failed. Which approach fits?
choices: Query the INFORMATION_SCHEMA jobs view with SQL, filtering by time and table
Count the rows in the destination table, since an empty table marks failures
Check only the latest job in the console; older jobs cannot be searched
Rerun every load job so each one reports a fresh status
questions.why: The INFORMATION_SCHEMA views are built-in tables of past activity that can be searched with SQL by time and destination, and they include the error details needed to find the failed loads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a Dataflow streaming job and a BigQuery load job are healthy, and name one limit of relying on each job's status alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: For the Dataflow streaming job I would check that its state is running and that record counts keep moving through each step, since a streaming job never finishes on its own. I would also scan its worker logs for repeated errors, because a job can look running while every record fails. For the BigQuery load I would check the job's state and then its error result, because a load can be marked done and still have loaded nothing. The limit with the streaming job is that a running state says nothing about freshness, so I also compare the output timestamps with the clock. The limit with the load is that job history only covers a retention window, so an older failure may be gone before anyone looks.
rubricPoints: Dataflow health is judged from job state plus step record counts and worker logs, not state alone
A streaming job is expected to keep running, so a running state is normal rather than proof of health
BigQuery jobs can show done while carrying an error, so the error field must be checked
Each status signal has a limit, such as freshness for streaming or the retention window for job history

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a live situation where a job looks finished but produced nothing adds more than a listed mission covers, since no current mission reviews cloud job status.

lessons.plain: Database Center is a single screen in Google Cloud that shows many of your managed databases at once, instead of opening each one separately. A managed database is one the cloud provider runs for you: it handles the underlying machines, patching and some backups, while you still care about whether it is healthy, secure and set up sensibly. Managing a fleet means keeping track of all of them together. The screen highlights problems such as availability risks, security or configuration gaps, and suggested fixes, so you can see where to look first. Think of it as a dashboard that gathers your database dashboards into one place.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run fifteen databases across three projects, and a customer reports slowness. Without opening each database one by one, what single view would you want to check first, and what would you hope it tells you?
lessons.teach:
A fleet is a group of resources you manage together. In Google Cloud, your database fleet is every managed database you own across your projects, whatever the engine: relational services such as Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, or others such as Spanner and Bigtable. Database Center is the console view that gathers these into one overview, so you do not have to visit each instance to learn its state.

It works because the service collects health and configuration signals from each database and summarizes them in one place. Each database appears with its status. Where the service detects a risk, such as a degraded instance, a backup setting that is off, or a high-availability setup missing (high availability means a standby copy that can take over if the main copy fails), it raises an issue and often a recommendation describing the fix. You can filter the list by project, location or database type, then open one resource to see its details and metrics.

Worked example: a team has forty databases. Step 1: open Database Center and scan the fleet summary for issues above zero. Step 2: filter to the production project to narrow the list. Step 3: open the one flagged database that has a high-availability recommendation. Step 4: read the recommendation and decide whether the fix is a configuration change you can make now or needs a planned maintenance window. Step 5: record the finding and the time, so you can check the database's metrics afterwards.

Common mistake: treating the overview as a complete audit. It shows what the service can detect and what it watches; a clean summary does not prove backups restore or that access rules are right. Those checks still need the database's own backup and logging views.

Consequence: a risk shown here is an early warning on a running system. Acting on it before an outage is the day-2 value of a fleet view.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs 14 databases across two projects. An engineer opens Database Center, filters the list to the project named bank-payments-prod and to the Spanner database type, then opens the one Spanner instance showing a backup-off issue and reads its recommendation. The planned maintenance window is Sunday at 02:00, so the engineer schedules the backup change for then. The missing step: once the change is applied, the engineer ____ before writing the finding down with the time. Choose the step that completes the check.
choices: Deletes the issue from the list so the summary reads zero.
Promotes the standby copy to primary so the risk cannot return.
Reopens the fleet summary to check the issue is gone.
Restores the newest backup to a test instance to prove access rules.
questions.why: Re-checking the fleet summary confirms the flagged issue has cleared, which is the verification the workflow needs before recording the finding.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud's Database Center, what is a fleet?
choices: A list of users who are allowed to open the console.
A single database instance together with its standby copy.
A group of managed databases you manage together, across projects and engines.
The set of backups kept for one database over its lifetime.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a fleet as a group of resources managed together, here every managed database you own across projects regardless of engine.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether its production database's backups can actually be restored. Which check is the right one to rely on?
choices: A filter on database type set to Bigtable.
The database's own backup and logging views.
The Database Center fleet summary showing zero issues.
The count of databases shown in the overview.
questions.why: The teaching text says a clean fleet summary does not prove backups restore, so the database's own backup and logging views are needed for that check.

questions.prompt: Database Center shows zero issues for a Cloud SQL instance. What can the engineer conclude?
choices: The backups are confirmed to restore correctly.
The access rules on the instance are confirmed correct.
The instance has high availability with a standby copy ready to take over.
The service has detected no risk it watches for, but backups and access rules still need separate checks.
questions.why: A clean summary only reflects what the service can detect and watches, so it does not prove backups restore or that access rules are right.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Database Center is for, and name one limit of relying on it alone when checking a database's health.
lessons.modelAnswer: Database Center gives us one place to see all our managed databases across projects, instead of opening each one. It collects health and configuration signals and lists risks, such as an instance with degraded availability, a missing high-availability setup, or a backup setting that is off, often with a suggested fix. We use it to triage: scan the summary, filter to the environment that matters, and open the flagged resource. The limit is that it only reports what the service checks. A clean overview does not prove a backup restores or that access is right, so I still confirm with the database's own backup and monitoring views, and I treat each recommendation as something to review before applying it.
rubricPoints: Describes Database Center as a single fleet-wide view of managed databases across projects
Explains that it surfaces health, risk and configuration signals with recommendations
Names a concrete limit, such as a clean summary not proving backups restore or access is correct
Says findings should be verified with the database's own backup and monitoring views

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console navigation and product facts, and no listed mission or planned engine covers the database fleet view.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. By default, Google Cloud encrypts your data and manages the keys itself. Customer-managed encryption keys, or CMEK, mean you create and control the key yourself, in a key service inside your own project, and the cloud service uses your key instead. You decide who may use it, when it rotates, and whether it can be turned off. The trade-off is that if you disable or destroy the key, the data it protects becomes unreadable, even to you. Think of it as a bank keeping the spare key to your safe, while you hold the right to take that key back.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a cloud service encrypts your files with a key that you control, what do you think happens to those files if you switch that key off, and why?
lessons.teach: A customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) is an encryption key that you create and manage in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS), and that a Google Cloud service uses to protect your data at rest. Cloud KMS groups keys into key rings and locations. Each key has one or more key versions, and the enabled version is the one used to encrypt new data.  Why it works: most services use envelope encryption. The service generates a data encryption key (DEK) to encrypt the actual data, then encrypts that DEK with your key encryption key (KEK), which stays in KMS. The wrapped DEK is stored next to the data. To read the data, the service must ask KMS to unwrap the DEK, which requires permission on your key. Cut off the key, and you cut off the data.  Worked example: you set a Cloud Storage bucket to use your key. (1) New objects get a DEK, wrapped by the key's current enabled version. (2) The storage service's own service agent needs permission to encrypt and decrypt with your key, or writes fail. (3) You disable that key version. (4) Reads of objects wrapped by it now fail with an error. (5) You re-enable the version and reads recover.  Common mistake: treating CMEK as a setting you can flip freely. Disabling a key version, scheduling its destruction, or deleting the key can make data permanently unreadable. Scheduled destruction has a waiting period, but it is not a safe undo, and changing the key for existing data usually means rewriting that data.  Consequence in a running system: a key problem looks like application errors from storage or database calls, not an obvious security alert. Check the key's state first, then the KMS audit logs that record who used the key.  A key you control is a key you can lose, so treat key lifecycle changes as production changes.

questions.prompt: A logistics company sets a Pub/Sub topic named shipment-events to use its own key, orders-kek, in the ops-keys ring. Pub/Sub is Google Cloud's managed message queue, which holds messages until consumers read them. The steps so far: (1) New messages are encrypted with a data encryption key that is wrapped by version 4 of orders-kek, the enabled version. (2) The Pub/Sub service agent, the Google-managed identity that the service uses internally, holds permission to encrypt and decrypt with orders-kek. (3) An engineer disables version 4 in Cloud KMS. (4) Consumers reading messages wrapped by version 4 start getting errors. Which action completes step 3 in the way that caused step 4?
choices: An engineer disables key version 4 in the ops-keys ring, so KMS refuses to unwrap the keys that depend on it.
An engineer deletes the whole ops-keys ring and recreates it with the same name, which re-encrypts existing messages.
An engineer revokes the Owner role of the consumer project, which removes the service agent's access to the key.
An engineer schedules version 4 for destruction with a 24-hour waiting period and then cancels the request.
questions.why: Disabling the key version that wraps the data keys stops KMS from unwrapping them, so reads of data protected by that version fail, which is the cause of step 4.

questions.prompt: In envelope encryption as used with CMEK, which item is the key encryption key (KEK)?
choices: The Cloud IAM policy attached to the storage bucket
The wrapped data encryption key that is stored beside the data
The data encryption key that encrypts the stored bytes directly
The customer-managed key held in Cloud KMS that wraps each data encryption key
questions.why: The KEK is the key you manage in Cloud KMS, and it is the one that wraps (encrypts) the data encryption keys, while the wrapped DEK is only the stored result.

questions.prompt: A web app's database calls begin failing with permission-style errors at 10:00, shortly after someone disabled a key version that the database's disk uses. Which first step fits how CMEK problems usually show up?
choices: Look only at the application's CPU and memory graphs, since key problems never appear as errors.
Delete the database and restore it from the most recent backup.
Open a security incident and rotate every application password before looking at anything else.
Check the state of the key version in Cloud KMS, then review the KMS audit logs to see who disabled it.
questions.why: The teaching text says to check the key's state first and then the KMS audit logs, because key problems look like storage or database errors rather than security alerts.

questions.prompt: A team wants to move existing objects in a Cloud Storage bucket from key A to key B. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Changing the bucket setting re-encrypts all existing objects instantly and at no cost.
Changing the key for data that is already written usually means rewriting that data so it is protected by the new key.
Existing objects are unaffected by the bucket setting, and only objects written later will ever use key B.
Old objects keep working under key A until it is deleted, so the switch to key B is harmless.
questions.why: Data already written is wrapped by the old key, so moving it to a new key generally requires rewriting it, and the bucket setting alone does not do that.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what CMEK is and name one limit or tradeoff of using it, in your own words, as if they are about to turn it on for a production storage bucket.
lessons.modelAnswer: CMEK means we create the encryption key ourselves in Cloud KMS, and the storage or database service uses that key to protect our data. Google's service generates a data key for the actual bytes, then wraps that data key with our key, so reading data requires KMS to unwrap it. The main tradeoff is control versus risk. We can rotate the key, limit who uses it, and audit every use, but if we disable or destroy the key version, or remove the service's permission to use it, the data becomes unreadable. Before enabling it on a production bucket, I would confirm the service agent has the encrypt and decrypt role on the key, check that the key and resource are in compatible locations, and agree on who is allowed to change key state.
rubricPoints: Defines CMEK as a key the customer creates and controls in Cloud KMS.
Explains envelope encryption: a data key protects the data and the customer key protects that data key.
States the main tradeoff: disabling, destroying, or losing access to the key makes data unreadable.
Mentions that the service's own identity must have permission to use the key.

suggested.rationale: The envelope-crypto lab would let the learner wrap and unwrap data keys hands-on, which is the mechanism behind CMEK.

lessons.plain: A subnet is a slice of a cloud network that holds a block of private IP addresses, such as 10.0.1.0/24, which is 256 addresses. Every virtual machine inside it takes one address from that block. When the block runs low, you cannot simply add addresses to the middle of it. Google Cloud lets you widen the block in place by lowering its prefix length, for example from /24 to /23, so the new addresses sit alongside the old ones and existing machines keep theirs. The catch is that widening is one-way: you can grow a subnet's range but you cannot shrink it back, so check that the new size will not collide with other networks first.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your subnet 10.10.0.0/24 is almost out of addresses. If you widen it to 10.10.0.0/23, do you think the virtual machines already running in it would need new IP addresses or be restarted? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A CIDR block is a range of IP addresses written as a starting address and a slash number, such as 10.10.0.0/24. The slash number is the prefix length: it says how many leading bits are fixed. The remaining bits are free, so a smaller prefix number means a bigger block. A /24 has 8 free bits, giving 2 to the power of 8, which is 256 addresses. A /23 has 9 free bits, giving 512 addresses. Expanding a subnet means lowering its prefix number, which doubles the size each time you drop one.

The primary IPv4 range is the main block of a subnet, and it is the one you resize with this step. A secondary range is a separate block attached to the same subnet, often used for containers, and it is managed on its own.

Why it works: a subnet is essentially a rule that says addresses inside this block are local to this network. Widening the rule makes more addresses local. The cloud already reserves the extra addresses, so existing virtual machines keep their current addresses and nothing moves.

Worked example: subnet app-subnet has 10.10.0.0/24, covering 10.10.0.0 to 10.10.0.255. Step 1: list the other subnets in the same network and see that the nearest one starts at 10.10.2.0/24. Step 2: expand to 10.10.0.0/23, which covers 10.10.0.0 to 10.10.1.255. Step 3: check that this new block does not overlap 10.10.2.0/24 or any other subnet, peered network or on-premises route. It does not, so the expansion is allowed, and the subnet now holds 512 addresses.

Common mistake: assuming the change is reversible, or that a larger block is always safer. Expanding into a range that overlaps a peered network or an on-premises network makes routing ambiguous, and traffic can go to the wrong place. Firewall rules that name the old range now match more addresses, so review them after any expansion.

In a running system, expansion is a live change that does not restart machines, but it permanently changes what the network considers local.

questions.prompt: A subnet named billing-subnet in the network fin-net has the primary IPv4 range 172.20.8.0/25, which covers 172.20.8.0 to 172.20.8.127 and holds 128 addresses. Step 1: the current block is 172.20.8.0/25. Step 2: the nearest other subnet in fin-net starts at 172.20.8.128/26. Step 3: the candidate expansion is 172.20.8.0/24, which would cover 172.20.8.0 to 172.20.8.255. Missing step: decide whether this expansion can be applied.
choices: Allowed, because the new block only adds addresses after 172.20.8.127 and the other subnet starts later in the range.
Not allowed, because 172.20.8.0/24 overlaps 172.20.8.128/26, which makes local routing ambiguous, so a different range must be chosen.
Allowed, because the virtual machines already in billing-subnet keep their addresses, so no overlap check is needed.
Allowed, but only after every virtual machine in billing-subnet is restarted to pick up the larger range.
questions.why: The expanded /24 would contain the existing 172.20.8.128/26 subnet, so the two would overlap and the change must be rejected.

questions.prompt: A subnet uses the primary range 192.168.40.0/26. An administrator changes it to 192.168.40.0/25. Which statement describes the result?
choices: The subnet now holds 32 addresses, which is an expansion because the number after the slash got smaller.
The subnet now holds 128 addresses, which is an expansion because the number after the slash got smaller.
The subnet now holds 128 addresses, which is a shrink because the number after the slash got larger.
The subnet now holds 64 addresses, which is a shrink because the number after the slash got larger.
questions.why: Going from /26 to /25 drops the prefix number, which adds one free bit and doubles the block from 64 to 128 addresses, so it is an expansion.

questions.prompt: A subnet has the primary range 10.50.0.0/23. An engineer wants to change it to 10.50.0.0/22. Another subnet in the same network uses 10.50.2.0/24. What should happen?
choices: Apply the change, then review only the firewall rules, since overlap inside a single network does not affect routing.
Apply the change, because a /22 covers 1024 addresses and is therefore safer than a /23.
Do not apply the change, because 10.50.0.0/22 overlaps 10.50.2.0/24 and routing to that space would become ambiguous.
Apply the change, because existing virtual machines keep their addresses so nothing in the network can break.
questions.why: The /22 block includes the 10.50.2.0/24 subnet, so the two ranges overlap, and the expansion is the wrong action here.

questions.prompt: A subnet has a primary range 10.60.0.0/24 and a secondary range 10.61.0.0/20 used for containers. The team wants more room for the primary range. Which action is correct?
choices: Expand the secondary range, because it is the range that holds the virtual machine addresses.
Shrink the secondary range to free space, because both ranges must share one block inside the subnet.
Lower the prefix on the primary range 10.60.0.0/24 toward a larger block, after confirming it does not overlap other subnets, since the secondary range is managed separately.
Change the total size of the subnet by editing the secondary range's prefix, because the two ranges must always keep the same size.
questions.why: Only the primary range is resized with this step, and it must be checked for overlaps before its prefix number is lowered, while the secondary range is handled on its own.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should expand our subnet from /24 to /16 so we never run out of IP space again. Explain to them what expanding a subnet does, what it cannot do, and the main tradeoff of making the range that large.
lessons.modelAnswer: Expanding a subnet lowers its prefix length, which makes the primary IPv4 block bigger without moving existing virtual machines. Their addresses stay the same, and new machines draw from the larger pool. But the change is one-way: we cannot shrink the subnet back down. Going from /24 to /16 would claim 65,536 addresses, which is far more than we need, and that range could overlap other subnets, peered networks or on-premises routes. An overlap would cause routing conflicts. Before expanding, I would check the target block against every other route and subnet, and choose the smallest prefix that gives us enough room for the next year.
rubricPoints: Expansion increases the primary range by lowering the prefix length, and existing VM addresses are kept.
The change is one-way: a subnet cannot be shrunk back to a smaller range.
The new range must not overlap other subnets, peered networks or on-premises routes.
Oversized expansion wastes address space and widens which firewall rules and routes match.

suggested.rationale: Choosing whether an expansion is safe is an exam-style reasoning task about overlaps and one-way changes, which a short situation adds more to than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Every computer on a network needs an address, like a house number, so other machines can send it messages. On Google Cloud, a virtual machine usually gets an address that is handed out when it starts and may change later. Reserving a static address means you claim one specific address for your project so it stays the same even when the machine stops, restarts, or is replaced. There are two kinds: external addresses that the internet can reach, and internal addresses that only your private network can use. A fixed address matters when other systems, such as a website name lookup or a partner's approved list, depend on it. Reserving one is a deliberate choice, because an unused reserved address still has a cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server is reachable at an address that changes every time its machine is restarted. Before reading anything else, what would you expect to break for users, and what single change would you make to stop it?
lessons.teach:
An IP address is a numeric label that lets machines find and talk to each other. On Google Cloud, a Compute Engine virtual machine (a rented virtual computer) gets addresses in two forms. An internal address sits inside your private network, within one subnet (a slice of that network's address range), and is reachable only from inside it. An external address can be reached from the internet. By default, both are ephemeral, meaning Google assigns them when the machine starts and they can change or be released when the machine stops or is recreated.

Reserving a static address means you claim a specific address for your project so it stays yours until you release it. You can attach it to a machine, move it to another machine, or keep it reserved while nothing uses it. External static addresses are either regional or global; regional is the usual choice for a single machine, and global is used with global load balancers. Internal static addresses are chosen from an unused address in a given subnet, either picked by you or assigned on request.

The reason this works is that a static address is a fixed identity. DNS records (the entries that map a name like example.com to a number), firewall allow-lists, partner configurations, and certificates can all point at a value that will not move.

Worked example: a team runs a web server with an ephemeral external address. Their DNS entry points at that address. The machine is stopped for maintenance and started again, and it comes back with a different address. Users now see failures until someone updates DNS. The fix is to reserve a static external address, attach it to the machine's network interface, and point DNS at the reserved value. Stops and restarts now keep the same address.

Common mistake: reserving an address and forgetting it. A reserved external address that is not attached to anything still incurs charges and appears in the IP address list as reserved but unused, so it should be checked during routine review.

In a running system, a silently changed public address can break partners and allow-lists at once, which is why static reservation is a routine day-2 check.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Logistics runs a reporting VM in europe-west1 with an ephemeral external address. A partner's firewall allow-list contains that current address. The team reserved a regional static external address and attached it to the VM's network interface. Afterward, the partner's traffic to the VM started failing. The team's runbook has these steps: (1) reserve a regional static external address, (2) attach the reserved address to the VM's network interface, (3) ______________________, and then they verify traffic. Step 3 was never done. Which step fills the blank?
choices: Give the partner the reserved address value so they update their allow-list to it
Lower the priority number of the firewall rule that allows the partner
Change the VM's machine type to a larger size
Create a global static address and attach it to a load balancer
questions.why: The partner still allow-lists the old ephemeral address, so updating their allow-list to the reserved value is the missing step that makes the fixed identity useful to them.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an ephemeral external address on a Compute Engine VM?
choices: An address the owner has claimed for the project so it stays fixed until released
An address that only works inside one subnet and cannot be reached from the internet
An address that is reserved in advance and billed even when no machine uses it
An address Google assigns at startup that can change or be released when the machine stops or is recreated
questions.why: Ephemeral addresses are assigned when the machine starts and may change or be released on stop or recreation, while the other options describe static or internal addresses.

questions.prompt: A team has a VM in a subnet with range 172.16.8.0/24 and wants a fixed internal address for it so a dependent service never sees the address change. What is the correct approach?
choices: Reserve an unused address from inside 172.16.8.0/24 and attach it to the VM
Attach a global external address, since global addresses are always internal
Create a new subnet and move the VM into it so the address is kept
Reserve an external static address and use it as the internal address
questions.why: Internal static addresses are chosen from an unused address within the given subnet, so reserving an unused address from 172.16.8.0/24 gives a fixed internal identity.

questions.prompt: A team reserved a regional external static address months ago for a test VM, then deleted the VM. The address still appears in the IP address list as reserved and the team is being charged for it. What should they do during routine review?
choices: Attach it to any running VM so the charges stop, without checking whether it is needed
Release the address if it is no longer needed, since a reserved but unattached external address still incurs charges
Assume the charge is a billing error because reserved addresses are free when unused
Wait for it to become ephemeral again, since reserved addresses expire on their own
questions.why: A reserved external address that is not attached to anything still incurs charges and appears as reserved but unused, so the routine check is to release it if it is no longer needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a static IP address is, why a team would reserve one instead of using the default, and one real limit or cost of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: A static IP is an address that you reserve for your project so it stays the same, even when the machine it is attached to stops, restarts, or is replaced. The default is an ephemeral address, which Google assigns when the machine starts and which can change after a stop or recreate. We reserve a static address when something outside the machine depends on the address staying put, such as a DNS record, a firewall allow-list at a partner, or a certificate. The main tradeoff is cost and tidiness. A reserved address that is not attached to a running resource is still charged and still shows in the console, so reservations need an owner and a periodic review. Internal static addresses work the same way inside a subnet, so other services on the private network can rely on a fixed target. The reservation does not make the workload itself highly available; it only keeps the identity stable.
rubricPoints: Defines an ephemeral address and says it can change when a machine stops or is recreated
Explains that a reserved static address stays fixed and can be attached or moved
Names a reason to reserve one, such as DNS records or allow-lists depending on a fixed value
States a real limit or cost, such as charges for reserved addresses that are not in use

suggested.rationale: A situation-based scenario, such as a changed address breaking DNS, teaches the decision to reserve and the cost check better than a definition alone.

lessons.plain: A route is a rule that tells a cloud network where to send a packet based on its destination address. Most routes are created for you automatically when you make a subnet. A custom static route is one you add yourself to say something like: traffic for this particular address range should go to that particular place, such as a network appliance or a VPN tunnel to an office. It stays fixed until someone changes it, which is why it is called static. Adding one changes where live traffic goes, so treat it as a real change with real impact on running systems.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your network has one rule that says send anything for 10.0.0.0/8 to gateway A, and a second, more specific rule that says send 10.1.2.0/24 to gateway B. Which gateway should a packet addressed to 10.1.2.50 use, and why?
lessons.teach:
A route is an entry in a routing table that maps a destination address range, written in CIDR notation such as 192.168.50.0/24, to a next hop, meaning the place the packet is handed to next. A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private network inside the cloud provider. The platform creates routes for each subnet automatically, and you can add custom static routes for destinations it cannot know about, such as a range behind a VPN or a network appliance.

When a packet leaves a machine, the network chooses the route whose destination range is the most specific match, meaning the longest prefix. If several matching routes tie on that length, the one with the lowest priority number wins; the default priority is 1000. Each custom route names a next hop type, such as an IP address inside one of your subnets, a specific VM, a VPN tunnel, an internal load balancer, or the default internet gateway. A route can also be limited to machines carrying a given network tag, so only some machines use it.

Worked example. Your subnet is 10.10.0.0/20 and an inspection appliance sits at 10.10.0.5. You add a route with destination 192.168.50.0/24, next hop IP 10.10.0.5, priority 1000, scoped to machines tagged clients. A tagged machine sends a packet to 192.168.50.7. Step one: the candidate routes include the default internet route 0.0.0.0/0 and your new /24. Step two: the /24 is more specific, so it wins. Step three: the packet is handed to 10.10.0.5.

Common mistake: assuming a route makes traffic flow. A route only chooses a next hop. The appliance must still forward the packet, and firewall rules still apply. Also, a custom route cannot compete with a subnet's own range, which is always preferred.

Consequence: if the appliance stops, the route still points at it, so packets silently time out. Operators diagnose this by checking the effective routes for the machine and reviewing flow logs for where packets go missing. Treat every static route as a traffic change, not a configuration note.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has subnet 172.16.8.0/22 and a firewall appliance at 172.16.8.9. A custom static route is set up for destination 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop 172.16.8.9 and priority 700. A second custom route for the same 10.50.0.0/16 uses a VPN tunnel as next hop with priority 1000. A VM with no network tags sends a packet to 10.50.9.4. Step one: both routes match, and both destinations are a /16, so the match length is equal. Step two: ___. Step three: the packet is handed to 172.16.8.9. Which choice correctly completes step two?
choices: The route with the highest priority number wins, so the VPN tunnel is chosen
The default route 0.0.0.0/0 wins because it is the broadest destination range
The VPN tunnel wins because VPN next hops always take precedence over IP address next hops
The route with the lowest priority number wins, so the route to 172.16.8.9 is chosen
questions.why: When destination lengths tie, the lowest priority number wins, and 700 is lower than 1000, so the route to the appliance is chosen.

questions.prompt: A team's VM at 10.20.200.9 needs to send to 10.20.200.9's neighbours. Its routes include 10.20.0.0/16 (next hop A), 10.20.128.0/17 (next hop B) and 0.0.0.0/0 (default internet). Which route does the VM use for a packet to 10.20.200.50? Note: a /17 covers addresses from 10.20.128.0 to 10.20.255.255.
choices: The 10.20.0.0/16 route with next hop A, because the shorter prefix covers more addresses
The default internet route 0.0.0.0/0, because it always applies first
Whichever of the two 10.20 routes was created first, because ties are broken by age
The 10.20.128.0/17 route with next hop B, because it is the longest prefix that matches the destination
questions.why: Both 10.20.0.0/16 and 10.20.128.0/17 match, and the more specific /17 has the longer prefix, so it wins over the /16 and the default route.

questions.prompt: A reporting VM tagged reporting uses a custom static route for 198.51.100.0/24 with next hop 10.30.2.11, a network appliance. That appliance was shut down last week but the route was never removed. Users report that requests to 198.51.100.x hang and then time out with no error message. Which action best helps diagnose this?
choices: Increase the route priority from 1000 to 100 so the route is preferred over the default route
Delete the default internet route 0.0.0.0/0 so the custom route becomes the only option
Check the effective routes for the reporting VM to confirm the route still points at 10.30.2.11, and review flow logs to see where the packets stop
Add a firewall rule allowing all traffic from the reporting tag, since the route is blocking the packets
questions.why: The route keeps pointing at a dead next hop, so packets silently time out; effective routes show the route and flow logs show where traffic disappears.

questions.prompt: A subnet 10.60.0.0/22 already exists in a project. An engineer adds a custom static route with destination 10.60.1.0/24 and next hop set to an inspection appliance at 10.60.0.5, expecting traffic to 10.60.1.x to go through the appliance. A tagged VM sends a packet to 10.60.1.30. Which statement is correct?
choices: The packet goes to the appliance only if the appliance has a matching firewall rule, since the route itself has no effect
The packet is still delivered within the subnet, because a subnet's own range is preferred over a custom static route, and the custom route does not change that
The packet is dropped, because custom routes cannot target destinations inside a subnet's range
The packet goes to the appliance, because the custom route is more specific than the subnet range
questions.why: A subnet's own range always takes precedence over a custom static route, so the custom route to 10.60.1.0/24 does not redirect that traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a custom static route does, how the network chooses between two routes that both match a destination, and one limit or risk of adding a route in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: A custom static route is a rule I add to a VPC that says packets for a specific destination range should be handed to a chosen next hop, such as a VM appliance, a VPN tunnel, or an internal load balancer. It is static because it does not change on its own. When more than one route matches a destination, the network prefers the most specific range, the longest prefix. If two matches tie, the lower priority number wins. The limit I would flag is that the route only decides where traffic goes. It does not check whether that next hop is healthy, and the next hop still has to forward the traffic and pass firewall rules. So if the appliance dies, packets quietly stop. The fix is to monitor the next hop and confirm the effective routes for the affected machines before and after any change.
rubricPoints: A custom static route maps a destination CIDR range to a chosen next hop.
The most specific (longest prefix) matching route wins, and ties go to the lowest priority number.
A route only selects the next hop; it does not check health or bypass firewall rules.
Routes can be scoped to tagged machines, and a custom route cannot override a subnet's own range.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner watch which route a packet takes, which this objective needs but no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: Cloud DNS is the phone book of your cloud. It turns a human name like api.example.com into the numeric address a computer needs, and you control those entries. Cloud NAT is a shared outbound door for machines that have no public address of their own. Those machines can reach the internet to fetch updates or call outside services, and replies come back, but nothing outside can start a connection to them. Day-2 work is checking that the names point where they should and that the outbound door is not running out of room.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has only a private address and no public address. Can it still reach a website on the internet, and can an outside client start a connection to it? Make your guess before reading on.
lessons.teach:
Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's managed DNS service. DNS, the domain name system, translates names such as api.example.com into IP addresses. A managed zone is a container in Cloud DNS that holds the records for one domain. A record is one entry, such as an A record that maps a name to an IPv4 address. Public zones answer queries from the internet; private zones answer only queries from chosen VPC networks. Each record has a TTL, the time-to-live in seconds, which tells resolvers how long they may cache the answer.

Cloud NAT (network address translation) lets virtual machines that have no external IP address send outbound connections. It is attached to a Cloud Router, a regional control component, and works through a NAT gateway that rewrites each outgoing packet's source to a shared public address and port. Replies come back to the gateway, which forwards them to the right machine. Unsolicited inbound connections are dropped, because the gateway has no mapping for them.

Worked example: api-vm has only a private address and calls a payment provider at a fixed hostname. Step 1: the VM asks DNS for the hostname and receives the provider's IP. Step 2: the VM sends the request to that IP, with its private address as the source. Step 3: the gateway rewrites the source to a NAT public IP and an allocated port, and records that mapping. Step 4: the reply returns to that IP and port, and the gateway restores the private address before forwarding it.

Common mistake: changing a DNS record and expecting every client to switch at once. Resolvers keep the old answer until the TTL expires, so you lower the TTL well before a planned move.

Consequence: when a NAT gateway runs out of ports for a busy VM, some outbound calls fail intermittently, and the symptom appears as timeouts inside the application rather than as an obvious outage.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics runs a batch VM named ledger-batch-7 in the europe-west1 region on the network corp-vpc. It has no external IP address, but it must download rate tables from a partner's hostname over HTTPS. The team follows these steps. Step 1: confirm ledger-batch-7 has only a private address. Step 2: create a Cloud Router named rtr-eu1 in europe-west1 on corp-vpc. Step 3: ______ (missing). Step 4: test that ledger-batch-7 can reach the partner, and confirm the partner cannot open a connection back to the VM unprompted. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Create a private zone for the partner's hostname so the VM resolves it locally.
Lower the TTL on the partner's A record to zero so the VM never caches the answer.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway on rtr-eu1 that covers the subnet ledger-batch-7 uses.
Give ledger-batch-7 an external IP address so it no longer needs translation.
questions.why: Cloud NAT works through a gateway attached to a Cloud Router, and that gateway must cover the subnet where the VM lives so it can translate the VM's outbound packets.

questions.prompt: A team at Kestrel Analytics asks what happens when an outside client tries to open a new connection to a VM that has only a private address and sits behind Cloud NAT. Which answer is correct?
choices: The NAT gateway forwards the connection to the VM because the VM's private address is known to it.
The connection succeeds only if the VM's DNS record has a TTL of less than 60 seconds.
The connection is accepted on any port the VM listens on, since NAT is transparent to inbound traffic.
The connection is dropped, because the gateway holds no mapping for a connection the VM did not start.
questions.why: Cloud NAT tracks only connections that a machine behind it initiated, so an unsolicited inbound connection has no mapping and is dropped.

questions.prompt: A nightly job on 40 VMs at Orchard Freight starts timing out on some outbound API calls. No VM is down, and the failures come and go, with no clear pattern in the logs of the job itself. Based on how Cloud NAT works, what is the most likely cause?
choices: The Cloud Router has been deleted, so every outbound packet is blocked at once with a clear error.
The TTL on the API's DNS record has expired, causing the API to reject every request outright.
The NAT gateway has run out of ports for the busy VMs, so some outbound calls fail intermittently.
The VMs' external IPs were removed, so the application cannot resolve any hostnames at all.
questions.why: Port exhaustion on the NAT gateway causes intermittent outbound failures that show up as application timeouts rather than a total outage, which matches the symptoms described.

questions.prompt: Lumen Health wants a hostname such as db.staging.internal.example to resolve only for its staging VPC networks and never be answerable from the internet. Which Cloud DNS setup fits this requirement?
choices: A private managed zone attached to the chosen staging VPC networks, so only those networks get answers.
