A private zone attached to every VPC network in the project, so that no network is left out.
A public managed zone, because any zone can be restricted later with a firewall rule.
A public zone with a very long TTL, so resolvers outside the company hold the answer longest.
questions.why: A private zone answers only queries from the VPC networks you choose, which keeps an internal name hidden from the internet while serving the staging networks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Cloud NAT does for a private-only virtual machine, and name one limit or tradeoff a day-2 operator should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud NAT gives a VM with no external IP a way to make outbound connections, such as downloading packages or calling an external API. The VM's traffic leaves through a NAT gateway attached to a Cloud Router, which swaps the private source address for a shared public address and a port, then maps replies back. Nothing from the internet can start a connection to that VM through NAT, so it is not a way to expose a service. The main limit is port capacity: each external address offers a finite number of ports, and a busy VM can exhaust its allocation. When that happens, outbound calls time out intermittently. A day-2 operator should check NAT logging and port allocation metrics when an application reports timeouts to external hosts, and should remember that DNS answers stay cached for the record's TTL after any change.
rubricPoints: Cloud NAT gives VMs without external IPs outbound internet access through a gateway tied to a Cloud Router.
The gateway maps private source addresses to shared public address and port pairs, and replies return via that mapping.
Inbound connections from the internet are not allowed through NAT, so it does not expose services.
Ports are finite; exhaustion causes intermittent outbound timeouts that need monitoring or logging to diagnose.
DNS record changes take effect only as cached answers expire, governed by the TTL.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path from a private VM through a NAT gateway to an outside host best builds the path-and-address reasoning this objective needs, and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise it.

lessons.plain: A cloud firewall is a set of gatekeeping rules that decide which network traffic may reach a machine and which may leave it. Day to day, the job is keeping those rules correct as the system changes: opening a port for a new service, narrowing a rule that is too open, and making sure a rule that blocks something important is not left in place by accident. Think of a building door policy: a list of checks read from the top down, with a default answer when nothing matches. Google Cloud offers VPC firewall rules for each private network, and newer Cloud Next-Generation Firewall policies that can be layered above them. Both need regular checking, because one careless edit can cut off a whole application.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have two firewall rules on the same machine. One allows SSH from your office address and has a low priority number. Another denies SSH from everywhere and has a high priority number. Which one decides whether your office can connect, and why?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private network inside the cloud. A VPC firewall rule is a rule attached to that network that allows or denies traffic. Each rule has a direction: ingress means traffic coming into a machine, and egress means traffic leaving it. It has a priority, a whole number from 0 to 65535, where a lower number is checked first. It has a target, the machines it applies to, often chosen by network tag. It has a source or destination address range, and a protocol and port such as TCP 22 for SSH. Rules that nothing else overrides are called implied rules: traffic into a machine is denied by default, and traffic out is allowed by default. Firewall rules are stateful, so replies to an allowed connection return without a separate rule. Cloud NGFW policies are a richer rule set that can be attached at the organization, folder, or network level. They can match on domain names and inspect traffic more deeply, and they are evaluated alongside your VPC rules.

Worked example: a web server has tag web. Rule A allows TCP 22 from your office range at priority 100. Rule B denies TCP 22 from all addresses at priority 1000. Your office connects. The check reaches priority 100 first, matches Rule A, and stops. A stranger connects. Rule A does not match, so the check moves on to Rule B, which denies the connection.

A common mistake is adding a broad deny rule with a low priority number. It is checked before the rules you meant to keep, so it silently blocks them. In a running system this can stop a load balancer's health checks from reaching the backends, which marks healthy instances as unhealthy and drops live traffic.

The priority order of rules decides the outcome, so every change should be checked against the rules that sit above and below it.

questions.prompt: A payments VM is tagged ledger in a network your team runs. An existing deny rule blocks all ingress TCP 5432 from 10.70.0.0/16 at priority 400. The reporting subnet 10.70.8.0/24 must reach the database on TCP 5432. Step 1: target the rule at machines tagged ledger, direction ingress. Step 2: create an allow rule for source 10.70.8.0/24, TCP 5432, at priority 300, which is lower than 400 so it is checked first. Step 3: before you finish, ___
choices: Set the priority to 65535 so the rule is checked last and cannot interfere.
Change the rule's direction to egress so that replies are covered.
Check which rules sit above and below priority 300 to confirm nothing earlier denies this traffic.
Delete the existing deny rule so the new allow is the only rule left.
questions.why: The teaching text says every change should be checked against the rules that sit above and below it, because priority order decides the outcome.

questions.prompt: An internal API VM is tagged api. Rule P allows TCP 8443 from 172.16.4.0/22 at priority 50. Rule Q denies all TCP from 0.0.0.0/0 at priority 20. A client at 172.16.5.9 connects to the API on TCP 8443. What happens?
choices: It is denied by Rule Q, because priority 20 is checked before priority 50 and the match stops there.
It is allowed by default, because ingress rules without a match fall back to allow.
It is denied only if the client is not tagged api.
It is allowed by Rule P, because the client is inside the allowed range.
questions.why: A lower priority number is checked first, so Rule Q at priority 20 matches and denies the connection before Rule P is reached.

questions.prompt: A batch worker VM sits in a network that has only the implied rules and no custom firewall rules. It starts an outbound HTTPS connection to a vendor API. Which outcome is correct?
choices: It is blocked until someone adds an egress allow rule for TCP 443.
It is denied, because no custom rule explicitly permits it.
It is allowed only when the worker VM carries a network tag.
It is allowed, because outbound traffic is allowed by default and the vendor's replies return without a separate rule.
questions.why: Implied rules allow egress by default, and firewall rules are stateful so replies to an allowed outbound connection come back without their own rule.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Cloud NGFW policies is accurate?
choices: They run only after all VPC rules have been checked and cannot affect traffic that VPC rules allow.
They replace VPC firewall rules entirely once any NGFW policy is attached.
They can only be attached to a single VM and cannot be shared.
They can be attached at the organization, folder, or network level, can match on domain names, and are evaluated alongside VPC rules.
questions.why: The teaching text describes NGFW policies as attachable at organization, folder, or network level, able to match domain names, and evaluated together with VPC rules rather than instead of them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find out why a new web server cannot be reached on port 443. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking the firewall rules that apply to that server. I look at the target tags or service account to confirm which rules even match it, then at direction, priority, port, and source range. Because rules are checked from the lowest priority number first, a broad deny with a low number can hide a correct allow further down. I also look at firewall logs, if logging is enabled on the rule, to see whether connections are being denied and by which rule. A tradeoff is that firewall logs cost money and add volume, so I would enable logging only on the rules I am investigating and turn it off again afterward. Also, logs show only what the rules did, not whether the application listens on 443, so I would confirm that separately before blaming the firewall.
rubricPoints: Check which rules apply to the target, using tags or service accounts
Evaluate by priority: lower number is checked first, and the first match wins
Use firewall logs, when enabled, to see which rule denied or allowed the traffic
Name a tradeoff such as log cost or volume, or that logs do not prove the app is listening

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet path through ordered rules is the core skill here, and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise exactly that.

lessons.plain: An alert is a rule that watches a number your system reports over time, such as how busy a server's processor is, and tells a person when that number crosses a line you chose. Think of a smoke alarm: it does not watch the whole house, it watches one reading, and it only sounds when that reading stays too high for long enough to matter. Creating an alert means choosing which number to watch, what level counts as trouble, how long it must stay there, and who gets told. Good alerts wake people for real problems and stay quiet otherwise.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's processor usage jumps to 95% for about ten seconds during a normal backup, then drops back to 20%. Should this alone wake an engineer at night? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number a system records repeatedly over time, such as CPU utilization (the share of a machine's processor in use) or a count of failed requests. A time series is the sequence of recorded values for one metric on one specific resource. An alert policy is a rule that watches one or more time series and opens an incident when a condition is met. The condition has parts you choose: a threshold (the level that counts as trouble), a comparison (above or below that level), and a duration (how long the value must stay past the threshold before the policy fires). Aggregation (combining several series into one number, such as an average across instances) is also set here. A notification channel is the destination that receives the alert, such as email, a chat tool, or a paging service. Documentation is free text attached to the alert that tells the responder what to check first.

Why it works: the duration separates a real problem from noise. Metrics fluctuate constantly, so a rule that fires on a single reading will fire all the time.

Worked example: a virtual machine's CPU utilization is recorded every minute. The alert has a threshold of 80% and a duration of 5 minutes. The recorded values are 70, 85, 88, 90, 91 and 86. Minute 1 is below the threshold, so nothing is counted. Minutes 2 through 6 are all above 80, which is five consecutive minutes, so the policy fires at minute 6. If minute 4 had dropped to 60, the streak would have reset and the alert would wait for a new five-minute run.

Common mistake: setting a threshold with no meaningful duration, or a duration so short that a routine batch job trips it every night. The result is alert fatigue, where people learn to ignore pages.

Consequence: a poorly tuned alert either floods the on-call engineer with false pages or, when set too loosely, fires only after users have already been affected. An alert is only as useful as its threshold, duration and destination taken together.

questions.prompt: A managed database's open-connection count is recorded every 2 minutes. An alert policy uses a threshold of 200 connections and a duration of 8 minutes. The readings are: minute 0 = 180, minute 2 = 210, minute 4 = 212, minute 6 = 214, minute 8 = 216, minute 10 = 218. Minute 0 is below 200, so nothing is counted. The readings at minutes 2 through 10 are all above 200, so the streak starts at minute 2. The policy fires once the streak has lasted 8 minutes. The step left out is the last one: at which minute does the policy fire?
choices: 6 minutes
8 minutes
12 minutes
10 minutes
questions.why: The streak starts at minute 2, so 8 minutes of continuous breach ends at minute 10, which is the reading where the policy fires.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Monitoring, what does the duration setting of an alert condition control?
choices: How long the value must stay past the threshold before the policy fires
How long the documentation text is kept attached to the alert
How many seconds the notification takes to reach a paging service
How often the metric is recorded by the agent
questions.why: Duration is the length of time the value must remain beyond the threshold before the alert policy opens an incident, so a single spike does not trigger it.

questions.prompt: A web tier records its error count every minute. The alert threshold is 20 errors with a duration of 1 minute. Every night a batch job pushes the count to 25 for 3 minutes, and on-call engineers are paged each night. Which change best stops the nightly pages without ignoring real trouble of similar length?
choices: Remove the notification channel so the pages stop reaching anyone
Set the duration to 10 minutes so the 3-minute batch spike never completes the required streak
Change the comparison to fire when the count drops below 20
Lower the threshold to 5 errors so the alert fires earlier
questions.why: A duration longer than the routine batch run stops the nightly spike from counting as a sustained problem, while the threshold and destination stay the same.

questions.prompt: A disk usage alert on a file server is set with a threshold of 90% and a duration of 0 minutes. What is the most likely result?
choices: The policy sends each notification to every channel twice
The policy fires only after the disk is completely full
The policy never fires because a zero duration disables the comparison
The policy fires on any single reading that crosses 90%, so brief spikes produce frequent pages
questions.why: With no required duration, one reading above the threshold is enough to open an incident, and metrics fluctuate constantly, so pages will be frequent and noisy.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants a CPU alert on our web servers. In your own words, explain how you would choose the threshold and duration so it does not page on short spikes, and name one tradeoff of making the duration longer.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from what a real problem looks like for our users, then pick a threshold that sits above normal peaks, for example 80% CPU. The duration is what stops brief spikes from paging anyone. I would require the value to stay above the threshold for something like ten minutes, so a short backup or deploy does not wake someone. I would also attach a note to the alert saying which dashboard to check first and who owns the service. The tradeoff of a longer duration is that we learn about a sustained problem later. A server that has been saturated for nine minutes will not page us yet, so users may feel slowness before anyone is notified. We would need to weigh that delay against the cost of false pages.
rubricPoints: Explains that threshold sets the level that counts as trouble and should sit above normal peaks
Explains that duration requires the condition to hold continuously, filtering out brief spikes
Names a real tradeoff: a longer duration delays notification of genuine sustained problems
Mentions that the alert needs a destination and useful documentation for the responder

suggested.rationale: Building and tuning threshold, duration and notification choices against simulated metric data is the core skill, and the planned metric alarm builder would let the learner practise exactly that.

lessons.plain: A custom metric is a number you define yourself and send to a monitoring service so it can graph that number and alert on it. Cloud products already report standard measurements such as CPU use, but your application knows things they cannot see, like how many orders are waiting in a queue or how long a business step took. You first describe the measurement by its name, what kind of number it is, and its unit. Then you send values over time, each with a timestamp. The service stores these as time series, which are lines of values for one set of labels, so you can chart them and set alarms on them just like built-in metrics.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web service already reports CPU usage, but on-call wants an alert when the number of orders waiting to be processed grows past 500. Where would that number come from, and what would you need to do before a dashboard could show it?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A metric is a named measurement recorded over time. A custom metric is one you define yourself rather than one the platform provides. Cloud Monitoring stores each metric as one or more time series: a sequence of timestamped values that share the same metric name and the same labels. A label is a key-value tag, such as queue=positions, that splits one metric into separate series. A metric descriptor is the definition of a custom metric: its name, which must sit under the custom.googleapis.com prefix, its kind (gauge for a current level, delta for change since the last report, cumulative for a running total), its value type, and its unit.

Why it works. Monitoring cannot see inside your code, so your application or agent sends points to it. Each point carries a value and a timestamp. Monitoring plots the points and evaluates alerts against them. The descriptor tells Monitoring how to interpret what you send, so a running total sent as a gauge will chart the wrong thing.

Worked example. A nightly intake job publishes its queue depth as a gauge named custom.googleapis.com/ingest/queue_depth. Step one: create the descriptor with kind gauge, value type int64, and unit 1. Step two: every minute the job reads its queue length, which is 412, and writes one point with the current timestamp, value 412, and label queue=positions. Step three: in Metrics Explorer you select the metric and filter on queue=positions to see the line. Step four: an alert policy can now use the same metric.

Common mistake. Putting a unique value into a label, such as an order ID, creates a new time series for every order. That inflates cost and makes charts slow and noisy.

Consequence. If you write points faster than the service accepts for a series, or with timestamps out of order, those points are rejected and the chart shows gaps at exactly the moments you were watching.

questions.prompt: A payments team creates the custom metric custom.googleapis.com/payments/declined_total to track a running count of declined card charges since the service started. Step 1: create the descriptor with kind cumulative, value type int64, and unit 1. Step 2: every 60 seconds the service reads its counter and writes one point with the current timestamp and the label processor=eu-west. At 09:00 the counter reads 1200, so the service writes a point with value 1200 at 09:00. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the team opens Metrics Explorer and filters on processor=eu-west to see the line. What should step 3 be, the write that happens at 09:01 when the counter reads 1215?
choices: Write a point with value 15, the difference since the last write, because a cumulative metric stores changes between reports
Write a point with value 1215 at a timestamp later than 09:00, still labeled processor=eu-west
Resend the 09:00 point with value 1200 so the chart has no gap at 09:01
Write a point with value 1215 and label the declined charge ID, so each decline gets its own series
questions.why: A cumulative metric is a running total, so each new point carries the current total (1215) at a later timestamp, keeping the same label so it joins the existing series.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Monitoring, what is a metric descriptor?
choices: The definition of a custom metric: its name under the custom.googleapis.com prefix, its kind, its value type and its unit
A key-value tag that splits a metric into separate series
A dashboard widget that displays one metric as a number
A timestamped value that is sent to Monitoring by an application
questions.why: The descriptor is the definition that tells Monitoring how to interpret the points you send, and the other options describe a dashboard, a point, and a label.

questions.prompt: A parcel company labels every scan point of its custom metric with the parcel_id, which is unique for each parcel. What is the most likely result?
choices: Monitoring merges all parcels into one time series, so the chart shows a single total
Monitoring rejects every point because labels must be numbers
Each parcel creates its own time series, which raises cost and makes charts slow and noisy
The descriptor's kind changes automatically from gauge to cumulative
questions.why: Each distinct label value creates a new time series, so unique values such as parcel IDs multiply series, which inflates cost and slows charts.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team keeps a running total of pallets moved since midnight and wants Monitoring to chart it correctly. Which descriptor kind should they choose?
choices: gauge
int64 value type
delta
cumulative
questions.why: A running total is a cumulative kind, and sending it as a gauge would chart the wrong thing, while delta reports change since the last report rather than a total.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a custom metric travels from your code into a Cloud Monitoring chart, and name one limit or tradeoff you would design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A custom metric starts with a descriptor that says what the number means: a name under the custom prefix, a kind such as gauge, a value type, and a unit. Our job then sends points, each a value plus a timestamp, tagged with labels that split it into series. Monitoring stores those series and lets us chart them in Metrics Explorer and build alerts on them. The main tradeoff is cardinality. Every distinct label value creates another series, so a label like order ID would multiply cost and clutter. I would keep labels to a small fixed set such as queue name or region. I would also respect the write rate for each series and send timestamps in order, because rejected points leave gaps in exactly the charts we rely on.
rubricPoints: A custom metric needs a descriptor defining its name, kind, value type, and unit before points are written.
Each point is a value with a timestamp, and labels split the metric into separate time series.
Charts and alert policies read the series that the application wrote, so the source of truth is what the job sends.
Unbounded label values create too many series, raising cost and degrading charts.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right metric kind, labels, and write pattern for a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, since no listed mission or planned engine builds custom metrics directly.

lessons.plain: Audit logs, VPC flow logs and firewall logs are the records a cloud provider keeps about what happened on your network and in your account. Audit logs answer who changed what and when, such as someone deleting a virtual machine. Flow logs record samples of network conversations between machines, so you can see which systems talked to which. Firewall logs record the connections that a particular firewall rule allowed or blocked. Configuring them means deciding which records to switch on, how much detail to keep, and where to read them later. Turning them on has a cost: more detail means more storage and more money, so you choose deliberately.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server cannot reach a database, and a colleague says a firewall rule must be blocking it. Without looking anything up, what record would you check first to confirm which rule dropped the traffic, and why might that record not exist yet?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Audit Logs record administrative and access events in your project. They come in four types. Admin Activity logs record changes to configuration, such as creating or deleting a resource; they are always on and cannot be turned off. System Event logs record actions the platform itself takes, such as automatic maintenance changes. Data Access logs record reads and writes of user data; for most services they must be switched on, because they can be large. Policy Denied logs record requests that an access policy refused. Audit logs are written to Cloud Logging, where you filter them by log name and resource.

VPC Flow Logs record network conversations between virtual machines. They are turned on per subnet, not for a whole virtual private cloud network at once. Flow logs are sampled, meaning the system records a fraction of traffic rather than every packet, and you control the sampling rate and the aggregation interval. Each flow record shows source and destination addresses, ports, protocol and byte counts, which helps answer which machines talked to which.

Firewall Rules Logging is switched on per firewall rule. When it is on, each connection matching that rule, whether allowed or denied, produces a log entry. This is the most direct way to see which rule handled a connection.

Worked example: a connection from 10.0.1.12 to port 5432 fails. Step one: check whether Firewall Rules Logging is on for the rules that could match. Step two: look for a DENY entry with that source and port. Step three: the entry names the rule that blocked it, so you change that rule, not the database.

Common mistake: assuming logs exist retroactively. Firewall logging and Data Access logging only record from the moment they are enabled, so a rule that was never logged leaves no trail.

Consequence: a busy subnet with full flow logging and per-rule firewall logging can generate large volumes and bills, while leaving logging off means you are blind during an incident.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a VM named ledger-worker-3 in the subnet ledger-core, which uses 10.60.8.0/24. Yesterday their reporting job stopped reaching a cache on 10.60.9.20, port 6379. The team wants to find out whether the calls were blocked by a firewall rule. Step 1: confirm that VPC Flow Logs is turned on for the subnet ledger-core, since flow logs are switched on per subnet and not for the whole network. Step 2: [missing step: state what to do here]. Step 3: read the matching record for its source address, destination address, port, and byte count, which tells you which machines talked and how much data moved.
choices: Filter the flow log entries by source address 10.60.8.x and destination port 6379 for yesterday's time window.
Change the flow log sampling rate to 100 percent so that past traffic is recorded again.
Turn on Data Access audit logs for the cache service so its client connections are recorded.
Enable VPC Flow Logs across the whole VPC network so that the subnet becomes covered retroactively.
questions.why: Step 2 is to narrow the flow records to the source and destination port in question for the time window of the failure, which is the only missing action that leads to the matching record in step 3.

questions.prompt: Which Cloud Audit Logs type is always on and cannot be switched off, recording changes to resource configuration such as creating or deleting a resource?
choices: Admin Activity logs
System Event logs
Policy Denied logs
Data Access logs
questions.why: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes and are always enabled, while the other three types are either optional or record different kinds of events.

questions.prompt: A network engineer creates a deny rule named block-legacy-ftp on a Monday with Firewall Rules Logging left off. On Wednesday an analyst searches for blocked FTP attempts from 198.51.100.23 and finds nothing for Monday or Tuesday. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The rule is working, so the blocked attempts must have been allowed through by a different rule.
Logs for Monday and Tuesday are hidden until the rule is updated to add a logging flag.
Firewall logging records only from the moment it is enabled, so earlier blocks left no entries and the analyst should turn on logging for the rule to see future blocks.
The firewall logs were deleted automatically when the rule was created, so they cannot be restored.
questions.why: Firewall Rules Logging is switched on per rule and only records connections from the time it is enabled, so the missing Monday and Tuesday entries are expected and no logs can be recovered for that period.

questions.prompt: A data science team runs a training subnet, ml-train, with VPC Flow Logs enabled. A VM there could not reach a VM on another subnet, and the team wants to know which firewall rule blocked the connection. Which action gives the most direct answer?
choices: Enable Data Access audit logs on the destination VM so that connection attempts are named by rule.
Turn on Firewall Rules Logging for the rules that could match, then look for a DENY entry with that source and port.
Increase the flow log aggregation interval so that each record includes the rule name.
Read the flow log byte counts, since a count of zero shows which rule dropped the packets.
questions.why: Firewall Rules Logging is the feature that names the rule handling each matching connection, while flow logs show addresses, ports, and byte counts but not the rule responsible.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would use audit logs, VPC flow logs and firewall logs to work out why a connection failed, and name one limit or cost tradeoff you would weigh before turning on more logging.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with firewall logs, because they show per rule whether a connection was allowed or denied, and they only exist for rules where logging is switched on. If there is no entry, I would check flow logs on the subnet to see whether packets reached the machine at all. Flow logs are sampled, so a short connection may be missing from them, and I would keep that in mind. For a question like who changed the firewall rule, I would check the Admin Activity audit log, since it records configuration changes. The tradeoff is cost and volume: logging every rule and every subnet produces a lot of data to store and pay for, and Data Access logs can be large. So I would enable only what a specific investigation or compliance need requires and set retention to match.
rubricPoints: Audit logs record configuration changes and access events, and Admin Activity logs are always on.
VPC Flow Logs are enabled per subnet and are sampled records of network conversations.
Firewall Rules Logging is enabled per rule and records matching allowed or denied connections.
Logs only exist from the moment logging is enabled, and more logging raises volume and cost.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a failed-connection scenario that uses all three log types adds more than reading console steps alone.

lessons.plain: Cloud Logging collects log messages from your cloud resources and keeps them for a set time. Exporting logs means setting up a rule that makes a copy of matching log messages and delivers those copies to another place. Common destinations are a BigQuery table for SQL analysis, a Cloud Storage bucket for cheap long-term archive, or a Pub/Sub topic that a system outside the cloud, such as one in your own data center, can read. Think of it like a mail forwarding rule: you say which letters to copy and where they should go. The copies start from the moment the rule exists, so older messages are not moved backward. Companies set this up for security review, long retention, or to feed tools they already run outside the cloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you create a rule today that copies error logs from an application into a BigQuery table. Do you expect last week's error logs to appear in that table, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A log sink is a rule inside Cloud Logging's log router. The sink has a filter, which is a text expression that selects the log entries it cares about (for example, only entries from one project with severity ERROR or higher), and a destination. Matching entries are copied to the destination, and the original stays in Cloud Logging. Supported destinations include BigQuery datasets, Cloud Storage buckets, Pub/Sub topics, other log buckets, and projects you do not own. For an on-premises system, the usual route is Pub/Sub: the sink publishes entries to a topic, and an agent or connector in your data center pulls them from a subscription.

Why it works: the router checks each new entry against every sink's filter as it arrives and writes a copy to each matching destination. Because it forwards only new entries, a sink never backfills history. Each sink also has a writer identity, a service account that Google creates for that sink. This identity must have permission to write into the destination, such as the BigQuery Data Editor role on the target dataset. Without that permission, delivery fails and nothing arrives.

Worked example. You want failed requests from project shop-prod sent to a BigQuery dataset named ops_logs. Step 1: write a filter that matches resources of the application and severity of ERROR or higher. Step 2: create a sink with the BigQuery dataset as its destination. Step 3: note the writer identity the sink shows. Step 4: grant that identity write access on ops_logs. Step 5: trigger an error. A row appears in the table a few minutes later, but errors from before the sink existed do not.

Common mistake: creating the sink and assuming data flows, without granting the writer identity access. The consequence is that during an incident the security or operations dashboard built on that table stays empty, and nobody notices until someone needs the data. Always verify a new sink by generating a test log entry and checking that it reaches the destination.

questions.prompt: A retail team runs a checkout service in project storefront-eu. They want its WARNING and higher entries delivered to their on-premises security tool. A log sink is a rule in Cloud Logging's log router that copies matching entries to a destination, and the writer identity is the service account Google creates for that sink. Steps 1 to 3 are done: the filter is resource.labels.service_name="checkout" AND severity>=WARNING, the sink's destination is the Pub/Sub topic siem-feed, and the sink shows its writer identity. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the setup so entries can reach the topic?
choices: Recreate the sink so it backfills last week's WARNING entries into the topic.
Change the filter to include DEBUG entries so the topic receives more data.
Grant the sink's writer identity the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic siem-feed.
Give the on-premises agent's Google account the Owner role on project storefront-eu.
questions.why: The writer identity must have permission to write into the destination, and for a Pub/Sub topic that means the Publisher role on that topic, which the other three choices do not provide.

questions.prompt: A platform engineer creates a new sink today in project ledger-core with the filter severity>=ERROR. Entries with ERROR severity were written to Cloud Logging last month. What happens to those older entries?
choices: They are copied to the sink's destination in one batch when the sink is created.
They are rewritten with the sink's writer identity so the destination can read them.
They are deleted from Cloud Logging once the sink starts matching new entries.
They stay in Cloud Logging, and the sink only forwards entries that arrive after it exists.
questions.why: A sink checks only new entries as they arrive and never backfills history, while the original entries remain in Cloud Logging.

questions.prompt: A sink in project fleet-telemetry sends matching entries to a BigQuery dataset. The filter is correct and new matching entries are being written, but the table has had no rows for a full day. Which cause is most likely?
choices: The log router is copying entries but BigQuery is hiding them until the table is refreshed.
The sink's writer identity lacks write permission on the target dataset, so delivery fails silently.
The sink was created before the project had any logs, so it is waiting for a restart.
The filter is too narrow, so Cloud Logging is storing the entries in a different project.
questions.why: Without write permission for the writer identity on the destination, delivery fails and nothing arrives, which matches the symptom of an empty table despite a correct filter.

questions.prompt: A team has just created a sink that forwards entries to an on-premises agent through a Pub/Sub topic. Before relying on it for alerts, what is the best way to confirm it works?
choices: Generate a test log entry that matches the filter and confirm it reaches the agent's subscription.
Copy an old ERROR entry from last month into the topic by hand and see if it is accepted.
Check that the sink appears in the list with a green status and move on.
Wait one business day and count whether any entries arrived at the agent.
questions.why: A test entry that matches the filter verifies the whole delivery path, while a sink's status alone does not prove that data is actually arriving at the destination.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would get our application logs into BigQuery for analysis and also into our on-premises security system. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Logs stay in Cloud Logging by default, so to send them elsewhere I create a sink in the log router. The sink has a filter that picks which entries to copy, and a destination. For BigQuery, I point the sink at a dataset and then grant the sink's writer identity permission to write to that dataset, because without that grant nothing lands. For the on-premises security system, I would not use BigQuery as a bridge. I would send entries to a Pub/Sub topic and have a pull subscriber in our data center read from it, which keeps the connection outbound from our side. The main limit is that sinks forward only new entries from the moment they exist, so history from before the sink needs a separate backfill or is simply not exported. A second tradeoff is cost and noise: a broad filter floods the destination, so the filter has to be narrow enough to keep only what the team actually needs.
rubricPoints: A sink is a log router rule with a filter and a destination, and it copies matching entries rather than moving them.
BigQuery needs the sink's writer identity granted write access to the target dataset, or delivery fails.
On-premises delivery usually goes through Pub/Sub with a subscriber that pulls from inside the data center.
Sinks forward only new entries and do not backfill history from before they were created.
A filter that is too broad increases volume and cost, so filters should be as narrow as the need allows.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine makes the learner configure a log sink, so the console steps and destination options are best learned from reading and then checking a real sink in the console.

lessons.plain: Cloud logs are the written record a running system produces: each request, error, and administrative action leaves a timestamped line. Google Cloud gathers these lines in one service called Cloud Logging. Log buckets are the storage containers that keep those lines, and you choose how long each bucket keeps them. Log routers decide, entry by entry, where a copy goes: into a bucket, into a file store, into a data warehouse, or onto a message feed. Log analytics lets you query stored lines with SQL instead of only scrolling through them. Together these answer a day-two question: where do the records live, how long do they last, and how do I get them to the people who need them?
lessons.guessPrompt: You want security audit lines kept for a year, but noisy debug lines deleted after a week. Without any prior knowledge, how would you separate these two kinds of logs, and what would you need to configure to make it happen?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A log entry is one timestamped record a service writes. A log bucket is a container in Cloud Logging that stores entries and sets how many days they are kept, called retention. Every project starts with two buckets: _Required, which holds administrative and access records for 400 days and cannot be changed or deleted, and _Default, which holds everything else for 30 days unless you change it. A log router is the set of sinks, which are rules that examine each new entry. A sink has an inclusion filter, which selects entries to copy, and may have exclusion filters, which drop entries before storage. A sink's destination can be a log bucket, a BigQuery dataset (a table store for SQL analysis), a Cloud Storage bucket (a file store), or a Pub/Sub topic (a message feed other programs subscribe to). Log analytics is a setting you turn on for a bucket so its entries can be queried with SQL.

Why it works: the router evaluates each entry as it arrives, so routing and exclusion only affect future entries, not history. Retention and routing are separate decisions: retention controls how long a stored copy lasts, and routing controls where copies go.

Worked example: an audit line arrives. Step 1, the audit sink's inclusion filter matches audit entries, so the line is selected. Step 2, it is written to a custom bucket configured for 365 days. Step 3, the _Default sink has no exclusion matching it, so a copy also lands in _Default. Step 4, a debug line matches the _Default exclusion filter and is discarded before storage.

Common mistake: assuming a sink works without permission. A sink writes as its own service identity, which needs write access to the destination; without it, entries fail to arrive, and the failure is easy to miss.

Consequence: if routing is wrong during an incident, the evidence you need was never kept, and nobody learns this until they go looking for it.

questions.prompt: Harbor Pantry runs a payments service. Its team creates a sink named payments-errors with an inclusion filter that matches only ERROR-severity entries from the payments service, sending them to a custom log bucket kept for 90 days and to a Pub/Sub topic that an alerting program subscribes to. Trace one ERROR entry. Step 1: the payments-errors inclusion filter matches the entry, so it is selected. Step 2: the entry is written to the custom bucket, where it is kept for 90 days. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the alerting program receives the entry from the topic. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The sink's service identity is granted permission to publish to the topic, because without that write access the copy fails to arrive.
The sink is recreated so that ERROR entries already stored from last week are copied to the topic.
The topic's own retention is set to 90 days so it matches the bucket before any message is delivered.
The _Required bucket is checked because it holds every entry from the payments service.
questions.why: A sink writes as its own service identity, which needs write access to its destination, so the topic copy only arrives once that permission is granted.

questions.prompt: A school district's platform team changed the _Default bucket's retention to 10 days. They later find that administrative and access records from 300 days ago are still available in Cloud Logging. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Changing _Default retroactively applied the 10-day limit only to entries older than 10 days, so the records should have been removed.
Those records were copied into a Pub/Sub topic, which keeps messages indefinitely and so preserved them.
Administrative and access records are held in _Required, which keeps them for 400 days and is not affected by the _Default setting.
Enabling log analytics on _Default converted the old records into permanent storage that ignores retention.
questions.why: The _Required bucket holds administrative and access records for 400 days and cannot be changed, so the _Default retention setting does not touch them.

questions.prompt: A logistics company routes its security entries through a sink to a Cloud Storage bucket. The sink's inclusion filter is correct, but for a week no new files have appeared in the storage bucket. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The inclusion filter must be rewritten to name the storage bucket directly, because filters select by destination.
The _Default bucket's 30-day retention is too short, so entries are deleted before they reach the storage bucket.
Log analytics must be turned on for the storage bucket before any entries can be written to it.
The sink's service identity lacks write permission on the storage bucket, so each write fails quietly and the failure is easy to miss.
questions.why: A sink writes as its own service identity, and missing write access on the destination makes entries fail to arrive without an obvious alert.

questions.prompt: A retail company adds an exclusion filter today to drop health-check entries from its log router. An engineer asks why health-check entries from last Tuesday are still in the log bucket. Which answer is correct?
choices: Entries stored in a BigQuery dataset ignore exclusions, so the older copies were sent there and remain.
The router evaluates each entry as it arrives, so the new exclusion affects only future entries and leaves stored history alone.
The exclusion must also be applied to the _Required bucket before it can affect older entries stored in other buckets.
Exclusion filters remove existing entries after 24 hours, so Tuesday's entries should already be gone by now.
questions.why: Routing and exclusion decisions are applied as entries arrive, so a newly added exclusion cannot remove entries that were already stored.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a log entry travels from a service to a stored, queryable record in Google Cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of log routing or retention that they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service writes an entry, and Cloud Logging passes it to the log router. The router checks each sink's inclusion filter, and any exclusion filters drop entries that should not be kept. Each matching entry is copied to the sink's destination, which can be a log bucket, a BigQuery dataset, a Cloud Storage bucket, or a Pub/Sub topic. Log buckets keep entries for a retention period, and log analytics lets you query a bucket with SQL. The main tradeoff is that routing only applies to new entries, so a filter added today does not recover lines already lost, and retention costs grow with longer periods. Also, a sink writes as its own service identity, so the destination must grant it write access, or the copies silently never arrive. Plan retention by how long the evidence must exist, and verify each sink with a test entry.
rubricPoints: Describes the path: entry, router, sink filters, then destination
Explains that log buckets control retention, separate from routing
Names a limit: routing and exclusions only affect new entries
Mentions the sink identity needing write access to the destination

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console configuration and product facts about buckets, sinks, and analytics, which a reading and a worked example cover better than an existing or planned hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Cloud Logging is the place where a Google Cloud project collects the messages its services and applications write while they run, such as startup notes, warnings, and errors. Each message is stored as a log entry, a small record that carries a time, a severity level, and details about which resource wrote it. Viewing logs means opening those records. Filtering means narrowing them to the few that matter, such as errors from one service in the last hour. Inspecting a log entry means opening one record and reading its fields to understand exactly what happened. When something breaks, this is how you find the evidence before changing anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server started returning errors at 09:14, but the central log store holds millions of messages from the last week. Without any tool knowledge, what three pieces of information would you use to find only the relevant messages, and why?
lessons.teach:
A log entry is one record written by a service or application. Its main parts are a timestamp (when it happened), a severity (how serious it is, such as INFO, WARNING, or ERROR), a resource (the thing that produced it, described by a type and labels such as project and instance ID), and a payload (the message itself, either plain text or structured fields). Some entries also carry a log name, which identifies the stream they belong to.

Cloud Logging is the service that stores these entries. The Logs Explorer page in the console lets you query them. A query is a set of conditions, and when you join them with AND the results must satisfy all of them. Useful fields include resource.type, severity, timestamp, and text search on the payload. Severity comparisons follow an order, so severity>=ERROR returns ERROR, CRITICAL, and anything more serious. The colon operator matches a substring, so textPayload:"timeout" finds messages containing that word, while an equals sign requires an exact match.

Worked example: you want errors from one Compute Engine VM after 09:00 UTC. Step 1: set resource.type to gce_instance. Step 2: add severity>=ERROR. Step 3: add timestamp>="2024-05-01T09:00:00Z". Step 4: open one matching result to read its payload, labels, and timestamp. The three conditions reduce thousands of entries to a handful you can actually read.

Common mistake: leaving the time range picker on a short default window, or using an exact equals on a message fragment, so the query returns nothing and you conclude nothing happened. Check the time range first, and use the colon operator for fragments.

In a live incident, an empty result from a wrong filter can make a failing service look healthy, so confirm the query is correct before trusting an empty list.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service named checkout-api (Cloud Run is Google's managed service for running containers, and each deployed version is a revision with resource type cloud_run_revision) wrote log entries on Tuesday. You want only WARNING or more serious entries whose payload contains the words connection refused. In Logs Explorer you have already entered resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND severity>=WARNING. The query still needs one more condition: matching the payload text. What should you add?
choices: textPayload:"connection refused", so that any payload containing those words matches
textPayload="connection refused", so that the payload must equal those words exactly
Nothing more; an empty result would mean no warnings were logged
severity="WARNING", so that only warning entries are returned
questions.why: The colon operator matches a substring, so it finds payloads that contain the phrase, while the equals sign would require the whole payload to match exactly.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Logging, what is the severity field of a log entry?
choices: The name of the log stream the entry belongs to
How serious the entry is, such as INFO, WARNING, ERROR, or CRITICAL
A label such as project ID or instance ID that identifies the producing resource
The time at which the entry was written, in UTC
questions.why: Severity records how serious an entry is, and it is compared against an ordered scale of levels, while the other options describe the log name, timestamp, and resource labels.

questions.prompt: You want to see every entry from a Cloud SQL database instance (a managed database service) that has severity ERROR or worse and whose payload contains the word deadlock. Which filter does this?
choices: resource.type="cloudsql_database" AND severity="ERROR" AND textPayload="deadlock"
resource.type="cloudsql_database" AND severity>=ERROR AND textPayload:"deadlock"
severity>=ERROR AND textPayload="deadlock"
resource.type="cloudsql_database" OR severity="ERROR" OR textPayload="deadlock"
questions.why: The AND joins require all three conditions, severity>=ERROR includes CRITICAL and above, and the colon matches the word inside the payload, whereas the other options use OR, an exact severity match, or an exact payload match.

questions.prompt: A teammate reports that no errors were logged by a VM in the last hour, based on a filtered Logs Explorer query that returned an empty list. The VM is known to be failing. What should you check before trusting that result?
choices: Whether the VM's external IP address has changed since the last deployment
Whether the severity field has been removed from the log entries by the service
Whether the time range picker covers the last hour and the filter is written correctly
Whether the payload is stored as structured fields rather than plain text
questions.why: An empty result can come from a short time window or a wrong filter, so the query must be confirmed correct before concluding that the failing service is healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find the errors from one service during a specific time window in Cloud Logging, and name one limitation of relying only on a filter that returns no results.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would open Logs Explorer, set the time range to cover the window, then build a query that combines the resource type, a severity of ERROR or higher, and a timestamp lower bound, joined by AND. I would open one matching entry to read its full payload, labels, and timestamp so I know the actual message instead of guessing from the list. The limitation is that a filter only finds what it matches. If the query uses an exact text match, the wrong time range, or the wrong resource type, it can return nothing even when errors exist. Before concluding the service was healthy, I would check the time range and widen the filter to confirm the query works, because an empty result only proves that nothing matched the query I wrote.
rubricPoints: Names the key filter parts: resource type, severity, and time range, combined with AND.
Explains that opening a single entry shows the payload, labels, and timestamp needed to read the actual message.
States that an empty result can come from a wrong filter, time window, or exact-match text, not from a healthy service.
Describes a check to confirm the query works before trusting the result.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you hunt through log messages to explain an API failure, which practises the same narrowing and reading of individual entries.

lessons.plain: When an application feels slow or breaks, you need evidence about where the time or the work is going, not guesses. Google Cloud offers diagnostic tools that each look at a different layer. Cloud Trace follows a single request as it passes between services and shows where the delay sits. Cloud Profiler samples what the code is doing inside a running service. Query Insights shows which database queries are slow or heavy. The index advisor suggests database indexes that could make those queries faster. You pick the tool that matches the symptom.
lessons.guessPrompt: An API endpoint that used to answer in 200 ms now takes 3 seconds, but only for some customers. Before reading anything, which layer would you suspect first (the network, the application code, or the database), and what single piece of evidence would you want to check first?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. Latency means how long an operation takes from start to finish. A trace is the record of one request's journey through a system. Each timed step inside it is a span, a piece of work with a start and an end, and spans nest so you can see which call waited on which. Cloud Trace collects these timings from instrumented services and draws them as a timeline. A profile is a statistical picture of where a program spends its CPU time or memory. Cloud Profiler takes periodic samples from running code, so it reveals which functions are busy without stopping the service. Query Insights is a view of database query performance: it ranks queries by how long they take and how often they run. The index advisor looks at queries that scan many rows and recommends an index, a sorted lookup structure on chosen columns, so the database can find matching rows directly.

Why it works: each tool measures a different layer, so you narrow down in order. Trace tells you which service or call is slow. Profiler tells you which code path inside that service uses the CPU. Query Insights and the index advisor tell you whether the database is the bottleneck and what change would fix it.

Worked example: an orders endpoint takes 1.2 seconds. Step one: open a trace for a slow request, and the timeline shows a 1.0 second span for a database call inside the orders service. Step two: open Query Insights for that database, and the top query scans about two million rows on each run, filtering on customer_id. Step three: the index advisor recommends an index on customer_id. After the change, the same query reads only matching rows and the endpoint drops to about 0.2 seconds.

Common mistake: treating one trace as typical behaviour. A single request can be unusual, so compare several traces and look at the spread. Another mistake is profiling the wrong layer, since a profile of the application will not reveal a slow database query.

Consequence: an unindexed query whose cost grows with table size can exhaust database CPU at a traffic peak, making every service that depends on it slow at once. Diagnostics show where the time goes; the fix still needs a change that you verify with the same tool.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service's search endpoint takes 3.1 seconds per request. Step one: a trace of one slow request shows a 2.8 second span for a database call inside the search service. Step two: Query Insights for that database ranks one query first, and it scans about 900,000 rows on each run while filtering on event_id and status. The index advisor recommends a composite index on event_id and status, and the team adds it. Step three, which is missing from this write-up: the team needs to confirm the change worked.
choices: Open Cloud Profiler on the search service to find the busiest CPU functions, since the database is now fixed
Pull several traces from after the change and compare the database span durations against the earlier spread
Treat one fast trace after the change as proof that the endpoint is healthy
Ask the index advisor for a second recommendation before looking at any traces again
questions.why: Comparing several traces after the change, and checking the spread of database span durations, verifies the fix with the same tool that found the problem, while a single trace or a profile of the application would not show whether the database query got faster.

questions.prompt: Which diagnostic tool ranks database queries by how long they take and how often they run?
choices: Query Insights
The index advisor
Cloud Trace
Cloud Profiler
questions.why: Query Insights is the database performance view that ranks queries by duration and frequency, whereas the index advisor recommends indexes and Cloud Trace shows request timelines.

questions.prompt: A team profiles their order-processing application, finds no slow functions, and still sees a slow endpoint. Which mistake most likely explains this?
choices: They traced too many requests and averaged away the one slow request
They profiled the application layer, but the slowness is likely in a database query the profile cannot reveal
They should have sampled the profile for a longer period of time than the trace
They used a sorted index on the wrong columns, which slows the application
questions.why: A profile shows where application code spends CPU time, so it will not reveal a slow database query; the team should move to Query Insights or the index advisor for the database layer.

questions.prompt: Which tool draws the timing of one request as nested spans, so you can see which call waited on which other call?
choices: Cloud Profiler
Cloud Trace
Query Insights
The index advisor
questions.why: Cloud Trace collects timings from instrumented services and draws each request as a timeline of nested spans, showing which step waited on which.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the checkout API is slow and suggests buying bigger servers. Explain to them which of these four tools you would open first, what that tool would show you, and one limit of the tool you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with Cloud Trace, because the complaint is slowness and I need to know which call in the request path takes the time. A trace for a slow checkout request shows each span with its duration, so I can see whether the delay is in the payment service, a downstream call, or a database query. If the trace points at a database call, I would move to Query Insights to see which query is slow and how often it runs, and the index advisor may suggest an index. The limit is that a trace shows one request's timing, not a pattern across all users, so I would compare several traces before drawing conclusions. Buying bigger servers might hide the symptom without fixing a slow query.
rubricPoints: Start with the tool matching the symptom: Trace for request-level latency across services
Explain that Profiler shows code-level CPU or memory use inside one service
Explain that Query Insights and the index advisor address slow database queries and indexing
Name a real limit, such as one trace not representing typical behaviour

suggested.rationale: Choosing which diagnostic tool fits a symptom is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style situation, which adds more than reading the tool list alone.

lessons.plain: Imagine a notice board from your building's power company that lists only outages affecting your street, not every outage in the country. The Personalized Service Health dashboard in Google Cloud works in a similar way. It shows known incidents and planned maintenance from the cloud provider that touch the products, regions, and resources you actually use, so you can tell whether a problem may be on the provider's side or inside your own system. It is a starting point for checking, not a complete monitoring tool.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application suddenly slows down in one region, and nothing in your recent code changes looks suspicious. Before you dig into your own code, what would you check first to find out whether the cloud provider itself is having a problem, and why would that check come first?
lessons.teach:
Service Health is the part of Google Cloud that reports on the health of the platform itself. Personalized Service Health narrows that feed down to your own footprint. Two kinds of event can appear. An incident is an unplanned disruption that is happening now or has already happened. Maintenance is scheduled work that the provider has announced in advance. Each event records which products, locations, and sometimes specific resources it affects, along with a timeline of status updates.

Why it works: the provider knows about its own failures and planned work before most customers do, and it knows which of its services each project uses. Matching those two sets of information lets the console show only what could affect you. An event is relevant when its product and location overlap with what your projects run.

Worked example: your team runs a web service in one region and sees errors rising at 14:05. Step 1: open the Service Health page in the console and use the personalized view. Step 2: look at the active incidents for the product your service depends on, such as Compute Engine, in your region. Step 3: find an entry that started near 14:00 and read its status updates. Step 4: if it matches, the error spike is probably caused by the provider, so you record the incident, follow its updates, and avoid rebuilding your own stack in a panic. If nothing matches, the cause is more likely in your deployment or code.

Common mistake: treating an empty dashboard as proof that everything is healthy. The feed only shows events the provider has published and can map to you, so your own metrics and logs still need checking.

Consequence: during a live outage you are seeing, a clean dashboard means you must investigate your own monitoring and logs rather than wait for the feed to explain it. The dashboard tells you whether the platform is part of the problem.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly batch job in europe-west1 that reads from Cloud Storage and writes to BigQuery. At 09:20 the job slows down. Its engineer works the case this way: Step 1, open the personalized Service Health view. Step 2, filter to Cloud Storage in europe-west1. Step 3 is missing from this trace. Step 4, the only matching entry is scheduled maintenance that was announced for Sunday, so it cannot explain a Tuesday slowdown and the cause is more likely in the job itself. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Conclude the feed is empty, so Cloud Storage is healthy, and skip the remaining checks.
Move the job's output to a new bucket and then recheck the feed for any changes at all.
Check the matching entry's type and start time against the 09:20 slowdown.
Delete the nightly job and recreate it in us-east1 to rule out the region entirely.
questions.why: Step 3 is where the engineer reads the matching entry and compares whether it is an incident or maintenance and when it started against when the symptoms began, which is what Step 4 relies on.

questions.prompt: In Service Health, what separates an incident from maintenance?
choices: Both are the same kind of entry and differ only in the colour of their status badge.
Incidents are announced days ahead while maintenance always appears without warning after it begins.
Incidents are for billing questions and maintenance is for quota increases, so they never touch running workloads.
An incident is an unplanned disruption; maintenance is announced work scheduled ahead.
questions.why: An incident is unplanned and is happening now or has already happened, while maintenance is scheduled work the provider announced in advance.

questions.prompt: A team's Cloud Run service in us-west2 returns errors, and the personalized Service Health view shows no entry for it. What is the right next step?
choices: Check the service's own metrics and logs; an empty feed does not prove the platform is healthy.
Conclude the platform is healthy and close the ticket, since the feed is the authority on platform health.
Wait for the feed to show an entry before looking at anything else in the system.
Disable Service Health for the project so that old entries stop hiding the real cause.
questions.why: The feed only shows published events it can map to you, so an empty view means you must investigate your own monitoring and logs.

questions.prompt: A project runs Pub/Sub only in us-central1. A maintenance entry appears that lists Pub/Sub in asia-south1 and nothing else. Is this entry relevant to the project, and why?
choices: Yes, because any Pub/Sub maintenance is relevant to every project in the organisation.
Not relevant, because the entry's product and location pair does not overlap with anything the project runs.
Not relevant, because maintenance entries never affect messaging products like Pub/Sub.
Yes, because maintenance always affects every region once it is announced.
questions.why: An event is relevant only when its product and location both overlap with what your projects run, and here the location does not match.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the Personalized Service Health dashboard shows nothing, the cloud is fine and the bug must be in our code. Explain to them what the dashboard can and cannot tell you, including one limit of it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The dashboard lists incidents and planned maintenance that the provider has published and that match the products, regions, and resources in our projects. So it can quickly tell us whether Google has a known disruption that could explain our symptoms, and it shows scheduled maintenance coming up. An empty list does not prove the platform is healthy. The feed only contains events the provider has posted and can map to us, so a problem may not be posted yet, or it may affect us in a way the feed does not link to our resources. That means we should still check our own error metrics, dashboards, and logs before deciding the bug is in our code. We use the dashboard to rule the platform in or out as a candidate cause, not as a final verdict.
rubricPoints: Explains that the dashboard shows provider incidents and planned maintenance filtered to the learner's own products, locations, and resources.
States that it helps decide whether a platform-side problem could explain the symptoms.
Names the limit: an empty feed does not prove everything is healthy, because events may be unposted or not mapped to the resources.
Says our own metrics and logs still need checking before blaming or clearing the code.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console navigation and the meaning of the feed's entries, which is best learned by reading rather than by a listed mission.

lessons.plain: Running software on a server or in a cluster is only half the job; you also need to see what it is doing. This objective covers two ways Google Cloud collects that picture. The Ops Agent is a small program you install on a virtual machine so it can send that machine's logs and performance numbers to the monitoring and logging services. Managed Service for Prometheus is a hosted way to collect metrics from applications that already expose data in the Prometheus format, mainly inside Kubernetes clusters, without running your own Prometheus server. Both put their data where you can graph it, search it and alert on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server on a virtual machine has been slow for an hour, but nobody can see its memory history or its error lines in the central console. Before reading anything, what would you need running on that machine to make those numbers and log lines show up in one central place, and why would the machine not send them on its own?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a small program that runs alongside your workload and forwards what it observes to a central service. The Ops Agent is Google Cloud's agent for Compute Engine virtual machines. It has two parts: a logging part that reads log files and system journals and sends the lines to Cloud Logging, and a metrics part that samples the machine (CPU, memory, disk, and any software you enable, such as a web server) and sends the values to Cloud Monitoring. A metric is a number sampled over time, such as memory use each minute. A log is a timestamped record of an event. By default a virtual machine reports only basic numbers seen from outside the guest. Memory use and the contents of in-guest log files are visible only from inside the operating system, so the agent must run there.

The agent reads its settings from a configuration file on the machine. You list which log files to collect and which metric receivers to enable, then restart the agent so it reloads. The machine's service account also needs permission to write metrics and logs. Without that permission the agent runs but nothing arrives.

Managed Service for Prometheus works differently. Prometheus is an open-source system in which applications expose a plain-text page of metrics, and a collector visits that page on a schedule. This visit is called scraping. In the managed version, a collector runs inside your Kubernetes cluster, and you declare which pods to scrape using a Kubernetes resource. The samples are stored in Cloud Monitoring, where you query them with PromQL, the Prometheus query language.

Worked example: a team wants memory graphs for a VM running nginx. First they install the Ops Agent on the VM. Second they enable the nginx receiver in the configuration file. Third they restart the agent. Fourth they check Cloud Monitoring for the new metrics a few minutes later. If the graph is empty, they check the agent and its permissions before blaming the application.

Common mistake: assuming installation is enough. If the configuration is wrong or the service account lacks write permission, the agent runs happily while the dashboard stays empty.

Consequence: without a working agent, a disk filling up on that machine produces no signal anywhere, so the team learns about it only when users complain.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a Python order service on a Compute Engine VM. The service writes its own log file at /var/log/orders/app.log, and the team wants those lines in Cloud Logging. Their steps are: Step 1, install the Ops Agent on the VM. Step 2, add the path /var/log/orders/app.log to the logging section of the agent configuration file. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, open Cloud Logging and filter for lines from that file. Which action completes the missing Step 3?
choices: Create a PodMonitoring resource so a collector scrapes the order service
Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API for the project
Restart the Ops Agent so it reloads its configuration file
Delete the VM and create a new one with the same name
questions.why: The agent reads its settings when it starts, so after the configuration file is edited it must be restarted before the new log path is collected.

questions.prompt: A VM's monitoring page shows CPU and network numbers but no memory graph. The VM has no agent installed. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The Monitoring API quota for memory was used up, so new samples are dropped
The machine's zone does not support memory metrics at all
Google Cloud blocks memory metrics on all Compute Engine machine types
Memory use is seen only from inside the operating system, so an agent must run there
questions.why: By default a VM reports only numbers visible from outside the guest, and memory use can only be sampled from inside the operating system by an agent.

questions.prompt: An Ops Agent is installed on a VM, its configuration file lists an nginx receiver, and the agent was restarted. A few minutes later Cloud Monitoring still shows no new metrics for that VM. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Cloud Monitoring keeps metrics only for the first hour after an agent is first installed on a machine
Nginx has to be reinstalled from its source package before any metric can be sampled at all
The machine type is too small to run the agent at all, so the restart silently failed
The service account lacks permission to write metrics, so the agent's samples never arrive
questions.why: An agent can run normally yet deliver nothing if the VM's service account is not allowed to write metrics and logs.

questions.prompt: In Managed Service for Prometheus, where are the scraped samples stored, and how are they queried?
choices: In Cloud Logging as text lines, queried with the log filter language
In the Kubernetes API server, queried with kubectl get
In Cloud Monitoring, queried with PromQL
In a local file on each pod, queried with SQL
questions.why: The collector inside the cluster scrapes application metrics, the samples are stored in Cloud Monitoring, and PromQL is the language used to query them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between the Ops Agent and Managed Service for Prometheus, when you would use each, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on either one.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Ops Agent is installed on a Compute Engine virtual machine and sends that machine's logs and system metrics, plus metrics for software like nginx, to Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring. You use it when the workload runs on a VM and you need things only the operating system can see, such as memory use or the contents of a log file. Managed Service for Prometheus fits applications that already expose Prometheus-format metrics, usually in a GKE cluster. A managed collector scrapes those endpoints on a schedule and stores the samples in Cloud Monitoring, where you query them with PromQL. A tradeoff of the agent is that it is configured per machine, needs a restart after changes, and needs correct service-account permissions. For Prometheus, you only get what the application exposes, and the scrape interval controls how often data arrives, so a long interval can hide short spikes.
rubricPoints: The Ops Agent runs on a VM and sends its logs and metrics to Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring.
Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes Prometheus-format endpoints, usually in GKE, and stores samples in Cloud Monitoring.
The agent needs a configuration change, a restart, and write permission on the service account to work.
Scrape interval or missing exposed metrics can hide data, so the choice of collection path has limits.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which collection path fits a day-2 situation and checking where its data appears adds more than any listed mission, and no planned engine covers agent setup directly.

lessons.plain: When a running system needs attention, someone has to notice what is going wrong, find out why, and decide whether the resources it uses are sized sensibly. Google Cloud offers two helpers for this. The first is an AI assistant you can question in ordinary language about your environment, including its logs and metrics. The second is a set of suggestion engines that study how your resources have actually been used and propose changes, such as shrinking a server that is far bigger than it needs to be. Think of the assistant as a knowledgeable colleague you can question, and the suggestion engines as an auditor's report whose advice you still have to approve before anything changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual server has used about 3 percent of its CPU every day for a month. Before you make it smaller, what would you check first, and why would one month of quiet days not be enough to decide?
lessons.teach:
Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI helper built into the Google Cloud console. You ask it questions in plain language about a project, such as why a service slowed down, and it reads relevant logs, metrics, and configuration to point you at likely causes. Its answers are a starting point for your own checking, not a verdict. Active Assist is the name for a family of recommenders. A recommender is an automated analysis that compares what you have configured with what you actually use, then publishes a suggestion with a reason and a risk note.

Worked example: a Compute Engine virtual machine (a rented server) has averaged very low CPU use for weeks. Step one, the recommender collects utilization history over a window of time. Step two, it compares observed use with the machine's configured size. Step three, it publishes a suggestion, for instance a smaller machine type, along with an estimated saving.
